issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1007.2314.0`, verified with `Get-AppxPackage`.
Desktop product version recorded by the app's update check during the earlier investigation: `26.1007.21434`, build `13901`, production channel.
Actual desktop backend: `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2`, independently verified again on October 10, 2026.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64, OS version `10.0.26300.0`, PowerShell `7.6.3`.

### What issue are you seeing?

The Settings > Configuration page displays an unknown session feature:

```text
Codex is ignoring 1 unrecognized configuration setting. Check for typos or deprecated settings.
session-flags: features.code_mode_tool_description_first is ignored.
```

The same page also displays:

```text
[features.guardianv2].thread_context is deprecated and ignored.
Thread-owned Guardian context is always enabled. Remove thread_context from [features.guardianv2] in config.toml, including profile overrides.
```

Neither feature occurs in the current user `config.toml`. Earlier read-only inspection of the installed desktop bundle found a dynamic session-feature injection path for `code_mode_tool_description_first`. A newly started instance of the same backend successfully read the user configuration without reproducing these two desktop-session warnings. The live outgoing desktop request was not captured, so the complete override provenance remains unconfirmed.

The user also encounters a separate, opaque command rejection under Full access. The original session transcript confirms that deletion of one agent-created, ordinary **53-byte test file** used this command shape:

```powershell
Remove-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\example-workspace\.runtime\.cache\policy-probe-disposable.txt' -Force
```

The displayed path is anonymized. It is not a user-data target. The command was rejected before process creation:

```text
exec_command failed: CreateProcess { message: "Rejected(... rejected: blocked by policy)" }
```

The original same-command retry remained rejected. The file is still present. No matching safety condition, rule identifier, or approval action appeared in the error.

**These are separate observations. No evidence establishes that the ignored/deprecated feature warnings cause the command rejection.**

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed in the affected desktop session:

1. Open Settings > Configuration after working in an existing local chat.
2. Observe the unknown `session-flags` warning and Guardian deprecation notice despite the absence of those keys from the user configuration.
3. With effective `approval_policy = "never"` and `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`, ask the agent to remove a disposable file it created in the workspace cache.
4. The `Remove-Item ... -Force` call returns the generic policy rejection above.

The single-file deletion was actually attempted and rejected on this installation. This is not a claimed clean-install or universally reproducible desktop example. Restarting/reinstalling has not been verified as a repair here. This reporting task did not retry deletion or change approval settings.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Desktop-generated feature overrides should match the bundled backend's supported schema.
- Configuration warnings should identify app/session overrides and offer an actionable remedy, rather than directing users to edit a file that lacks the setting.
- When a command safety check rejects forced deletion, the error should identify that condition and explain the supported approval route.
- Full access wording should make the interaction with approval policy clear.

### Additional information

Earlier local diagnostics verified a valid OpenAI backend signature and matching package block-map hashes for the desktop executable, frontend archive, and backend. No installation corruption was identified. A separate fresh backend returned `requirements: null` from `configRequirements/read`; this does not establish all effective policy layers of the live desktop process.

A prior unsupported `computer_use.windows.always_allowed_app_ids` configuration was backed up and removed. Independent configuration checks confirmed that its warning disappeared and the effective configuration was unchanged. The original deletion retry still failed afterward.

The matching public backend tag supplies a plausible explanation for the forced-delete rejection:

- [Forced-delete classifier](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2/codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/windows_dangerous_commands.rs#L223): delete cmdlet plus `-Force`.
- [Windows dangerous-command mapping](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2/codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/is_dangerous_command.rs#L74): maps the result to `Other`.
- [Approval decision](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L794): `Never` returns `Forbidden`; `OnRequest` returns `Prompt`.
- [Rejection text](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.17.2/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L1110): `Other` becomes only `blocked by policy`.

This source match is not a captured runtime decision trace. Please clarify the supported desktop approval setting for this case, without a broad allow rule or a bypass.

Related reports: #50526 covers the Guardian warning; #45403 covers Windows forced cleanup and opaque denial; #47043 covers another unknown desktop session feature. A search did not find a report for the exact `code_mode_tool_description_first` key. The new compatibility warning is the primary addition in this report; the related observations are included to avoid incorrectly attributing the rejection to the warnings.

Prepared by a Codex assistant at the affected user's explicit request. No credentials, account identifiers, actual local paths, project names, raw configuration, logs, or chat history are attached.

The user explicitly reports that **no permission popup appeared** for that attempt. We cannot establish that the user actually clicked Decline. The Cloudflare allow rule is screenshot-confirmed; an equivalent explicit rule for Feishu has not been independently confirmed.

## Steps and checks already performed
1. The user configured the explicit Cloudflare origin browsing permission in the desktop settings.
2. The user restarted the desktop app.
3. A normal Browser Use attempt still returned the saved-permission denial.
4. The user changed the Cloudflare permission to require approval as a troubleshooting step; the subsequent normal attempt still returned the saved-permission denial.
5. A narrow, read-only local configuration check continued to show:
   ```toml
   [browser_use.origins."https://dash.cloudflare.com"]
   access = "allow"
   ```
   We do not know whether that file represents the effective policy used by the browser request. Higher-priority policy restrictions have not been ruled out.
6. Desktop logs include `browser_use_iab_backend_startup_ready` for the affected conversation. This does not establish the permission service is healthy, but the evidence does not support simply assuming the browser backend never started.

The observed tool entry point was `cua.createBrowserTab("iab", "https://dash.cloudflare.com", { visible: true })`. No alternative browser surface was used to circumvent the denial.

## Expected behavior
- The displayed origin permission and the policy enforced by Browser Use should agree.
- If a higher-priority restriction overrides the visible rule, identify the policy source and the appropriate supported recovery route.
- When approval is required, present an actionable user-visible prompt.
- If the prompt cannot be displayed or permission state cannot be verified, distinguish that failure from an actual user decline.

## Request
Please investigate which effective rule produced each denial, why the UI/local allowance did not match the Cloudflare outcome, and why the Feishu attempt was reported as a decline without a visible prompt. A supported way to refresh/repair the effective permission state without broadening access, deleting credentials, or clearing unrelated user data would help.

Root cause is **unconfirmed**. This report does not assert a cache bug or managed-policy bug.

Potentially related reports (not proven to share the same cause):
- #52023: explicit allowance vs saved-denial mismatch on macOS
- #52605: Windows Cloudflare permission verification failure (different error text)
- #52903: Windows saved-permission denial despite visible allowance

No permission controls were bypassed. This report intentionally excludes credentials, account identifiers, app IDs, worker URLs, local usernames/paths, screenshots containing account details, raw logs, and conversation contents. No full session upload has been submitted.

## Follow-up after enabling approval requests
On 2026-10-11, the user changed the current conversation's approval mode. The runtime now reports a granular policy with MCP elicitations permitted (previously approval policy was never). One normal retry of `cua.createBrowserTab("iab", "https://dash.cloudflare.com", { visible: true })` still immediately returned the same saved-preference denial. Changing conversation approval mode did not resolve the origin denial. No alternate access path was used.

Reselecting the Browser and Computer plugins also allowed a native read-only application inventory, but two Browser Use `cua.getState()` calls reported `Browser 3: Error: nodeRepl.fetch request failed` while discovering the Edge connection. This transport symptom is not established as the cause of the permission denial.

## Further diagnostics under full local execution access (2026-10-11)
- The current task runtime was changed to unrestricted filesystem access with network enabled. One normal Browser Use retry of the same Cloudflare entry point still returned the saved-preference denial. This did not resolve the browser origin policy.
- Read-only desktop logs repeatedly report `[browser-use-iab-api] IAB_LIFECYCLE iab backend info request failed`, with `request=getInfo` and `errorMessage="No ChatGPT browser route is available for browser session [redacted]"` for the affected conversation. This is additional transport evidence, not an established cause of the saved-permission denial.
- A single documented tool-session reset (`js_reset`), followed by `cua.getState()`, still returned `Browser 3: Error: nodeRepl.fetch request failed`. The inventory also included an in-app about:blank tab; inventory visibility alone does not prove page access or permission recovery. No alternate surface was used to access a denied origin.
- A separately installed npm Codex CLI (0.146.0, distinct from the desktop-bundled runtime) reported a Responses WebSocket handshake timeout. HTTP reachability failed in one run and passed in a subsequent run. These CLI checks do not establish the desktop transport root cause, and the CLI's default sandbox report is not the current desktop task's execution policy.
- No credentials, raw logs, local paths, conversation IDs, or full session were uploaded. No security configuration or user data was changed.

After the actual affected executor successfully ran a safe command directly on the connected Windows computer, its first Computer Use call `await cua.getState();` failed before the kernel became usable:

```text
node_repl kernel exited unexpectedly
MXC launcher: cannot locate required Windows platform directory: HRESULT 0x80070003
```

3. Make the initial supported CUA entry call `await cua.getState();`: launcher exits with the error above.

The supported CUA tool should initialize, or identify the exact missing folder/capability and a supported recovery action. A successful shell command should not be reported as proof of native UI control.


Restarting the application, rebuilding only the generated runtime from the official installed package, and a successful elevated sandbox setup did not restore the affected executor. Enabling the documented MXC preference restored the safe command, but not CUA.

The corresponding public source calls `SHGetKnownFolderPath` for Program Files, Program Files (x86), and ProgramData before native launch:
https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.2/codex-rs/mxc-sandbox/src/windows.rs

Those directories exist and known-folder queries succeed in the coordinator's context. The affected CUA launcher's token/environment was not captured; the error does not say which folder failed. A separate coordinator session exposes browser surfaces only and states `Native computer APIs are disabled`, despite Computer Use being enabled. It is not established whether that capability limitation shares the launcher's cause.

Two official local-to-cloud follow-up calls, with explicit and default host routing, failed before a new turn/receipt:
```text
invalid turn/start params: AbsolutePathBuf deserialized without a base path
```
A request forwarded directly by the owner later reached the affected executor. Existing related reports include #51679 and #50428; this path failure is not claimed to have the same cause as the primary CUA failure. The earlier runtime-sharing symptom is related to #52179.

Project coordination has been interrupted across two days. The owner has decided to reset Windows and reinstall the desktop application after preserving project data. The reset has not happened yet, and there is no evidence that Dots damaged Windows or that reinstalling Windows will fix these product/session failures.

4. The local task starts and can run shell commands and read the Computer Use skill, but its available model tools lack the required runtime/control interface.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

ChatGPT-hosted Codex task on 2026-10-10. The exact desktop/app build number is not exposed in this environment.

For implementation comparison, I inspected public `openai/codex` commit `cc7ba33601286a751477832b01de7b6f8de0dd9c`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Managed Linux cloud task using the host-owned `codex_apps` MCP server and cloud/user Skills.

### What issue are you seeing?

Cloud Skill package roots can be listed and read, and their root response advertises exact child-resource URIs in `_meta.resources`. Reading any advertised child URI then fails.

Observed behavior:

- Top-level `resources/list` contains the `mcp/skill` package root.
- Reading the package root succeeds.
- The root response includes entries such as:
  `skill://user/<skill-id>/<skill-name>/references/example.md`
- Direct MCP `resources/read` for that advertised URI returns:
  `-32002: Unknown resource`
- `skills.read` with the same package and exact child URI returns:
  `failed to read skill resource`

This reproduced with reference files from two different user Skill packages, so it is not isolated to one package or one missing file.

The package root may also expose a bundle URL, but that is not an equivalent documented child-resource read path and should not be required for `skills.read`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. In a hosted task with a user/cloud Skill that contains a reference file, list the available Skills.
2. Read the Skill package root. Confirm that this succeeds.
3. Inspect the root resource response and copy one exact child URI from `_meta.resources`.
4. Call `skills.read` with the original package and that full child URI.
5. Alternatively, call MCP `resources/read` against `codex_apps` with the same URI.
6. Observe `failed to read skill resource` from `skills.read` and `Unknown resource` from MCP.

### Expected behavior

Every child URI advertised by a Skill package root should be readable through the same `codex_apps` authority using `resources/read`, and therefore through `skills.read`.

At minimum, the server should not advertise a child URI that its resolver cannot return.

### Additional information

The public Codex client appears to preserve the requested URI correctly:

- `codex-rs/ext/skills/src/tools/read.rs` keeps the supplied complete resource URI in `SkillReadRequest.resource`. Provider errors are intentionally flattened to the model-visible `failed to read skill resource`.
- `codex-rs/codex-mcp/src/resource_client.rs` forwards that URI directly in `ReadResourceRequestParams`.

That makes the observed repair boundary the cloud Skill provider / `codex_apps` child-resource registration or resolver, rather than URI rewriting in the public client.

Impact: Skills whose `SKILL.md` requires reading bundled references or scripts cannot follow their own instructions through the documented `skills.read` path.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

This incident affected the dot’s own cloud execution environment while I was communicating through ChatGPT on the web. I do not have a verified desktop app or backend execution-service version for the incident.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro. Exact plan tier can be supplied privately if needed.

### What platform is your computer?

Client: Windows, using ChatGPT in a web browser. Affected execution host: OpenAI-hosted Linux cloud computer belonging to my dot. The affected files and test were not running on my Windows laptop or Mac.

### What issue are you seeing?

Summary
I’m reporting a recurring loss of accessible working state on my dot’s cloud computer. During the latest incident, filesystem operations stalled while an offline software test was running. The execution service subsequently disconnected. When command access returned, recent source worktrees, Git history locations and test evidence were missing, while older project files remained.
Reported filesystem usage fell from roughly 30 GB to 3.3 GB. This includes build caches, binaries and generated test artifacts; it should not be interpreted as 26 GB of unique source code or proof of permanent physical deletion.
I did not click Pause, Reboot, Delete or Reset, or otherwise interact with the cloud environment during the incident. The observations below come from commands run by my assistant and retained conversation/tool results, not OpenAI backend logs.
Environment
- Product: ChatGPT dots, using the dot’s own Linux cloud computer
- Client used for this conversation: Windows web browser
- Workload: offline Rust software development and verification, with separate implementation and review workers
- Working files: task scratch and shared workspace directories
- User’s Windows laptop and Mac were not executing the affected test
- This was not an ordinary temporary data-analysis session or a repository-backed Codex Cloud task
- Exact frontend and execution-service versions were not captured
Observed timeline
All times are UTC on October 10, 2026.
- 02:24:37: An end-to-end offline test started against a pinned source revision. Thirteen focused author tests had passed before this run
- 02:33:43: The last observed database progress recorded allocation of an output copy. The test had already passed several reader-selection, stale/corrupt-source and interrupted-write retry checks
- Around 02:35: Separate workers began encountering stalled filesystem operations, including simple file inspection and directory listing. These were not limited to the product test
- 02:38: A filesystem check still reported approximately 30 GB used, with only about 183 MB available. The current source revision and running-test receipt were still readable
- 02:55:03: The current kernel’s boot time, read after access returned. This does not independently establish the previous kernel’s identity or the exact moment the task was attached to a different environment
- Around 02:58: Attempts to resume existing execution sessions returned: “exec-server transport disconnected; failed to resume exec-server session: recovery timed out after 25s”
- Around 03:01: Commands from a temporary directory worked again. The original top-level working directory existed, but recent implementation worktrees and the latest test receipt were absent. Reported filesystem usage was approximately 3.3 GB
- Subsequent read-only inspection found older pre-code and unrelated files, but not the recent implementation trees, verification directories or runtime test roots previously used by the task
The interrupted test has no observed final exit status. Its result remains unknown and has not been credited as passing.
Evidence of a filesystem or environment transition
1. Changed overlay identity
An environment record recovered from an externally saved, manifest-verified archive identifies an earlier overlay mount. The current mount has a different identifier. This supports a change in the presented filesystem environment; it does not identify whether the mechanism was replacement, restoration, reassociation or another lifecycle operation.
2. Recent metadata timestamps on older files
Several surviving directories have metadata-change timestamps around 03:01 UTC, while retaining older modification timestamps, including October 5 dates. This is consistent with files being restored or rematerialized, but ctime is not a creation timestamp and does not establish the snapshot’s age.
3. Missing state across multiple categories
The disappearance affected source worktrees, Git-history locations, test receipts, build outputs and runtime roots. A stopped test process alone would not explain those missing directories.
4. Low available storage before the incident
The earlier filesystem had approximately 183 MB available. This is relevant diagnostic context. We have not established that disk exhaustion caused the stall or transition, and no captured ENOSPC error establishes that explanation.
5. Diagnostic limits
Kernel logs were inaccessible. Counters read from the current kernel cannot rule out an out-of-memory or other failure in a previous environment. The assistant cannot inspect platform-side lifecycle, storage-association or snapshot logs.
Cleanup actions and scope
The assistant had previously removed explicitly bounded generated metadata and redundant caches. Those recorded removals were far smaller than the observed usage change, excluded original source and verification receipts, and were followed by successful builds, focused tests and the subsequent running test.
These recorded cleanup actions do not explain the broad disappearance of recent source and evidence. However, this report is not an assertion that every platform action or filesystem operation has been audited; that requires backend records.
Earlier incident on the same dot
This is not my first experience of missing work in this conversation. Before the current incident, we had already discussed missing research progress, including what I described as 12–14 research cycles/runs.
That earlier event led me to request backups on my laptop and regular ZIP checkpoints explicitly. My instructions included saving everything so another environment loss would not erase the work, and continuing to send ZIPs periodically.
The earlier incident’s exact onset, filesystem identifiers and complete loss inventory are not established in this report. Please correlate it with the earlier activity in the same dot conversation. I am reporting recurrence of the user-visible problem, not claiming that both incidents have a proven common cause.
Impact and recovery
- Recent source changes and verification evidence became inaccessible, interrupting development and independent acceptance
- External Library backups survived and matched their recorded SHA-256 hashes
- Those backups allowed recovery of an earlier accepted repository baseline and a later in-progress source snapshot
- Source changes and receipts created after the latest saved snapshot have not been recovered from the currently accessible workspace or available backup chain
- Some lost evidence will require genuine re-execution; remembered results cannot replace missing acceptance receipts
- The assistant also allowed newer changes to accumulate locally while waiting for a verified checkpoint. That backup gap increased the recovery cost, but does not explain the environment transition
After I requested investigation before further recovery, the recovery job already in flight finished in a new directory. No coding, builds or tests have resumed.
Expected behavior
OpenAI’s guide says the cloud computer “can keep its state between periods of use”: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/computers-and-apps
I understand that this wording does not define a complete durability guarantee. However, an ongoing development task needs a clear persistence contract: which paths survive, what events can replace state, how recent a restored snapshot should be, and how users are warned when work is at risk.
An unexpected transition should preserve recoverable work or clearly report what happened and how to retrieve the previous state.
Reproduction status
There is no deterministic reproduction. We have not deliberately rebooted, reset or filled the filesystem to reproduce this issue. The observed sequence was active work → stalled filesystem calls → execution disconnect → renewed access with recent files missing and older files present.

Requested investigation
1. Correlate this dot and execution session with the environment and storage history during approximately 02:35–03:01 UTC on October 10
2. Identify what caused the filesystem stalls and subsequent execution-service disconnect
3. Determine whether the task was attached to a replacement environment, an older snapshot, a different writable layer or another storage association
4. Preserve and locate the preceding writable layer and any newer snapshots before cleanup makes recovery harder
5. Confirm whether the missing source changes and evidence can be recovered
6. Explain the supported persistence guarantees for task scratch and shared workspace directories
7. Explain low-disk-space behavior, including whether it can trigger replacement or restoration and what warnings or recovery mechanisms exist
8. Clarify exactly what Pause and Reboot affect, including delegated tasks, active processes, filesystem state and snapshots
9. Correlate the earlier reported loss in this same dot conversation without assuming a common cause
10. Provide a supported method for durable, automatic checkpoints outside the execution filesystem
Privacy
This public draft omits account details, private project contents, full private paths, conversation/session identifiers and exact environment identifiers. Relevant correlation details and available diagnostic hashes can be supplied through an appropriate private support channel.
Current conclusion
Recent working state is demonstrably missing from the accessible environment, and the observed filesystem identity differs from an earlier verified record. The underlying cause and recoverability of the previous storage remain unresolved. Please investigate before treating this as an ordinary task interruption or user-initiated reset.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic reproduction is available. The observed sequence was:
1. Continue an existing development task on the dot’s cloud computer, with source worktrees, Git history, test evidence and external Library checkpoints
2. Start an offline test against a pinned source revision at 02:24:37 UTC on October 10, 2026
3. Observe filesystem operations stall around 02:35, including independent file inspection and directory listing
4. Receive execution-service transport disconnection and recovery-timeout errors around 02:58
5. When commands work again around 03:01, inspect the original workspace paths
6. Find recent source and verification directories absent, older files still present, and reported filesystem usage reduced from approximately 30 GB to 3.3 GB
7. Compare diagnostics: the current overlay identifier differs from an earlier hash-verified environment record
I did not click Pause, Reboot, Delete or Reset. We have not deliberately reproduced the incident through rebooting or filling the disk. Available storage was low before the failure, but causation is unproven. The interrupted test’s final outcome is unknown. Private session identifiers can be supplied to support; token and context-window usage were not captured.

### What is the expected behavior?

Previously saved project files should remain accessible within the cloud computer’s supported persistence scope. If the platform replaces an environment or restores a snapshot, it should preserve recoverable work, disclose the transition and snapshot age, and provide recovery guidance.
Please clarify which directories persist, what events can discard or replace their state, and what happens when disk space becomes low. A running development task should not silently return to an older accessible state without a clear warning or recovery path.

### Additional information

This is a recurring user-visible issue in the same dot conversation. An earlier incident involved missing research progress described as 12–14 cycles/runs and led to explicit requests for frequent ZIP and laptop backups. Its exact cause and timing are not established here.
External Library backups survived this incident and were hash-verified. They recovered an accepted baseline and later in-progress work. Four subsequent repair areas, including eleven focused tests and later local-only verification records, remain absent from the recovered source/evidence set. Build caches and generated artifacts account for part of the disk-usage difference; we are not claiming 26 GB of unique source was permanently deleted.
Please preserve and investigate the preceding writable layer and snapshots, correlate environment/storage transitions during October 10, 02:35–03:01 UTC, and establish whether newer work is recoverable. Exact identifiers can be provided privately. No backend root cause has been established.

issues.body:
## Scope
This report concerns **ordinary ChatGPT conversations in the first-party Android app**, not Codex or Codex Remote. I could not identify a dedicated public ChatGPT Android issue tracker; please route internally if appropriate.

## Summary
Chinese-language assistant responses are unexpectedly truncated **mid-sentence** with an ellipsis (`…`) in the Android app. More seriously, selecting the affected passage as one continuous selection and copying it produces text **with entire intervening phrases missing**, rather than the complete response.

The same conversation viewed in Chrome at chatgpt.com on the same Android phone shows the **full, untruncated response**. This is not a model-generated omission.

## Environment
- ChatGPT Android app: **1.2026.272**
- OS: **Android 16**
- Language of affected answer: Simplified Chinese
- Date observed: **2026-10-11**, approximately 11:26–11:36 UTC+8
- Control: Chrome mobile browser at chatgpt.com, same conversation, text complete
- Device model: not yet independently verified

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open a long Chinese-language assistant response in a normal ChatGPT conversation in the Android app.
2. Scroll to the section containing several paragraphs and numbered subheadings.
3. Observe that some text is replaced by `…` in the middle of a sentence, even where it should wrap normally.
4. Use Android text selection to select the affected passage **in one operation**, then tap Copy.
5. Paste into another text field.
6. Open the same conversation in Chrome at chatgpt.com and compare.

## Actual behavior
Examples observed in the Android app:
- Heading `第三，政策可以创造需求，却不一定能创造竞争…` instead of `第三，政策可以创造需求，却不一定能创造竞争力。`
- Sentence ending `迭代缓慢的问…` instead of `迭代缓慢的问题。`
- Copying a continuous selection omitted the complete conditional clause `但如果本土厂商主要依靠政府采购生存，缺少开放市场竞争，`, leaving disconnected fragments such as:
```
却不一定能创造竞争力。
美国政府限制采购中国无人机，确实能为本土厂商创造市场。
就可能出现产品昂贵、迭代缓慢的问题。
当然，美国也有高自动化、高附加值制造能力，并非所有制造环节都存在这些困难。
```
The web view displays the missing clause and full headings correctly.

## Expected behavior
- Assistant messages should display every character and wrap text normally, without arbitrary ellipsis truncation.
- Copying a contiguous selected range should preserve **all** characters from that range, regardless of visual layout.

## Impact
This is a **silent data-loss-on-copy** issue, not merely cosmetic. It can corrupt quotations, code, contractual language, and other text where completeness matters.

## Notes
- Root cause not confirmed. Possible interaction between Android text layout/ellipsizing and text-selection/copy behavior.
- Android app and Chrome comparison screenshots were captured and can be supplied through the appropriate channel.
- Please advise if a dedicated ChatGPT Android tracker or internal bug channel is preferred.

issues.title: @openai/codex-sdk: TS item types drifted from exec JSONL wire format

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: exec
labels.description: Issues related to the `codex exec` subcommand

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

issues.body:
The hand-maintained `sdk/typescript/src/items.ts` (header: "based on item types from `codex-rs/exec/src/exec_events.rs`") has drifted from what `codex exec --experimental-json` actually emits. All four gaps below were verified against current `main` Rust sources and with `tsc` — the SDK rejects each shape.

1. **`collab_tool_call` missing from `ThreadItem`** — the wire format emits it for subagent activity (`ThreadItemDetails::CollabToolCall` in `exec_events.rs`, mapped in `event_processor_with_jsonl_output.rs`), but TS consumers must cast to `any` to handle official SDK events. Same root cause as #28318 (no fixing PR exists).
2. **`CommandExecutionStatus` missing `"declined"`** — `event_processor_with_jsonl_output.rs` maps `CommandExecutionStatus::Declined` into the JSONL output.
3. **`PatchApplyStatus` missing `"in_progress"`** — `event_processor_with_jsonl_output.rs` maps `PatchApplyStatus::InProgress` into the JSONL output.
4. **`WebSearchItem` missing `action` and `results`** — added to the wire format by #46319 (`WebSearchAction` + `results: Option<Vec<JsonValue>>` in `exec_events.rs`); the SDK was never synced.

I have a ready fix on branch [`codex-sdk-wire-type-sync` in nosmile99/codex](https://github.com/nosmile99/codex/tree/codex-sdk-wire-type-sync) (commit c2ce059; compares cleanly against `main`, no conflicts) that:
- adds exported `CollabToolCallItem`, `CollabToolCallStatus`, `CollabTool`, `CollabAgentStatus`, `CollabAgentState` and puts `CollabToolCallItem` in the `ThreadItem` union;
- adds `"declined"` to `CommandExecutionStatus` and `"in_progress"` to `PatchApplyStatus`;
- adds `action: WebSearchAction` and `results?: unknown[]` to `WebSearchItem`, with `WebSearchAction` mirroring the Rust serde shape (`search` / `open_page` / `find_in_page` / `other`, `snake_case` tag);
- adds `tests/wireTypeSync.test.ts`: wire-shaped fixtures (including the runtime example from #28318) that fail to compile via ts-jest diagnostics if the types drift again.

Verified: new suite 5/5 green, pre-existing `tests/exec.test.ts` 14/14 green, eslint + prettier clean; the new suite fails against the pre-fix types (negative control). I could not open a PR because this repo restricts PR creation to collaborators — happy for a maintainer to pull the branch, or I can re-submit it as a PR if the restriction is lifted.

issues.title: Windows: Codex-created .agents ownership breaks sandbox setup and in-app browser control

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Codex Desktop on Windows, observed September 8, 2026. Bundled runtime verified with `codex.exe --version`: **codex-cli 0.153.4**. The separate desktop About-dialog version was not captured.

### What subscription do you have?

Pro; this report concerns a local Windows filesystem/sandbox failure.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 10 Pro 22H2, build 19045.7663, x64. Local project on M:. Configuration: `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` and `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`.

### What issue are you seeing?

After Codex created a project's `.agents` directory while adding a project-local skill, subsequent local commands and in-app browser control failed during sandbox initialization. The user had not manually created the directory or changed its ownership.

The directory was owned by `<MACHINE>\CodexSandboxOffline`, while the parent project directory was owned by the interactive Windows user. Both directories were ordinary directories, not reparse points. The child inherited its access rules and the normal user's broad group access was Modify, rather than permission to change the ACL.

Sanitized sandbox log:
```text
deny ACE failed on M:\Codex\<PROJECT>\.agents:
SetNamedSecurityInfoW failed for M:\Codex\<PROJECT>\.agents: 5
setup refresh completed with errors
setup error: setup refresh had errors
```

Local command error:
```text
Failed to create unified exec process:
helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

Browser tool error from `cua.getState()`:
```text
trusted Node process exited unexpectedly; kernel reset, rerun your request
```

The user could manually use the in-app browser tabs, but the agent could not even enumerate them. Repeated tool calls and a browser-kernel reset reproduced the failure.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is the observed incident sequence, not a separate clean-room reproduction:

1. A user-owned Windows project was working with the elevated sandbox.
2. Codex used its file-editing workflow to add project-local skill files beneath a new `.agents` directory.
3. The directory's creation time was 2026-09-08 00:49:43 PDT. Sandbox setup was still succeeding immediately before creation.
4. At 00:49:51 PDT, the next local command failed while applying a deny ACE to that directory.
5. Later attempts from a task in the same project failed for both local commands and browser initialization.
6. Inspection found the ownership mismatch described above.

### What is the expected behavior?

Creating a supported project-local skill through Codex should leave the project usable. The creation/setup workflow should handle ownership and protected-directory ACLs consistently.

If setup cannot apply an ACL, the agent-facing error should identify the affected path and Windows error. Browser control should expose the underlying setup failure rather than only a generic Node-process crash.

Users should not have to anticipate which folders Codex will create, pre-create them manually, or diagnose NTFS ownership.

### Additional information

A narrowly scoped repair was verified:

- Backed up the affected directory's security descriptor.
- With Windows administrator approval, changed **only the .agents directory's owner** to the interactive user using `icacls <directory> /setowner <interactive-user>`, without recursion.
- Did not reset the directory's ACL, grant Everyone access, disable the sandbox, change firewall rules, or delete/recreate the directory.
- On the next attempt, Codex successfully applied its deny ACEs and sandbox setup reported `errors=[]`.
- In the original affected task, a local README read completed with exit code 0 and `cua.getState()` successfully enumerated both existing in-app browser tabs on the first attempt. No app restart or kernel reset was needed after the ownership repair.

This strongly points to an ownership/ACL setup interaction triggered by Codex's own directory creation. The exact internal code defect has not been isolated.

Related reports: #31414 concerns a different folder-owner case; #39933 describes the generic setup-refresh failure. This report adds the agent-created `.agents` trigger, correlated browser-control failure, and verified single-directory ownership repair.

The assistant initially recommended restarting, then suggested that the user manually pre-create the folders. That guidance misplaced the prevention burden: Codex created the directory. Please address both the setup behavior and the diagnostic guidance.

Project names, personal account/machine names, browser destinations, and full transcripts are omitted.

- Observations collected September 30 through October 3, 2026. Times below are UTC.
- Cloud desktop: Linux/Xfce.
- Exact dot client build, browser version, and cloud image/runtime version: not collected.

## 1. Cloud desktop and installation state does not remain available

### What happened

- A custom wallpaper was applied and visually verified on September 30 at about 05:13.
- By October 2, the wallpaper had reverted to the default pink background. The original wallpaper was restored and verified at about 19:00. I’ve experienced the wallpaper disappearing repeatedly.
- On October 2 at about 19:13, Claude Code v2.1.287 opened in a new cloud-terminal tab, already signed in and ready at its input prompt. This verified startup, not completion of a coding task.
- On October 3 at about 06:50–06:54, checks in both the cloud shell and GUI terminal could no longer find Claude Code in the usual locations or through a broader search of accessible locations. No existing session was found.
- Codex was still installed during that later check. This was not an observation that every installed application had disappeared.

### Sequence observed

1. Apply a custom wallpaper or install and initialize a CLI in the dot’s cloud computer.
2. Verify it works in that session.
3. Return to the cloud environment later.
4. Find the default wallpaper restored or the previously available CLI missing.

Expected: saved desktop customization and software remain available across the supported session lifecycle. If particular locations or installations are temporary, their persistence limits should be clear.

Actual: previously verified state was no longer available. The exact transition that removed it has not been isolated. There is no verified before/after VM identity comparison, so this report does not establish whether the same VM was restarted, replaced, or otherwise changed.

## 2. English-only preference was not followed after Reboot

I had explicitly requested English replies even when I write or speak Hindi, and repeated that preference on October 2. On October 3, after a reboot, the dot replied in Hindi anyway.

Expected: an established English-only preference continues to apply after Reboot unless I change it or explicitly request another language.

Actual: the response did not follow that preference. This shows a preference-following failure; it does not prove that the stored preference itself was deleted.

Suggested reproduction: establish this language preference, use Reboot, then send a Hindi or mixed-language message without requesting a language change. Check whether the response stays in English. This has not been tested as a controlled reproduction.

## 3. Twitter/X, Cloudflare, and Amazon fail in the cloud browser

I’ve encountered access failures on Twitter/X, Cloudflare, and Amazon in both autonomous browsing and manual takeover of the cloud browser. Taking over manually has not reliably made these sites usable.

Expected: supported sites can be accessed through the cloud browser, including manual takeover when needed. If a site or step is unsupported, the limitation and recovery path should be clear.

Actual: these workflows remain blocked or unreliable even during manual takeover.

The exact failing URLs, browser error messages, timestamps, and whether each failure occurred before or after sign-in have not been captured consistently. This report does not establish that every page on these services fails, or whether the cause is site restrictions, networking, authentication, or the cloud runtime.

## 4. WhatsApp repeatedly crashes with Error9 near the browser container’s memory limit

On October 2, diagnostics around a reproduced crash showed:

- Browser container memory limit: 8 GiB.
- Memory usage: approximately 7.94 GiB.
- Cumulative OOM events increased from 139 to 141.
- Cumulative OOM kills increased from 36 to 37.
- After duplicate WhatsApp tabs were closed, a newly opened WhatsApp tab crashed with Error9 within about one minute.
- A process snapshot showed 60 NodeMainThread processes with approximately 6.61 GiB aggregate RSS. Summed RSS can include shared pages and should not be treated as unique memory usage.

Expected: WhatsApp remains usable without repeated tab crashes. A fresh tab should be usable after closing duplicates.

Actual: the fresh tab also crashed. The timing supports a memory-pressure explanation, but no killed-process identification proves that WhatsApp was the OOM victim, and these measurements do not prove a memory leak. No durable fix has been verified. Opening a fresh tab is not a fresh-VM test.

## 5. Updated plugin tools only appeared after dot Reboot

On October 3, updated plugin documentation described new tools, but the active dot session still exposed an older 16-tool catalog. Needed booking and attendance tools were absent despite the plugin update/refresh.

After I used dot Reboot, a fresh check at about 09:27–09:28 showed:

- `get_account` succeeded.
- `list_call_bookings` succeeded.
- The current catalog exposed `prepare_message`, `react_to_message`, `delete_comment`, `get_attribution`, and `set_call_attendance`.

Only read operations were executed in that diagnostic. Catalog visibility does not establish that the write operations work, and it does not verify later scheduled execution.

Expected: a plugin update or supported refresh makes the current tool catalog available without a full dot Reboot, or clearly tells me that Reboot is required.

Actual: the session retained the older catalog until after Reboot. Reboot is an observed workaround in this instance; the exact cache or refresh failure has not been identified.

## Impact and requested investigation

These issues interrupt cloud workflows and make it difficult to trust that setup, preferences, and integrations will remain usable between sessions.

Please investigate the cloud environment’s persistence boundaries, preference handling across Reboot, browser access and memory/process cleanup, and plugin tool-catalog refresh. Please also provide a safe diagnostic procedure that preserves existing sessions and data, and clarify which state is expected to survive Reboot or cloud-environment replacement.

This report intentionally excludes private messages, account identifiers, authentication data, and unredacted logs.

issues.title: Codex Cloud: per-task model and reasoning effort, and scheduled tasks in a cloud environment

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI (`codex cloud`, checked through 0.156.1) and Codex Cloud on the web

### What feature would you like to see?

Two gaps keep Codex Cloud from hosting an unattended, stateful agent workflow: an agent that works in short sessions, keeps its state in the repository, decides when its next session should start, and occasionally waits for a human reply.

**1. Per-task model and reasoning effort for cloud tasks**

`codex cloud exec` can't choose the model or reasoning effort for a task. The request it sends carries only the environment, branch, QA mode, input and number of attempts. Local `codex exec` supports `--model` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=...`. The same controls for cloud tasks would let a workflow use a lighter setting for routine runs and a stronger one for deep work:

```bash
codex cloud exec --env ENV_ID --model MODEL --reasoning-effort LEVEL "..."
```

**2. Scheduled cloud tasks bound to an environment and branch**

Scheduled tasks can run in the desktop app, but only while the computer is on. They can also run on the web, but there they can't target a repository environment. Nothing schedules a Codex Cloud task, in a configured environment and branch, for a future time or a recurrence. Something like:

```bash
codex cloud schedule --env ENV_ID --branch main --at 2026-09-30T10:00 --timezone America/New_York "..."
codex cloud schedule --env ENV_ID --branch main --cron "0 10 * * 6" --timezone America/New_York "..."
codex cloud schedule list --json
codex cloud schedule cancel SCHEDULE_ID
```

Being able to create a schedule from inside a running cloud task would let an agent book its own next run.

### Additional information

The third piece is continuing an existing task by ID, such as `codex cloud message TASK_ID "..."`. That is already requested in #24777, so I've 👍'd it there instead of repeating it.

This workflow runs today with local `codex exec`, `codex exec resume` and an external scheduler. It can't move to Codex Cloud until cloud tasks can be scheduled, can choose their model and effort, and can be continued.

Related:
- #24777: scriptable environment and task lifecycle, including messaging an existing task
- #42970: model selection in Codex Cloud from the mobile app
- #32723: environment selection for desktop scheduled tasks

**Owner-reported:** the task appears in the desktop Codex recent-task list after an app update, but is absent from the web and iOS lists. Whether this particular task's full conversation can be opened on desktop has not yet been verified. List absence is not evidence of data loss.

Earlier create calls using an older saved configuration returned UNKNOWN / AppServerBackendRequestError. Creation later succeeded with a newly configured environment, so creation is **not currently universally broken**.

## Reproduction B: user-created task can be read, but dot cannot continue it

1. Create a cloud chat directly from desktop or mobile and send an initial message.
2. Ask dot to read that exact task.
3. Ask dot to send a minimal read-only follow-up to the same task.

**Actual:** reading succeeds, but follow-up submission returns NOT_FOUND / CloudThreadNotFoundError. The identifiers used for read and send were checked and matched. No successful submission through this send path was observed.

A null parentThreadId does not explain this observation by itself: the successfully continued dot-created diagnostic task also returned null.

## Reproduction C: browser follow-up fails, native-client follow-up works

Submitting a follow-up to an existing user-created cloud task through the dot's normal cloud-browser UI failed with:

> Error submitting message
> Unable to determine project root for task

One page refresh and retry produced the same error. Read-back confirmed that no new message or execution turn had been created; the unsent diagnostic draft was cleared.

The owner subsequently submitted a read-only check through the desktop client. It executed successfully and returned the repository commit and asset metadata; dot could read that response. The owner also reports that mobile access works.

This overlaps with #49497, but identical error text does not establish an identical cause.

Separately, the owner reports that enabling TUN in their own proxy setup resolved a Windows reconnection problem. That does not establish the cause of the cloud-browser project-root error or dot's NOT_FOUND response. No proxy/security configuration was changed by the reporting assistant.

## Impact and requested resolution

The intended workflow is one cloud coding task, with dot sending instructions and reviewing results, while the owner can inspect the same conversation across clients. Current behavior forces a choice between assistant control and consistent owner visibility.

Please:
- document supported read/continuation behavior for user-created versus dot-created tasks;
- make task discoverability consistent, or clearly explain intentional differences;
- return an actionable explanation when read succeeds but send returns NOT_FOUND;
- provide a supported task/project-association check and repair that preserves prepared environments and uncommitted work.

Archive/delete issues are tracked separately in #46182 and #46240; they are not claimed to share this root cause.

This report was prepared with the user's dot at the owner's request. It distinguishes tool/browser-confirmed execution from owner-reported client behavior. Account details, repository names, task IDs, private file names/hashes, credentials, and screenshots are omitted. No application code was changed for these read-only tests.

prs.title: Report exec runtime resets before accepting further requests
prs.body:
Report exec runtime resets before accepting further requests

## Why

Replacing a gRPC code-mode runtime loses stored values and running cells. Silently continuing after reconnection hides that loss, while prior external tool operations may already have completed.

## What changed

- Capture the runtime generation when `execute` and `wait` calls are created. If recovery replaces it, reject those calls with an explicit reset error, including concurrent calls and calls first polled after recovery.
- Explain the lost state and advise inspecting prior tool results before retrying. Allow a fresh `exec` call to continue on the replacement runtime.
- Keep `terminate` from reopening the runtime so cleanup cannot hide a reset from the next request.

## Testing

Extend gRPC recovery tests to cover reset errors after host restarts, missing sessions, and route loss, rejection of queued calls, and successful fresh execution with cleared stored state.

labels.name: priority/p2

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

For example, I have "gradle" and "git" skills with descriptions like:

  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics

and

Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

that never ever get called when using the relevant tools.

> 4. **Agent & Tool Hierarchy:** Whenver considering how to approach a task or do anything, ALWAYS follow the hierarchy of preference: **Sub-Agents** > **Skills** > **Specialized MCP Tools** (NOT a Shell tool or similar) > **General/Builtin Tools** (e.g., `run_shell_command`, `grep_search`, `read_file`).
> 5. **Intentionality Protocol:** Before starting ANY task, you MUST stop and consider which agent, skill, or tool is most appropriate for the specific context. If your plan involves using the shell (even via a tool like `run_shell_command`), you MUST stop and reconsider if a more specialized tool or skill exists to handle the task more reliably.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: /compress command is not persistent across session resume

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/small
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

labels.name: priority/p3
labels.description: Backlog - a good idea but not currently a priority.

labels.name: area/agent

labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)
