issues.body:
## Version

OpenClaw 2026.6.11 (e085fa1) · macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64) · Telegram long polling (grammY), single account

## Environment

The gateway routes outbound traffic through a local HTTP proxy (`127.0.0.1:10080`) provided by a VPN client. A custom watchdog restarts the proxy process on failure (with backoff). A `crontab` entry restarts the gateway daily at 05:05 via `launchctl kickstart`. The local router also reboots daily at 05:00 (now reduced to weekly).

## Summary

Under normal operation, the Telegram health-monitor cycles the polling lease every ~10 minutes: a `released stopped Telegram polling lease` log line is followed within 10-15 seconds by `starting provider`. **Occasionally that follow-up restart silently never happens.** The health-monitor keeps ticking and logging `health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)` every ~300s ad infinitum, but no `starting provider` line is ever emitted, and the bot stops calling `getUpdates` entirely. Inbound Telegram messages arrive at Telegram's servers but are never fetched. The only known recovery is a full gateway process restart (`launchctl kickstart`).

## Clearest reproduction (2026-07-17)

```
# 05:05  gateway restarted via crontab
# 05:10  health-monitor's first periodic check after restart fires — 
#        proxy is momentarily unreachable (router rebooting at 05:00)
05:10:03 [health-monitor] [telegram:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: disconnected)
05:10:08 [telegram] [default] released stopped Telegram polling lease
#        ^^^^^ NO "starting provider" follows — polling is dead from here on

# health-monitor keeps trying every ~300s, but restart never completes:
05:15:03 [health-monitor] [telegram:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)
05:20:03 [health-monitor] [telegram:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)
05:25:03 [health-monitor] [telegram:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)
# ... (repeats every 5-10 minutes, 63 times over 5.3 hours)

# 10:31  manual gateway restart → polling immediately recovers:
10:31:55 [telegram] [default] starting provider (@jason9054_claw_bot)
10:31:57 [telegram] [diag] isolated polling ingress started
10:31:59 [telegram] Inbound message telegram:5557212069 -> @jason9054_claw_bot (direct, 5 chars)
```

**Net effect:** bot unresponsive to inbound messages for **5 hours 21 minutes** (05:10:08 → 10:31:55). Gateway stayed up and healthy the whole time — other plugins/providers worked normally.

## 9 occurrences across ~7 weeks

Automated scan pairing every `released stopped` line with the next `starting provider` line, flagging gaps >60s:

| Timestamp (`released stopped`) | Gap until `starting provider` |
|---|---|
| 2026-06-29T05:39:01 | ~15.6h |
| 2026-07-03T18:48:44 | ~16.1h |
| 2026-07-06T05:43:38 | ~2.6h |
| 2026-07-11T05:10:08 | ~23.9h |
| 2026-07-12T05:10:07 | ~4.4h |
| 2026-07-13T10:00:08 | ~19.1h |
| 2026-07-14T05:10:07 | ~7.2h |
| 2026-07-14T12:27:45 | ~0.7h |
| 2026-07-17T05:10:08 | ~5.4h |

All 9 follow the same pattern: `released stopped` fires, `starting provider` never follows, health-monitor repeats `restarting (reason: stopped)` forever without effect.

## Suspected trigger: race with a concurrent network disconnect

4 of 9 occurrences (07-11, 07-12, 07-14, 07-17) happened at exactly 05:10 — one health-monitor interval after a daily 05:05 cron-triggered gateway restart — and within 1-2 seconds of a local proxy restart (triggered by a 05:00 router reboot causing a brief connectivity drop). The remaining **5 occurrences have no such correlation**: 06-29 and 07-03 predate the proxy watchdog entirely, and 07-06, 07-13, and 07-14T12:27 had no concurrent proxy restarts. This is **not specific to our proxy setup** — it's a generic race between "health-monitor detects disconnect → calls restart path" and "the restart path actually completing," triggered by any sufficiently-timed transient network interruption.

## Hypothesis

`released stopped Telegram polling lease` is logged unconditionally as part of the restart routine, but the subsequent "start provider" call either:

- **throws/rejects** without being logged or caught, *or*
- **hangs indefinitely** without a timeout

and the health-monitor's follow-up ticks just observe `stopped` again and re-log `restarting` without completing. Unlike the documented recoverable network error path for `getUpdates` (`TypeError: fetch failed` / `Network request for 'getUpdates' failed!` which are retried), this restart-after-disconnect path has **no retry, no backoff, no error visibility**.

A likely location: `releaseLease` sets state to `stopped`, then `startProvider` is called, but something between those two — perhaps the provider start itself hitting the same transient network failure that triggered the health check — throws without being caught, leaving the state as `stopped` permanently.

## Ask

1. Is this a known issue / fixed in a newer release?
2. Could the restart-after-`released stopped` path get the same retry/backoff treatment as the `getUpdates` network error path?
3. Could a failed/hung restart attempt log an **explicit, searchable error** (not just the periodic `health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)`)?
4. Is there a lighter-weight way to restart just the Telegram channel/provider via CLI? (`openclaw channels` only has add/capabilities/list/login/logout/logs/remove/resolve/status — no restart.)

## Workaround

We've deployed an external watchdog that detects "`released stopped` without `starting provider` within 3 minutes" and force-restarts the gateway via `launchctl kickstart`. It works but is a heavy hammer for a single-channel state bug. Script available if useful.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Automatic WhatsApp replies produced through the Codex runtime can appear as one bubble where an OpenClaw-runtime A/B produced multiple bubbles. The difference is real, but current source and shipped behavior do not expose first-class paragraph boundaries from Codex and intentionally pack adjacent paragraphs in the shared outbound planner.

This needs an explicit product decision about paragraph-to-message semantics, not a Codex-projector or WhatsApp-only repair.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure automatic visible replies and WhatsApp block streaming with `chunkMode: "newline"` and coalescing limits that do not join already separate chunks.
2. Configure `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` with `agentRuntime.id: "codex"`.
3. Through a real inbound WhatsApp turn, have the agent return two short paragraphs separated by a blank line.
4. Observe that both parts can arrive in one WhatsApp bubble.
5. Change only the model runtime to `agentRuntime.id: "openclaw"`.
6. Repeat through the same real WhatsApp path and compare outbound message IDs and bubbles.

The reported A/B produced one bubble with Codex and separate bubbles with OpenClaw. Codex reproduced both with and without live stream delivery.

### Expected behavior

Product decision required:

- Keep the current shared contract, where adjacent paragraphs may be packed into one send up to the channel limit; or
- Define a new typed preserve-paragraph-sends policy that applies consistently across runtimes and channels.

The earlier expectation that Codex should preserve upstream logical paragraph blocks is not supported by the upstream protocol: Codex exposes one accumulated text item plus deltas, not first-class paragraph boundaries.

### Actual behavior

Current shared planning in `src/auto-reply/chunk.ts` packs adjacent paragraphs up to the configured or channel limit. `src/infra/outbound/message-plan.ts` applies that planner to newline mode. Existing tests require one send for short adjacent paragraphs.

The reply coalescer can join streamed block chunks, but it cannot split one final payload after paragraph packing.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.2-beta.1; current main checked at `318807a96965e6fbeafcb389ab22cabc7ff52067`

### Operating system

Linux 7.0.0-27-generic x86_64

### Install method

npm global

### Model

openai/gpt-5.6-sol

### Provider / routing chain

Failing observation: OpenClaw -> Codex agent runtime -> OpenAI -> WhatsApp Web provider

Working A/B observation: OpenClaw -> OpenClaw agent runtime -> OpenAI -> WhatsApp Web provider

### Additional provider/model setup details

The A/B changed only `agentRuntime.id`. `messages.visibleReplies` remained `automatic`, and the WhatsApp streaming configuration remained the same. Live stream delivery was not the differentiating setting.

### Logs

```shell
Codex runtime:
assistant reply contains two short paragraphs
WhatsApp result: one automatic visible bubble

OpenClaw runtime, same channel settings:
one inbound run
multiple automatic outbound text deliveries
distinct outbound WhatsApp message IDs
```

Fresh redacted current-main A/B with exact prompt, output, timestamps, and outbound IDs: `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

- The original run used a real WhatsApp Web inbound path and showed distinct outbound IDs after changing only the runtime.
- Current main intentionally packs adjacent paragraphs in the shared newline planner.
- That packing behavior was introduced by #68844 / `73a69d9e64cb3dd6fbf8e5b75cab3ee3be0bca14` and is present in 2026.7.2-beta.1.
- Direct upstream Codex source check at current `95637f7056835fea66bdd0044414af480fc0fd74` confirms `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs` exposes one `AgentMessage.text` and concatenates all text entries. `AgentMessageDeltaNotification` carries one `itemId` plus a string delta. The protocol exposes no paragraph/block boundary.
- OpenClaw's Codex projector therefore cannot preserve a boundary upstream does not expose. Splitting on blank lines would be a heuristic and should not bypass shared channel policy.

### Impact and severity

Affected: users who expect one WhatsApp bubble per paragraph when using automatic replies.

Severity: medium UX difference; content is delivered.

Frequency: reproduced in the reported runtime A/B, but a fresh current-main live A/B is not attached.

Consequence: conversational grouping can differ across runtimes.

### Additional information

- #109543 and #110203 proposed related repairs and closed unmerged.
- PR #110402 remains the active external fix candidate at `8e3700901e0507c70d43c300da5d4030705218b9`. GitHub currently reports it conflicting/dirty against main. It still has compatibility and message-delivery risk and needs the maintainer product decision before any conflict repair should define a new shared delivery contract.
- #43271 is different. #42667 and #68844 cover the inverse behavior: intentionally combining short adjacent chunks/paragraphs.
- No fix should live only in WhatsApp. No Codex-projector split should be added unless a typed boundary contract is deliberately introduced.
- A shared planner change is valid only after maintainers decide the global newline-to-message contract.

issues.body:
## Summary

Sending a message to a `claude-cli`-runtime agent via `sessions_send` (including over the `/tools/invoke` HTTP endpoint with `delivery.mode: "announce"`) causes the target session to process **2-3 turns per single dispatched message**, burning tokens and in one case exhausting a daily session limit with no new user content involved.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)
- Two independent Gateway instances (Windows, `claude-cli` runtime, `anthropic:claude-cli` OAuth auth profile), dispatched to from a third MainPC Gateway via `POST /tools/invoke` → `sessions_send`
- Target model: `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5`

## Reproduction

From MainPC, dispatch a single message to a remote agent's main session:

```
curl -X POST "https://<target-host>/tools/invoke" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tool":"sessions_send","args":{"message":"test","sessionKey":"agent:<agentId>:main"}}'
```

Response comes back `status: "ok"` with a `delivery: {"status":"pending","mode":"announce"}` field.

## Observed behavior (from the target session's own transcript)

For a single dispatched message, the target session receives:

1. `[Inter-session message] sourceSession=agent:<target>:main sourceTool=sessions_send ... "Agent-to-agent announce step."` — this looks like the delivery/announce completion signal being re-injected into the *same* session as a new inbound turn, rather than being a passive UI-only notification. It is consistently accompanied by:
   `OpenClaw resumed this CLI session after prompt content changed. Follow the current turn's instructions; changed=system-prompt.`
2. The actual dispatched message content, delivered as its own inter-session turn.
3. In roughly half of our repeated tests, **the same message content was delivered a second time**, again wrapped with the "resumed after prompt content changed" drift note — with no further config or system-prompt change made in between.

So a single logical "send one message" action costs 2 turns minimum (real message + announce-step echo) and sometimes 3 (message delivered twice).

## Suspected root cause

- `resolveCliSessionReuse` (`cli-session-*.js`) computes a `reuse-with-drift` state whenever `extraSystemPromptHash`/`promptToolNamesHash` differs from what's bound to the stored CLI session. For `claude-cli`-backed agents, `canTransportSystemPrompt(backend)` is false, so instead of transparently updating the system prompt, the runtime injects a `"OpenClaw resumed this CLI session after prompt content changed..."` user-context note and reprocesses the turn (`prepare.runtime-*.js`, `buildCliSessionDriftUserContext`).
- Because `extraSystemPromptHash` is a hash of `params.extraSystemPrompt`, which appears to be rebuilt per-turn with call-specific inter-session metadata (e.g. `sourceChannel` varying between `"unknown"` and `"webchat"` across dispatches in our logs), near-consecutive inter-session dispatches can each look like a "prompt change" even when no user-facing config changed — causing the drift/replay path to fire repeatedly.
- Separately, the `"announce step"` completion marker appears to be delivered as a first-class inbound inter-session message into the same session, which seems unintended — a delivery-status/completion signal shouldn't itself need a full agent turn.

## Impact

- One remote PC in our multi-Gateway setup hit its daily session limit purely from these amplified/duplicated turns, with the human user not sending any of the extra messages.
- Cost/latency roughly 2-3x per cross-Gateway dispatch, discouraging legitimate agent-to-agent coordination use cases.

## Suggested fix directions

1. Don't reprocess the `"Agent-to-agent announce step."` completion marker as a new inbound turn on the target session — it should be a passive/UI-only receipt, not something requiring a fresh CLI agent turn.
2. Make `extraSystemPromptHash` stable across dispatches that don't change actual system-prompt content — exclude per-call metadata unrelated to the system prompt (e.g. `sourceChannel`) from the hashed value, or hash only the true prompt bytes.
3. If drift really is intentional per inter-session dispatch, consider suppressing the duplicate full-message redelivery we observed in ~50% of repeated tests (message delivered twice back-to-back with the same content).

Happy to share full transcript excerpts/screenshots if useful.

issues.body:
## Summary

WhatsApp group messages never reach OpenClaw's inbound handling — `gateway.call health` never updates `lastInboundAt`/`messagesHandled` for group traffic, and `directory groups list --channel whatsapp` always returns `[]` — even though WhatsApp's own delivery receipts confirm the message reached the linked device. Direct messages (DMs) on the same account work perfectly and instantly. This reproduces across a fresh QR relink and across a full gateway + plugin version update.

## Environment

- OpenClaw gateway: upgraded during triage from 2026.6.11 → **2026.7.1**
- `@openclaw/whatsapp` plugin: upgraded from 2026.6.11 → **2026.7.1** (via `plugins install @openclaw/whatsapp --force`)
- Deployment: self-hosted, Docker Compose, prebuilt GHCR image
- WhatsApp account type: WhatsApp Business, linked via QR (companion/multi-device session, not the Cloud API)
- Multi-agent setup: a second agent (`household`) routed via a top-level `bindings[]` entry: `{type: "route", agentId: "household", match: {channel: "whatsapp", accountId: "ferdinand"}}`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Link a WhatsApp Business account via `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp --account <id>` (QR).
2. Confirm DM works: message the linked number directly — pairs via `dmPolicy: pairing`, replies correctly. `gateway call health` shows `lastInboundAt` populated, `messagesHandled` incrementing.
3. Add the linked number to a WhatsApp group as a normal member.
4. Send a message in that group.
5. Check `openclaw directory groups list --channel whatsapp --account <id> --limit 50 --json` → returns `[]`.
6. Check `gateway call health --json` for that account → `lastInboundAt: null`, unchanged.
7. On the sending phone, check the message's delivery info for the linked number specifically → shows delivered / read (double-grey then blue ticks), confirming WhatsApp did deliver it to that device.

## What was ruled out

- **`groupPolicy` setting**: tested all three values (`disabled`, `allowlist` with empty `groupAllowFrom`, and `open`/no filter at all). Same null result in every case — including fully `open`, which should bypass all filtering.
- **Stale/interrupted session state**: fully logged out (`channels logout`) and relinked from scratch via a fresh QR pairing. Same result on the new session.
- **Plugin/gateway version**: reproduced on both `2026.6.11` and, after updating, `2026.7.1` (gateway core) with the plugin explicitly reinstalled at `2026.7.1` too.
- **Config/binding mistake**: the account-level binding routes correctly for DMs (same account, same binding path), so the routing config itself is not the issue — it's specifically group-type messages that never arrive at the inbound handler.

## Hypothesis (unconfirmed)

WhatsApp's newer privacy feature addresses group participants via an LID (`@lid`) identity rather than the plain phone-number JID (`@s.whatsapp.net`) used for DMs. This account's self-identity has both (from `gateway call health`): `32456872514@s.whatsapp.net` and LID `33986831237279@lid`. Given DMs (JID-addressed) work perfectly and only group messages (which involve LID-based participant addressing) silently fail to register, a parsing/routing gap specific to LID-addressed group messages seems like the most likely root cause — though this wasn't confirmed against the plugin's source directly.

## Impact

WhatsApp group support is effectively non-functional for this setup — the provider reports healthy/connected the whole time, so there's no error surfaced anywhere; it just silently never sees group traffic.

issues.body:
### Summary

Adding `acp` config to `openclaw.json` while gateway is running triggers a
restart loop: gateway auto-enables acpx, detects the enable as a config change
requiring restart, then acpx fails to load after the self-triggered restart,
causing another detection and another restart.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start gateway (systemd service) with existing config that has no `acp` key
2. Add `"acp": {"enabled": true, "backend": "acpx", "defaultAgent": "claude"}`
3. Gateway detects ACP config, auto-enables acpx, logs "config change requires
   gateway restart (acp)"
4. After restart: "http server listening (13 plugins)" — acpx absent
5. Gateway detects ACP config again, triggers another restart
6. Loop continues

### Expected behavior

After one restart, gateway should load acpx (14 plugins) and stabilize. No
further restart should occur.

### Actual behavior

```
config change requires gateway restart (acp)
http server listening (14 plugins: acpx, ...)  ← first start ok
[restart]
http server listening (13 plugins: ...)  ← acpx gone after self-restart
ACP runtime configured, enabled automatically
config change requires gateway restart (acp)  ← detects again
[restart loop]
```

"embedded acpx runtime backend registered lazily" only appears in the first
startup, never after the self-triggered restart.

### Root cause (traced to source)

`src/config/plugin-auto-enable.shared.ts:446-458` —
`hasAcpxSetupAutoEnableRelevantConfig` returns true when `cfg.acp.enabled`.
`resolveRelevantSetupAutoEnablePluginIds:478` adds acpx to the auto-enable set.

`src/gateway/config-reload-plan.ts:403` — the auto-enable is treated as a
`kind: "restart"` change. Gateway self-restarts.

`extensions/acpx/register.runtime.ts:79-90` — acpx lazy registration depends
on the plugin `start()` lifecycle hook. After the config-reload-triggered
restart, this hook is not re-invoked, so `registerAcpRuntimeBackend` is never
called again. The acpx backend stays unregistered despite the auto-enable
detection succeeding.

### OpenClaw version

2026.6.11 (dev checkout, commit 1586910)

### Operating system

Linux RHEL 8, Node 24.13.1

### Install method

Source checkout, systemd service

### Model

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Provider / routing chain

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Impact and severity

Affected: Any user adding ACP config to a running gateway
Severity: High — ACP dispatch completely unavailable after first restart
Frequency: Reproduced on 6/6 restart attempts
Consequence: ACP cannot be used; gateway enters restart loop requiring manual
intervention (remove acp config, stop gateway, restart)

### Additional information

Workaround: stop gateway before adding acp config, then start fresh. The first
startup loads acpx correctly (14 plugins). Avoid triggering config reload while
gateway is running with ACP enabled.

issues.body:
After updating from OpenClaw 2026.6.11 to 2026.7.1 on macOS, my managed/user-space install under ~/.openclaw failed because parts of the install still pointed at the old embedded Node runtime.

Environment:
macOS
Managed install under ~/.openclaw
Previous OpenClaw: 2026.6.11
Updated OpenClaw: 2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)
Old embedded Node: ~/.openclaw/tools/node-v22.22.0
New embedded Node after repair: ~/.openclaw/tools/node-v24.15.0

What happened:
`openclaw update` installed 2026.7.1 but failed doctor because OpenClaw now requires Node >=22.22.3, while the managed runtime was still v22.22.0.
Re-running `install-cli.sh` with `--node-version 24.15.0` installed the new runtime and OpenClaw package.
My shell still found the old binary first because ~/.zprofile had a hardcoded old path:`export PATH="$HOME/.openclaw/tools/node-v22.22.0/bin:$PATH"`
After fixing PATH, gateway startup still failed due to startup migration blockers.
Gateway startup then failed because the WhatsApp plugin peer link still pointed to the old Node 22 OpenClaw package.

Relevant error:

Plugin "whatsapp" failed post-core payload smoke check (missing-openclaw-peer-link): Plugin declares peerDependency "openclaw" but peer link audit failed: /Users/attila/.openclaw/extensions/whatsapp/node_modules/openclaw points to /Users/attila/.openclaw/tools/node-v22.22.0/lib/node_modules/openclaw instead of /Users/attila/.openclaw/tools/node-v24.15.0/lib/node_modules/openclaw. Run `openclaw update repair` to retry plugin repair.

Recovery steps that worked:

`curl -fsSL --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 https://openclaw.ai/install-cli.sh | bash -s -- --prefix "$HOME/.openclaw" --version latest --node-version 24.15.0`
`# remove old node-v22.22.0 PATH entry from ~/.zprofile
source ~/.zprofile

openclaw doctor --fix --allow-exec
openclaw update repair
openclaw gateway restart`


Expected behavior:
The update or recovery path should update all managed references from the old embedded Node/OpenClaw package root to the new one, including plugin peer links, or automatically run/surface `openclaw update repair` as part of the failed update recovery.

Actual behavior:
The update partially succeeded but left stale references to node-v22.22.0 in shell/plugin state, causing the CLI and gateway to fail until PATH and plugin peer links were repaired manually.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

An IRC account whose login becomes **non-recoverable** on reconnect (bad server password `464`, banned `465`, erroneous nick `432` — already classified fatal in `extensions/irc/src/client.ts`) makes the IRC monitor retry **every 1000 ms forever** with no error classification, no attempt cap, and no backoff, while the gateway keeps reporting the account as `running` / healthy. The operator gets no signal that the channel is permanently stuck.

### Steps to reproduce

Grounded in current source (`upstream/main` @ `dabc40d42c`); no live IRC capture — see Logs.

1. Configure a `channels.irc` account that connects successfully (valid nick + credentials). Start the gateway; it reaches `001` and logs `connected to <host> ... as <nick>` (`extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:191`).
2. Make the login fatal for subsequent reconnects, then drop the live connection: e.g. the server bans the nick/host (`465`) or applies a K-line, or the server password is rotated so the next `PASS` yields `464`; then the server closes the socket (or a network blip closes it).
3. The socket `close` event fires with `ready === true`, so `client.ts` invokes `onDisconnect` (`extensions/irc/src/client.ts:431-440`), and the monitor's `onDisconnect` calls `scheduleReconnect()` (`extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:116-124`).
4. 1000 ms later `connect()` runs again; `connectIrcClient` now rejects with the fatal `464`/`465`/`432` before `001` (`extensions/irc/src/client.ts:339-343`). The `.catch` in `scheduleReconnect` logs `IRC reconnect failed: ...` and calls `scheduleReconnect()` again (`extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:84-90`) — an unbounded 1/second retry with no classification, cap, or backoff (`IRC_MONITOR_RECONNECT_DELAY_MS = 1000`, `extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:23`).
5. Run channel status (CLI `/status` / `channels status`): the IRC account still shows `running: true` / healthy.

### Expected behavior

- A non-recoverable login error (`464`/`465`/`432`, already treated as fatal in `client.ts`) should stop the retry loop or apply a capped backoff rather than reconnect every 1 s indefinitely.
- On disconnect/failure the account's status should reflect `connected: false` + the error, consistent with the other channels: `whatsapp`/`discord`/`slack`/`feishu`/`mattermost` all push `connected: false` + `lastError` on disconnect (e.g. `extensions/whatsapp/src/login-qr.ts` pushes `connected: false` on login end/failure). IRC's `statusSink` type only carries `lastInboundAt`/`lastOutboundAt` (`extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:19`) and is never called with a disconnect signal.
- Gateway/CLI status should not report the account as healthy while it is stuck in a fatal-retry loop.

### Actual behavior

- `extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts`: `monitorIrcProvider` awaits the first `connect()` then returns a `{ stop }` handle; `runStoppablePassiveMonitor` → `runPassiveAccountLifecycle` (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-lifecycle.core.ts`) then `await waitUntilAbort(...)` and never re-derives health.
- `scheduleReconnect()` (monitor.ts:78-93) uses a fixed `IRC_MONITOR_RECONNECT_DELAY_MS = 1000` from both the `onDisconnect` path and the `void connect().catch(...)` path — no error classification, no cap, no backoff.
- `IrcMonitorOptions.statusSink` is typed as `{ lastInboundAt?; lastOutboundAt? }` only (monitor.ts:19); it is never invoked with `connected: false` / `lastError` on disconnect.
- `src/gateway/server-channels.ts` sets `running: true` once at task start (server-channels.ts:630) and never re-derives it from IRC connection health; `src/channels/status/read-model.ts:95` reports the account healthy when `account.running === true`. So the account reads healthy for the entire duration of the fatal-retry loop.

### OpenClaw version

`upstream/main` @ `dabc40d42c` (2026-07-07)

### Operating system

Any — IRC channel runtime; not OS-specific.

### Install method

Source checkout (`upstream/main`).

### Model

N/A — channel connection-lifecycle bug; reproduces regardless of model/provider (not on the model request path).

### Provider / routing chain

N/A — IRC channel transport; independent of provider/model routing.

### Logs

```shell
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO — no captured live IRC log in this report. Reproducing the fatal
reconnect loop requires a live IRC server that returns 464/465/432 on reconnect
(e.g. a ban/K-line or rotated server password), which was not available. The
report is grounded in static file:line evidence at upstream/main @ dabc40d42c:
  - extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:23,78-93,116-124 (fixed-1000ms scheduleReconnect loop)
  - extensions/irc/src/client.ts:13,339-343,431-440 (fatal 464/465/432 classification; onDisconnect only when ready)
  - extensions/irc/src/monitor.ts:19 (statusSink cannot carry connected:false)
  - src/gateway/server-channels.ts:630 and src/channels/status/read-model.ts:95 (running:true set once → healthy forever)
```

### Impact and severity

- Affected: operators running an IRC channel account that becomes non-recoverable while live (nick/host banned, K-line, rotated server password) or that drops and cannot re-authenticate.
- Severity: Medium. Silent permanent outage on the affected account, with a status surface that reports healthy while the channel is dead, plus ~1 log line/second of reconnect spam.
- Frequency: deterministic once the reconnect login is fatal; the loop never self-terminates.
- Consequence: missed inbound/outbound on that IRC account with no operator-visible signal (status lies), and continuous log noise. Same "reports healthy while actually dead" class as the qqbot (#100127) / twitch (#100343) status fixes, in a channel those PRs did not cover.

### Additional information

**Scope note (path distinction, grounded):** a login that is fatal from the very first `connect()` propagates *out* of `monitorIrcProvider` via `runPassiveAccountLifecycle` (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-lifecycle.core.ts`) to the gateway's generic account lifecycle — it does not enter this internal loop. The fixed-1000ms `scheduleReconnect` loop described here is specifically the **post-successful-connection reconnect** path (`onDisconnect` → `scheduleReconnect`).

**Why filed as an issue rather than a PR:** the core fix turns on a maintainer product decision (below), and a real fix could span `monitor.ts` (classification + backoff), `client.ts` (fatal-code surfacing), the `statusSink` contract, and `server-channels.ts` health derivation. `monitor.ts` was just changed by #100799 (merged 2026-07-06, the *opposite* "stays disconnected after socket close" bug), raising regression sensitivity. Filing for a policy call before a blind PR.

**Open questions for maintainers (decision points):**
1. On a fatal login (`464`/`465`/`432`), should the account **give up permanently** (mark failed) or **keep retrying** (operator may fix server-side) but with capped backoff + honest status?
2. Should IRC's `statusSink`/status be widened to carry `connected: false` + `lastError` on disconnect (mirroring other channels), and should `server-channels.ts` re-derive `running` from IRC connection health?
3. If backoff is preferred over give-up, what cap/policy — matching which existing channel?

**Least-controversial first slice (if a narrow PR is wanted regardless of the give-up decision):** replace the fixed 1000 ms reconnect with capped exponential backoff **and** surface `connected: false` + error on disconnect/failure (status honesty only, no permanent give-up). That slice is defensible without settling question 1.

### Summary / Problem Statement
In `src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts`, `writeFile` pipes the complete input Buffer directly as `stdin` into `runCheckedCommand`. For large assets (e.g., binaries or model weights), this duplicates the memory buffer and violates Node's `exec` payload limits, triggering Out-of-Memory crashes.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Vulnerable Code Location:** [src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts#L111)
- **Mechanics:**
  ```typescript
  const result = await runCheckedCommand("sh", [], { stdin: params.data }); // Huge buffer copied to stdin string
  ```

### Impact Analysis
- Process instability: large file uploads inside the sandbox crash the host gateway manager.
- Out-of-memory crashes on resource-constrained host machines.

### Proposed Solution
1. Stream large file payloads in chunks to the sandbox filesystem wrapper instead of passing the entire buffer via stdin.
2. Enforce a maximum file size write limit for direct buffer operations.

### Affected File References
- [fs-bridge.ts:L100-L120](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts#L100-L120)

issues.body:
## Summary

OpenClaw's thinking/effort ladder is `off, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max`. When a
requested level exceeds what the resolved model/provider actually supports, OpenClaw silently
substitutes the nearest supported level. The substitution is correct (providers genuinely have
different effort ceilings), but it happens with **no warning, log, or field in any result**, so
the caller cannot tell that the effort they requested was reduced. This makes it hard to align
expectations, especially for `xhigh` and `max`, which behave very differently per family.

## Where the silent substitution happens

All of these are pure return values with no diagnostic at the call site:

- `clampThinkingLevel` — nearest-supported-level substitution (walks the ladder).
- `clampReasoning` / `clampReasoningLevel` — `xhigh -> high` (and `max -> high`).
- Anthropic effort fallback — `xhigh -> high` unless the model natively supports xhigh;
  `max -> high` unless the model natively supports max.
- OpenAI request builders — `max` is rewritten to `xhigh` before the request; `xhigh` then
  survives only on the newest reasoning models and otherwise clamps to `high`.
- Generic OpenAI-compatible / custom providers — same `max -> xhigh` rewrite, then clamp to
  `high` (or the reasoning param is dropped entirely if the model is not flagged
  reasoning-capable).

## Observed expectation gaps (per family)

- `max` is honored natively only on the Claude reasoning models that gate it. On OpenAI it is
  never sent as "max" (rewritten to `xhigh`, then often clamped to `high`); on DeepSeek reasoning
  is effectively binary (enabled/disabled) so `max` is advisory only; on generic providers it
  clamps unless the catalog row declares xhigh/max.
- `xhigh` is honored only on the newest reasoning models per family and clamps to `high`
  elsewhere.

None of these emit a signal, so a user who sets `max` and a user who sets `high` can end up with
identical requests and no way to know.

## Suggested improvement

Emit a one-time (or debug-level) warning / include an `effortApplied` (vs `effortRequested`)
field wherever a level is clamped or rewritten, so callers can see when the effective effort
differs from what they asked for. This does not change routing behavior, only observability.
The interactive `/think` path already surfaces "using X (Y not supported)"; the same signal is
missing on the programmatic/agent-turn and spawn paths.

---
_Reported from OpenClaw 2026.6.11. Behavior confirmed by source reading; generic, no private infrastructure details._

issues.body:
## Summary

When a parent agent session on Telegram spawns subagents, the subagent **completion announces** and **subagent status lists** are delivered to the Telegram chat, but they are never recorded/mirrored into the parent session's Control UI chat transcript — not live, and not after reopening the session or refreshing the UI. The dashboard transcript therefore cannot reconstruct what the user was actually told in the channel.

This is the announce-specific slice of the broader cross-surface mismatch reported in #104544 (I posted the full live repro there). It is also distinct from #83494 (message(action=send) rendered only as toolCall/toolResult blocks): in that issue the outbound text at least exists in the transcript as a tool block; here the announce/status deliveries are absent from the parent transcript entirely.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.7.1-beta.5`
- Channel: Telegram direct chat
- Surface: Control UI (macOS app) chat transcript for the parent session
- Observed: 2026-07-12, ~18:05–18:15 local time

## Steps to reproduce

1. Telegram DM session with a main agent; have it spawn subagents (`sessions_spawn`) for a longer task.
2. Let at least one subagent complete so its completion announce is delivered to the Telegram chat.
3. Have the subagent status list ("active subagents / recent subagents (last 30m)") delivered to the chat as well.
4. Open the same session in the Control UI and compare the transcript with the Telegram chat.

## Actual behavior

Telegram received three bot messages:

1. `18:06` — an assistant text message (end of the parent turn's explanation).
2. `18:08` — the subagent status list ("**active subagents:** … **recent subagents (last 30m):** …", 5 entries with model/tokens/status).
3. `18:11` — a subagent completion announce ("Review completed: `tmp/scan-cli-repair-review.md`. Merge verdict: **DO NOT MERGE**. Key blockers: …").

The Control UI transcript for the same (selected, live) session ends at `18:05` with the parent turn's Activity/tool blocks (`sessions_spawn`, several Read/Exec tool outputs, and a `Yield` block). None of the three channel deliveries appear.

Reopening the session and refreshing the UI does **not** make them appear, so this is not the pagination/hydration gap from #104543 — the messages seem to never be part of the parent session's `chat.history` at all.

## Expected behavior

Channel deliveries that originate from the session's own orchestration (subagent completion announces, subagent status lists) should be mirrored into the parent session transcript — or at least be visible somewhere in the Control UI timeline — tagged with their origin (e.g. "announce from subagent X"), so the dashboard matches what the channel user actually saw.

## Why this matters

For orchestration-heavy sessions the user-visible outcome is often *only* delivered via announce. An operator auditing the session from the Control UI sees the parent's internal yield but none of the messages the user actually received, which reads like lost state and makes incident review / verification of channel behavior impossible from the dashboard.

## Related

- #104544 — Telegram and Control UI can show different final content (full live repro of the same window posted there)
- #83494 — Control UI renders message(action=send) visible replies only as toolCall/toolResult blocks
- #104543 — Control UI chat transcript ignores chat.history pagination (ruled out for this report: refresh doesn't restore the messages)


## Screenshots (cropped for privacy)

**Control UI transcript for the session (selected, live) — ends at 18:05 with the parent turn's Activity/tool blocks incl. the `Yield`; none of the three delivered messages are rendered (unchanged after reopening the session / refreshing the UI):**

![Control UI transcript ending at 18:05](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/aaajiao/27c401b3311338a5e1539fc512007967/raw/354f5b5cebec8b87566cdf767bbded732e51536b/control-ui-transcript.png)

**What Telegram actually received in the same window — 18:06 assistant text, 18:08 subagent status list, 18:11 completion announce:**

![Telegram deliveries at 18:06, 18:08 and 18:11](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/aaajiao/27c401b3311338a5e1539fc512007967/raw/354f5b5cebec8b87566cdf767bbded732e51536b/telegram-received.png)

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The native Codex parent-local inference relay rejects an image-heavy request above its 32 MiB decoded-body limit, but converts the deterministic size error into a generic HTTP 502; Codex and OpenClaw repeatedly retry the oversized conversation before the agent fails without a model reply.

### Steps to reproduce

Two evidence levels are available: an observed real-provider conversation failure and an executed, isolated reproduction of the installed decoder boundary. No private conversation payload is attached.

**Observed conversation path:**

1. Use OpenClaw 2026.9.9 with `@openclaw/codex` 2026.9.9, managed Codex 0.160.0, ChatGPT OAuth, and `openai/gpt-6-astra` through the native Codex app-server.
2. The affected native conversation accumulated eight inline PNG data URLs in four `exec` tool-result records.
3. Continue that conversation. Codex logs a request of **33,599,844 uncompressed bytes** and approximately **20,639,399 compressed bytes**, then receives the local relay's generic 502. Further attempts keep replaying oversized requests.
4. OpenClaw logs three same-model retries, exhausts its transient retry window, and surfaces the final transport error. This agent has no configured model fallbacks.

The image-producing workflow itself is not included as a portable reproduction. The following boundary reproduction is deterministic and was executed against the installed dispatch implementation:

```sh
node --input-type=module -e '
import { readdirSync } from "node:fs";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";
import { zstdCompressSync } from "node:zlib";
const dir = process.env.HOME + "/.openclaw/extensions/codex/dist/.setup/";
const file = readdirSync(dir).find(name => /^inference-dispatch-.*\.mjs$/.test(name));
if (!file) throw new Error("Installed Codex inference-dispatch module not found");
const { createCodexInferenceDispatch } = await import(pathToFileURL(dir + file).href);
const dispatch = createCodexInferenceDispatch({ context: {}, assertCurrent() {} });
for (const size of [33554432, 33599844]) {
  const wire = zstdCompressSync(Buffer.alloc(size, 32));
  const req = {
    headers: { "content-encoding": "zstd" },
    async *[Symbol.asyncIterator]() { yield wire; }
  };
  try {
    const upload = await dispatch.prepareHttp(
      req, false, "/responses", new AbortController().signal, () => {}
    );
    upload.settle();
    upload.releaseModelExecution();
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ decodedBytes: size, compressedBytes: wire.length, result: "accepted" }));
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ decodedBytes: size, compressedBytes: wire.length, result: "rejected", code: error.code, message: error.message }));
  }
}'
```

This intentionally bypasses sampling/authorization preparation to isolate the actual decoder. It uses synthetic bytes, sends nothing upstream, and does **not** claim to reproduce a full provider turn. The `prepareHttp` signature above is for the installed 2026.9.9 build; current main has a different signature.

Observed output:

```json
{"decodedBytes":33554432,"compressedBytes":1043,"result":"accepted"}
{"decodedBytes":33599844,"compressedBytes":1047,"result":"rejected","code":"ERR_BUFFER_TOO_LARGE","message":"Cannot create a Buffer larger than 33554432 bytes"}
```

### Expected behavior

Keep bounded request admission, but identify an oversized decoded request as a deterministic size failure rather than a transient connection failure. Surface an actionable size-specific error without repeatedly resending the same oversized history. Do not silently discard conversation content or unconditionally remove the memory bound.

Known-good controls: the installed decoder accepts exactly 33,554,432 bytes; a fresh one-shot Gateway request with the same agent credentials and `openai/gpt-6-astra` returns the requested `OPENCLAW_TRANSPORT_OK` marker successfully.

### Actual behavior

The compressed request is below 32 MiB, but its decoded body is **45,412 bytes over** the limit. zstd decompression throws `ERR_BUFFER_TOO_LARGE` before forwarding. The HTTP proxy catches the local exception and returns the same sanitized 502 used for transient transport failures. Native Codex retries internally; OpenClaw subsequently retries the model turn as `server_error`.

The affected run terminates after about **147 seconds**, with three outer retries and no model reply. A fresh connection cannot make this unchanged oversized body fit.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.9 (bcfc888); `@openclaw/codex` 2026.9.9; managed `@openai/codex` 0.160.0.

### Operating system

Linux 7.2.9-1-cachyos, x64; Node v26.8.2.

### Install method

npm global OpenClaw, installed Codex plugin.

### Model

openai/gpt-6-astra

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw Gateway -> native Codex app-server (stdio) -> private loopback parent-local inference relay -> ChatGPT/Codex backend.

### Additional provider/model setup details

ChatGPT OAuth. Agent primary explicitly selects `openai/gpt-6-astra` with no agent-specific fallbacks. Credentials are usable, and a fresh same-model request succeeds.

The last successful inference reported 85,638 input tokens; the native effective context window at failure was 258,400 tokens. Rejected requests have no provider-reported token count because they fail locally. The measured violation is the relay's **byte** limit, not a demonstrated token-context overflow. No compaction records were found in the affected native conversation.

### Logs

Sanitized Gateway excerpts, October 11, 2026, UTC:

```text
01:09:10 [agent/embedded] transient same-model retry 1/8 for openai/gpt-6-astra reason=server_error: delayMs=599
01:09:42 [agent/embedded] transient same-model retry 2/8 for openai/gpt-6-astra reason=server_error: delayMs=1239
01:10:16 [agent/embedded] transient same-model retry 3/8 for openai/gpt-6-astra reason=server_error: delayMs=4447
01:10:52 [agent/embedded] transient retry window elapsed for openai/gpt-6-astra after 3/8 retries; stopping same-model retries
01:10:52 Embedded agent failed before reply: unexpected status 502 Bad Gateway: Codex parent-local inference transport failed; retry on a fresh connection., url: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<redacted>/backend-api/codex/responses
```

Native Codex request log fields:

```text
Compressed request body with zstd pre_compression_bytes=33599844 post_compression_bytes=20639399
Request completed method=POST url=http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<redacted>/backend-api/codex/responses status=502 Bad Gateway
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Only sizes/types were inspected for the large tool results; no image or transcript content is included:

| Measurement | Bytes |
| --- | ---: |
| Relay decoded-body limit | 33,554,432 |
| Initial failed request before compression | 33,599,844 |
| Amount over the limit | 45,412 |
| Eight inline PNG data URLs in native history | 33,247,720 |

Inline image data is 98.95% of the initial failed request size.

**Latest-release and current-main source inspection:**

The latest GitHub release checked was [v2026.10.1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/releases/tag/v2026.10.1), published October 10. This is a source comparison, **not** a claim that the newer release was installed or the full conversation reproduced on it.

- [v2026.10.1 inference-upload.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.10.1/extensions/codex/src/app-server/inference-upload.ts#L4): `MAX_BODY_BYTES = 32 * 1024 * 1024`.
- [v2026.10.1 inference-dispatch.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.10.1/extensions/codex/src/app-server/inference-dispatch.ts): zstd decoding uses `maxOutputLength: MAX_BODY_BYTES`; rewritten payloads are bounded too.
- [v2026.10.1 inference-proxy.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.10.1/extensions/codex/src/app-server/inference-proxy.ts): non-authorization local exceptions before response headers become a generic 502.
- Current main was also inspected and retains these bounds and error mapping. The checked main revision was [6b13e9e4142d](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/6b13e9e4142d02427949b5ffbb10db574997686e).

### Impact and severity

Affected: one observed native Codex-backed Telegram conversation with large inline tool images.

Severity: blocks model replies in that conversation. The Gateway remains running and fresh same-model requests succeed.

Frequency: four failed runs across October 10-11 have the same terminal relay error; retained request-size logs confirm oversized bodies for the latest two. The decoder rejects the measured above-limit body deterministically.

Consequence: futile native and outer retries, about 147 seconds of delay on the quoted run, and terminal failure without a model reply. No data loss or additional billing impact is established.

### Additional information

This is distinct from these related items:

- [#150940](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/150940): image-heavy native history and storage-retention gap; related, but not this decoded relay limit and retry classification.
- [#125308](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/125308): long-session byte-budget and compaction recovery problems; related, but not this exact decoder boundary.
- [#142823](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/142823): merged omitted-`instructions` fix for Responses Lite requests. The same public 502 string can represent different causes; the installed build already accepts omitted instructions.
- [#155987](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/155987): merged request-byte reuse optimization explicitly preserves the 32 MiB body limit.

Last known good/first known bad release: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO. This report does not establish a regression.

Temporary operational workaround: start a fresh conversation and carry forward text rather than the old inline images. Only the fresh same-model inference control was exercised; resetting the affected production conversation was not performed.

A useful repair would preserve memory/admission bounds while distinguishing decoded-size failures from transient transport failures, and define a supported path for oversized image-bearing replay context. No production code was patched during this investigation.

issues.body:
## Summary

Allow an OpenClaw agent to safely change, validate, and repair its own LLM provider configuration without becoming unusable when the new configuration is invalid.

## Problem to solve

I use multiple LLM providers and switch between them depending on workload, availability, cost, rate limits, and model capabilities.

I asked my OpenClaw agent to configure itself to use a different LLM provider with a different API credential. The agent made an error while updating its configuration. After the invalid configuration was applied, the agent could no longer use the intended model correctly.

At that point, OpenClaw’s security restrictions also prevented the agent from correcting the configuration it had just modified. This creates a recovery deadlock: the agent is authorized to initiate a provider change, but if that change is incorrect, it may lose the ability to diagnose or repair the resulting configuration.

The current behavior makes agent-managed LLM configuration risky. A small mistake in a provider name, model identifier, endpoint, credential reference, or related setting can require manual intervention outside the agent. In some environments, the user may not have convenient access to the host or configuration files, so the agent can effectively lock itself out.

## Proposed solution

OpenClaw should provide a secure and recoverable workflow for agent-initiated LLM provider changes.

Before activating a new configuration, OpenClaw should validate its structure and perform a minimal connectivity test against the selected provider and model. The existing working configuration should remain active until the candidate configuration has passed validation.

Configuration changes should be transactional. OpenClaw should preserve the last known working configuration and automatically roll back when validation fails, authentication is rejected, the configured model does not exist, the endpoint is unreachable, or the agent cannot successfully complete a basic inference request.

After applying a valid configuration, OpenClaw could use a short confirmation window. If the new provider becomes unusable during that window, the system should automatically restore the previous provider.

The agent should also have access to a narrowly scoped recovery operation that can inspect and repair only the LLM routing configuration it previously changed. This capability should not grant unrestricted access to security-sensitive settings. It should operate through a dedicated configuration API with schema validation, an audit trail, explicit secret handling, and clear permission boundaries.

API credentials should never be displayed back to the model or written into conversation history. The agent should work with secret references or credential identifiers, while the OpenClaw runtime securely stores and validates the underlying credentials.

A recovery command or safe mode would also be useful. It could restore the last known working provider, select a user-defined fallback provider, or temporarily start with a locally configured emergency model when the primary model configuration is broken.

## Alternatives considered

The current alternative is to manually edit OpenClaw’s configuration files or environment variables after a failed provider change. This works for users with direct access to the host, but it is inconvenient and may be impossible in remotely managed or automated deployments.

Another alternative is to prohibit agents from changing LLM configuration entirely. This reduces risk, but removes a valuable capability for users who intentionally operate several providers and need dynamic routing or provider migration.

Users can also maintain an external script that tests and replaces the configuration. However, this duplicates logic that OpenClaw is better positioned to handle because it already understands its configuration schema, provider adapters, security model, and runtime state.

## Impact

This affects users who operate OpenClaw with multiple LLM providers, frequently change models, rotate credentials, respond to provider outages, or optimize workloads according to cost and capacity.

The severity is high when an invalid change prevents the agent from starting or responding, because the normal conversational interface can no longer be used to recover.

The problem occurs whenever an agent-generated provider configuration contains an invalid value or when a provider accepts the configuration initially but fails during activation.

The practical consequences include service interruption, manual configuration repair, remote host access, longer recovery times, and reduced trust in agent-managed configuration.

A safe self-reconfiguration workflow would make multi-provider setups significantly more reliable and would allow OpenClaw agents to adapt to provider availability without risking permanent lockout.

## Evidence/examples

A representative scenario is an installation with two providers, Provider A and Provider B. Provider A is currently working. The user asks the agent to switch to Provider B and supplies or selects a securely stored credential.

The agent writes an incorrect model identifier or provider setting. OpenClaw activates the invalid configuration immediately, and subsequent LLM requests fail. The agent is then unable to repair the configuration because it no longer has a functioning model connection or because security rules prevent it from modifying the affected settings.

The expected behavior is that OpenClaw validates Provider B before activation, keeps Provider A available during the transition, and automatically returns to Provider A if Provider B cannot complete a test request.

## Additional information

This feature should remain backward-compatible with existing provider configuration keys and should preserve OpenClaw’s security boundaries.

The goal is not to let the model freely modify arbitrary security settings. The goal is to offer a constrained, auditable, and reversible mechanism specifically for LLM provider and model configuration.

Useful implementation concepts may include staged configuration, schema validation, provider health checks, secret references, least-privilege configuration scopes, automatic rollback, a last-known-good snapshot, and an emergency fallback provider.

issues.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Android and Apple mobile implementations duplicate several deterministic
protocol and business-rule paths while the native UI and device integrations
must remain platform-owned. Existing near-duplicates already differ in edge
behavior, so an unplanned extraction risks a protocol regression.

## Proposed Solution

Create an evidence-backed, contract-first migration record before introducing
KMP. It defines the initial pure-logic boundary, a Swift-friendly SKIE plus
hand-written facade, ABI and Swift-parity gates, required Android/iOS proof,
and a per-PR net-negative production diff gate.

## Alternatives Considered

- Share mobile UI: rejected because platform-native UX and OS integrations are
  first-class requirements.
- Use Kotlin Swift Export as the production boundary: deferred because it is
  currently Alpha.
- Keep duplicate logic: rejected for deterministic protocol and business rules
  where a single source of truth has clear maintenance value.

## Impact

No runtime or UI behavior changes are proposed by the planning PR. The plan
gives maintainers a safe sequence for reducing future Android/iOS business-logic
duplication without exposing generated Kotlin APIs to Swift callers.

## Evidence

- Repository mapping found direct Talk directive and Bonjour parser overlap plus
  behavior differences that require characterization before extraction.
- Official Kotlin guidance supports incremental logic sharing while retaining
  native UI; Swift Export remains Alpha.
- Docs formatting, MDX, glossary, and link validation pass; autoreview reported
  no actionable findings.

issues.body:
## Consumer and failure mode

A backend transport bridge calls `chat.send` with a stable `idempotencyKey` and retries transient or retryable failures with that same key. If the original request finishes with a retryable error, the Gateway stores that result in its dedupe cache. A subsequent attempt receives the same stored error.

Without a wire-level replay signal, the client cannot distinguish the stored result from a fresh failure and continues retrying until its retry budget is exhausted. The required client decision is:

```ts
if (error.retryable && !error.replayed) {
  retryWithSameIdempotencyKey();
} else {
  surfaceError();
}
```

This is the concrete consumer contract that was missing from #98203 and #98206. The earlier live WebSocket proof established the transport gap, but #98206 was correctly closed because forwarding the entire internal `RespondFn` metadata record would expose diagnostic/plugin values and break strict clients.

## Proposed contract

- Add a client capability named `response-replay`.
- Clients advertising it may receive `meta: { replayed: true }` on an idempotent `chat.send` replay.
- Keep the metadata schema closed and JSON-only. No arbitrary values and no `runId`; method payloads remain the source for run identifiers.
- Keep responder log metadata and wire metadata as separate typed arguments.
- Do not send `meta` to clients that omit the capability, preserving strict older response-frame schemas.
- Have the official TypeScript Gateway client advertise the capability and surface `GatewayClientRequestError.replayed` so the contract has an in-tree consumer.

Example opted-in response:

```json
{
  "type": "res",
  "id": "request-id",
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "UNAVAILABLE",
    "message": "stored failure",
    "retryable": true
  },
  "meta": { "replayed": true }
}
```

## Non-goals

- Publishing the existing internal `RespondFn` metadata record.
- Exposing diagnostic `error`, `channel`, plugin metadata, or log-only `runId` values.
- Changing protocol version or sending additive fields without capability negotiation.
- Defining a general-purpose metadata bag before another concrete consumer exists.

## Acceptance evidence

- Strict schema accepts only `{ replayed: true }` and rejects legacy/arbitrary metadata.
- A client without `response-replay` receives the unchanged response envelope.
- An opted-in client receives only the typed replay object, even when log metadata contains additional fields.
- A cached `chat.send` response supplies replay metadata through the dedicated wire argument.
- The official TypeScript client advertises the capability and exposes `replayed: true` on request errors.

If this shape matches the intended protocol boundary, I have a tested draft implementation ready to link.

issues.body:
## Summary
Under conditions we can now reproduce in production roughly weekly, the agent's reply lane wedges: new *real* inbound WhatsApp messages are accepted by the gateway but never dispatched to an agent turn, while scheduled heartbeat polls continue to dispatch and return normally the whole time. The gateway reports healthy. Only a gateway restart recovers the lane.

## Environment
- OpenClaw gateway on macOS (Apple Silicon), WhatsApp channel via Baileys
- Agent backend: claude-cli (Max plan), primary model opus-class
- Heartbeat: 30-min scheduled poll, 08:00–23:00 IST

## Two observed incidents
1. **2026-07-02 22:46 IST → 2026-07-03 00:31 IST** — burst of back-to-back inbound messages hung the agent; only manual "send one message at a time" pacing worked around it.
2. **2026-07-09 09:40 → 13:37 IST** — 5 consecutive real inbound messages went unanswered for ~4 hours (including an explicit "whats happeneing ?" chase), while heartbeat polls dispatched and returned `HEARTBEAT_OK` normally throughout the same window. Session JSONL shows the inbound user events recorded with no corresponding agent turn started. `openclaw gateway restart` (pid 67352 → 87136) immediately recovered dispatch; the queued messages were then processed.

## What we ruled out
- **Model/auth:** direct model probe during the wedge returned OK in seconds; the same model produced crisp 15–40s replies earlier the same morning (08:29–08:54). claude-cli auth valid.
- **Gateway liveness:** `openclaw status` healthy; outbound sends (heartbeat replies, watchdog pings) flowed the entire time.
- **Burst-typing as sole trigger:** incident 2 was NOT a burst — messages arrived minutes-to-hours apart.

## Hypothesis
Looks like a dispatch-queue wedge specific to the inbound-user-message lane — work is queued but no run is ever started for it (`queued_work_without_active_run` class), while the scheduled-poll lane uses a path that keeps dispatching. Possibly a lost wakeup / stuck lease on the per-conversation run lock after an aborted or overlapping run.

## Impact
Highest-severity failure mode for a personal-assistant deployment: the agent looks alive (heartbeats, crons, outbound all fine) while silently ignoring the principal. Detection required building an external watchdog probe (real-inbound-age vs heartbeat-flow comparison over session JSONL).

## Asks
1. Dispatch-lane instrumentation: log an explicit error/event when an inbound user message sits queued >N min with no run started (silent starvation is currently invisible).
2. Self-heal or watchdog hook: expose lane health (last inbound dispatched vs last inbound received) so operators can probe it without parsing session files.
3. Root-cause the run-lock/wakeup path for the inbound lane under overlapping runs.

Happy to share sanitised session JSONL excerpts and watchdog probe code.

issues.body:
## Problem

OpenClaw currently has a hard boundary around some protected config paths when changes are initiated from inside an agent session. That boundary is good in spirit: an agent should not be able to silently or autonomously grant itself more authority.

But the current implementation creates a sovereignty problem for owner-operated deployments: even when the human owner explicitly asks and confirms in chat, the agent has no valid approval path for protected changes such as enabling the `/mcp` command or registering an MCP server. The only available outcomes are:

1. refuse the owner request, or
2. bypass the OpenClaw config tool by raw-editing `openclaw.json`, which normalizes exactly the wrong precedent.

That is the wrong tradeoff. The system should preserve the guardrail while giving the owner a first-class, auditable approval path.

## Concrete example

Goal: register a locally installed MCP server after auditing/smoke-testing it.

The owner tried to run:

```text
/mcp set agentic-aqua={"command":"/Users/senemaro/.local/bin/aqua-mcp","args":[]}
```

OpenClaw replied:

```text
⚠️ /mcp is disabled. Set commands.mcp=true to enable.
```

The agent inspected the schema and confirmed:

```text
commands.mcp: boolean
Allow /mcp chat command to manage OpenClaw MCP server config under mcp.servers (default: false).
```

Then the agent attempted the sanctioned config path:

```json
{"commands":{"mcp":true}}
```

Gateway refused:

```text
gateway config.patch cannot change protected config paths: commands.mcp
```

This left no legitimate agent-mediated owner approval flow. The owner explicitly authorized the change, but OpenClaw still forced the choice between human manual editing and agent-side bypass.

## Why this matters

This is not a request to let agents freely self-escalate.

It is the opposite: owner-approved escalation should be explicit, structured, logged, and harder to confuse with autonomous agent behavior.

Right now, the hard block makes the safe path unavailable. A capable owner can still edit the file directly, but then OpenClaw loses the chance to:

- show the exact diff before approval,
- require an explicit human confirmation gesture,
- restart/reload safely,
- record an audit trail,
- distinguish owner intent from agent initiative,
- apply extra checks for dangerous MCP servers or command flags.

For local-first/open-source deployments, sovereignty means the owner can authorize changes to their own machine without teaching the agent to step around the runtime boundary.

## Current implementation clue

The gateway tool appears to allow only a small allowlist of config paths for agent-side mutation and rejects others as protected.

Observed in the installed build:

```ts
const ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS = [
  "agents.defaults.systemPromptOverride",
  "agents.defaults.promptOverlays",
  "agents.defaults.model",
  "agents.defaults.thinkingDefault",
  "agents.defaults.subagents.thinking",
  "agents.defaults.reasoningDefault",
  "agents.defaults.fastModeDefault",
  "agents.list[].id",
  "agents.list[].systemPromptOverride",
  "agents.list[].model",
  "agents.list[].thinkingDefault",
  "agents.list[].subagents.thinking",
  "agents.list[].reasoningDefault",
  "agents.list[].fastModeDefault",
  "channels.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.*.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.*.*.*.requireMention",
  "messages.visibleReplies",
  "messages.groupChat.visibleReplies"
];
```

And:

```ts
if (disallowedPaths.length > 0) {
  throw new Error(`gateway ${params.action} cannot change protected config paths: ${disallowedPaths.join(", ")}`);
}
```

That hard error is the core UX/security problem: it treats all protected edits as impossible from the agent path, even with live owner confirmation.

## Proposed fix: owner-approved protected config changes

Add a first-class approval flow for protected config mutations instead of hard-failing immediately.

Suggested behavior:

1. Agent calls `gateway config.patch` or a new action such as `gateway config.propose`.
2. Gateway computes the exact changed paths and classifies risk:
   - normal allowlisted path → current behavior
   - protected path → requires owner approval
   - dangerous path/flag → requires stronger approval or remains blocked depending on policy
3. Gateway returns an approval card to the current human/operator surface showing:
   - exact config path(s), e.g. `commands.mcp`
   - old value and new value
   - full JSON patch/diff
   - risk label and explanation
   - whether restart is required
   - requesting agent/session identity
4. Human explicitly approves via the native approval UI or an owner-only command.
5. Gateway applies the change itself, writes an audit record, and restarts/hot-reloads as needed.

## Specific MCP handling

For MCP-related paths, add extra review fields:

- command path
- args
- environment variables/secrets referenced
- cwd
- whether command is absolute or PATH-resolved
- whether executable exists
- package provenance if known
- tool list if the server can be smoke-tested before enabling
- warning if tools include destructive/financial actions

Example approvals that should be possible:

```json
{"commands":{"mcp":true}}
```

and later:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "agentic-aqua": {
        "command": "/Users/senemaro/.local/bin/aqua-mcp",
        "args": []
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Safety requirements

This should not become a blanket escape hatch.

Recommended constraints:

- default deny for protected paths unless an explicit owner approval arrives;
- approvals expire quickly;
- approval must include exact patch hash/base config hash to prevent TOCTOU surprises;
- approval should be bound to the requesting session and patch contents;
- dangerous flags may require typed confirmation or config-level opt-in;
- all protected approvals should be logged in an audit trail;
- channel identity should matter: group chat confirmation should be treated differently from a local TUI or authenticated owner DM;
- optional config policy could disable this feature entirely for hosted/shared deployments.

## Why this is better than the current state

The current state is neither fully safe nor sovereign:

- It blocks legitimate owner-directed work through the sanctioned tool.
- It pressures users toward manual edits or alternate agents.
- It gives agents an incentive to consider raw file bypasses.
- It provides no structured diff, approval, or audit trail for the actual change.

A protected-edit approval flow would make the safe thing also the easy thing.

## Acceptance criteria

- An agent can propose a protected config change without applying it.
- The owner sees an exact diff and risk explanation.
- The owner can approve or deny through a first-class OpenClaw mechanism.
- Approved changes are applied by Gateway, not by raw agent file editing.
- The approval is logged with session/agent/path/old/new metadata.
- Existing hard-block behavior remains available via config policy for deployments that want it.
- The MCP registration flow works without requiring manual `openclaw.json` edits when owner approval is present.

issues.body:
## Summary

WhatsApp DM (and group) channels currently can't participate in the
`threadBindings.spawnSessions` feature shipped in 2026.5.x because the
framework requires native thread/topic primitives (Discord channels, Slack
threads, Telegram topics). WhatsApp exposes a thread-like proxy —
**reply-quote** — via `contextInfo.quotedMessage.stanzaId` on inbound
messages, which OpenClaw already extracts but doesn't currently use for
session routing. Proposing this be wired into the `threadBindings` flow so
a reply-quoted inbound routes to the session that originally sent the
quoted message.

## Motivation

Recurring crons that target non-main sessions (`isolated`, `current`, or
`session:<custom-id>`) can deliver outbound messages reliably via
`announce`, but user replies always land in `agent:<id>:main` per
WhatsApp DM routing. This breaks any pattern where a scheduled nudge and
the user's response need to share session context — daily standups,
recurring research workflows, scheduled reviews, debrief flows, etc.

The current workarounds are all unsatisfying:

- Use `sessionTarget: "main" + payload.kind: "systemEvent"` and rely on
  the cron-event prompt path. Fragile — payload-loss issues like #73189
  recur intermittently when the main session is busy / the cron-event
  prompt builder gets pre-empted by bare heartbeats.
- Use `isolated + announce` and have the agent's main session detect
  reply content via heuristics. Works for distinctive content shapes
  (e.g. pasted dumps) but fails on ambiguous replies ("ok here you go").
- Use `isolated + announce` plus an external state-marker file that
  main reads on every inbound. Works but couples cron and main via
  out-of-band state and isn't natively supported by the framework.

## Related

- #65300 (open) — *"ACP thread-bound replies missing threadId on
  non-native-thread channels"*. Describes the same root primitive gap.
- #13892 (open) — *"cron sessionTarget support for specific session
  keys"*. Adjacent (already partially landed via `session:<id>`
  sessionTarget values).
- #73189 (closed) and #75964 (closed) — illustrate the recurring-cron
  fragility on `main + systemEvent` that the proposed feature would
  obviate.

## Proposed design

Mirror the existing Discord `threadBindings` shape, using reply-quote as
the WhatsApp-equivalent of a thread.

### Storage

A persistent binding store (sqlite or JSON) keyed by outbound `stanzaId`:

```json5
{
  "<outbound stanzaId>": {
    sessionKey: "session:<id>",
    agentId: "<id>",
    accountId: "default",
    boundAt: <ms>,
    lastActiveAt: <ms>,
  },
  ...
}
```

Pruned periodically by `idleHours` (no activity since `lastActiveAt`)
and `maxAgeHours` (hard cap from `boundAt`).

### Outbound hook

When any session-originated outbound WhatsApp message is sent (the
existing `deliverWebReply` / outbound send path), record:

```ts
recordThreadBinding({
  stanzaId: sentMessage.id,
  sessionKey: ctx.sessionKey,
  agentId: ctx.agentId,
  accountId: ctx.accountId,
});
```

Single write per outbound. No-op when
`channels.whatsapp.threadBindings.spawnSessions === false`.

### Inbound hook

In the WhatsApp inbound processing path, before the existing
session-target resolution:

```ts
const quotedStanzaId = extractContextInfo(message)?.stanzaId;
if (quotedStanzaId && cfg.channels.whatsapp.threadBindings?.enabled) {
  const binding = await lookupThreadBinding(quotedStanzaId);
  if (binding && !isExpired(binding, cfg)) {
    overrideSessionKey(binding.sessionKey, binding.agentId);
    bumpLastActiveAt(binding);
  }
}
// else: existing DM routing (defaults to agent:<default>:main)
```

If the binding lookup fails (unknown stanzaId, expired, or session has
since been pruned by `cron.sessionRetention`), fall back to the current
default routing and log a structured note.

### Config schema

Mirror `channels.discord.threadBindings`:

```json5
"channels": {
  "whatsapp": {
    "threadBindings": {
      "enabled": true,
      "idleHours": 2,
      "maxAgeHours": 24,
      "spawnSessions": true,
      "defaultSpawnContext": "isolated"
    }
  }
}
```

### CLI

A small admin surface for visibility/cleanup:

```
openclaw channels whatsapp threadbindings list   [--account <id>]
openclaw channels whatsapp threadbindings clear  --stanza-id <id>
openclaw channels whatsapp threadbindings expire [--idle | --max-age]
```

## Tradeoffs

**The user has to use WhatsApp's reply-quote feature** for the routing
to fire. Replies typed without quoting fall through to default routing.
This is a real friction point but acceptable as a default because:

1. WhatsApp users on mobile already understand long-press → reply.
2. Non-quoted replies preserving today's behavior is a safer migration
   story than overriding routing on heuristics.
3. An optional follow-up enhancement could maintain an "active
   conversation window" so subsequent unquoted replies within
   `idleHours` continue to route to the bound session — equivalent to
   how Slack thread-mode behaves once a user has replied in-thread.
   Recommend shipping deterministic-only first, adding the activity
   window later if it's needed.

## Group chat scope

Same `stanzaId → sessionKey` mapping conceptually works in group chats,
but the routing fallback (which session is "main" for a group binding)
differs. Recommend shipping DM-only first and treating group support as
a follow-up.

## Edge cases

- **Self-quoting:** user quotes their own earlier message — no
  binding entry, fall through to default. Correct behavior.
- **Multi-message nudges:** cron sends N messages — each gets its own
  binding entry pointing at the same `sessionKey`. Replying to any of
  them routes correctly.
- **Pruned session:** binding lookup succeeds but the target session
  was pruned by `cron.sessionRetention`. Fall back to default routing
  and emit a structured warning (`thread-binding.session_missing`) for
  observability.
- **Idempotency:** same stanzaId recorded twice (e.g. via retry) →
  upsert; do not error.
- **Slash escape:** `/main` (or equivalent) forces the next inbound to
  bypass thread-binding and route to default, for "this isn't about
  that thread" recovery.

## Implementation estimate

Roughly mirrors the existing Discord thread-binding plumbing: storage
layer + outbound hook + inbound override + config schema + TTL sweep +
CLI. Probably ~200 LoC of new code, plus tests. Most of the routing
plumbing already exists for Discord and only needs WhatsApp-side
adapter wiring.
