milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
Phase 3: The Gateway. Separate the web surface from the agent core so the gateway is optional and can restart independently.

Source of truth: [#7432 - v0.9.0 gateway](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432#v090-gateway), including existing issues/PRs, missing work, sequencing, and acceptance evidence.

Deliverables: agree the full core IPC contract first; finish the supported local IPC server; ship standalone zeroclaw-gw; migrate vendor webhook behavior into channel plugins; and have Tauri package and manage both processes.

Completion requires a core artifact without web assets or HTTP server code, a working IPC-connected gateway, core/channel operation when the gateway is absent, and demonstrated two-process desktop lifecycle. Existing OIDC, principal-isolation, and ZeroRelay work must integrate with this boundary. WATI is already retired. Feature acceptance and normal review/CI/release holds still apply.

issues.body:
Related: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/10007

At reviewed commit `3df6e2db994e2d9c48af3741f4d88751060f3797`, the primary consolidation merge chooses `survivor.kind.clone().or_else(...)`. An existing typed `Preference` survivor therefore bypasses classification of the incoming update. The merge helper can append incoming content or replace a contained survivor with the longer incoming text while retaining that subtype. The atomic-fact merge also preserves a Preference survivor for incoming Fact content.

This survivor-first behavior exists at the comparison base. #10007 does not add an autonomous production consolidation caller: its current callers are channel orchestration and WebSocket chat, whose stored classifications are unchanged. It adds no Preference-based authorization decision. This existing metadata limitation can be addressed separately; no complete preference-provenance guarantee should be inferred for merged rows in the meantime.

Acceptance criteria:

- Define and enforce a merge rule that does not assign incoming autonomous or differently classified content human-preference provenance solely because the survivor is typed Preference. Rejecting an incompatible merge, preserving provenance per contribution, or conservatively classifying the composite are possible outcomes.
- Cover the primary Core and atomic-fact merge paths consistently, including an existing typed survivor and the untyped fallback.
- Add a persistence-level regression with typed memory enabled, `dedup_on_write = true`, merge action, a Preference survivor, and an autonomous incoming update. Check the final stored content and kind, including append and containing-text replacement cases; retain coverage for ordinary compatible merges.
- Ensure any downgrade diagnostic reports the classification actually selected for storage rather than assuming the incoming classifier ran.

The merged #10009 changes Conversation autosave and does not fix typed consolidation merges. #9048 is related broader memory-lifecycle work.

Routing: memory consolidation and memory storage maintainers.

issues.title: [Bug]: Core conflict supersede hides unrelated memories when recall has no vector scores (the default)
issues.body:
### Affected component

memory

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

With the default `embedding_provider = "none"`, `consolidate_turn` can soft-hide existing Core memories that are unrelated to the new Core update. `conflict::check_and_resolve_conflicts` marks every Core recall candidate scoring above `conflict_threshold` (default 0.85, documented in `schema.rs` as a "Cosine similarity threshold") and `consolidate_turn` then calls `supersede` (`conflict_supersede_enabled`, default on). Recall filters `superseded_by IS NULL`, so those rows disappear from injection and search.

When a recall returns no vector results (always, with no embedding provider), the candidate scores are keyword scores the threshold has no meaning for:
- `SqliteMemory::recall_scoped` normalizes FTS-only results with `normalize::bm25_to_unit`, which divides by the batch maximum, so the top hit always scores 1.0.
- The FTS query ORs every token (`fts5_search_scoped`), and `memories_fts` uses FTS5's default tokenizer with no stop-word list, so a single shared common word ("is", "to", "user") is a hit.
- When FTS finds nothing, recall falls back to `LIKE` substring matching and gives every hit `score: Some(1.0)`, so an update with no words in common can still supersede rows ("on" matches "ph**on**es" and "Timez**on**e").
- Before #8898 added the normalization, raw BM25 scores cleared 0.85 as well (1.27 and 1.11 in the first case below); the threshold has never been calibrated for keyword scores.

Whether unrelated rows are hidden depends on how the model words the turn's `history_entry`. `consolidate_turn` writes that Daily row before the conflict check, and the check's recall includes it. When it repeats the update's words it becomes the top hit and Core rows score below 0.85 relative to it; when it is worded differently, the best-matching Core rows score 1.0 and just below, and are hidden.

Default config, four unrelated filler Core facts plus "User's dog is named Pixel" and "User prefers Pixel phones", then one `consolidate_turn` with a scripted model reply:

| `history_entry` | `memory_update` | Rows superseded |
|---|---|---|
| "Gave advice on drawing sprites for a retro game." | "User is learning Pixel art techniques" | dog, phone |
| "Recommended some albums." | "User enjoys listening to jazz" | dog, phone |
| "Turn summary." | "Enjoys listening to jazz on weekends" | phone, filler_editor, filler_tz (all 1.0 via the `LIKE` fallback) |
| "The user asked for tips on learning pixel art techniques for a game." | "User is learning Pixel art techniques" | none |
| "Discussed the user's new job." | "User started a new job at Acme" | none |

Across 8 pairs with hand-written, realistic history entries, 2 superseded unrelated rows (both with a history entry sharing no words with the update) and 6 superseded nothing. That is a small sample, not a frequency estimate. The same check also runs for typed facts when `consolidation_extract_facts` is on. The existing supersede tests use `conflict_threshold: 0.01` ("Keyword-only scores vary with corpus statistics"), so the default threshold is never exercised on this path. Only `SqliteMemory` was tested.

### Expected behavior

An unrelated Core memory is never superseded, whatever the wording of the history entry. Conflict detection should require an absolute similarity signal rather than a batch-relative one. Possible fixes, in order of preference:
1. Skip conflict supersede when the recall has no vector scores, since keyword overlap is not a conflict signal. This also covers the `LIKE` fallback. The trade-off is that genuine conflicts are no longer resolved without embeddings.
2. Or compare candidates with an absolute measure when embeddings are off; `conflict::find_text_conflicts` (Jaccard similarity) already exists and is used by `dedup_gate`.
3. At minimum, document that `conflict_threshold` assumes embeddings and warn in `validate_memory_semantics` when supersede is on without them.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Add to `mod consolidate_turn_tests` in crates/zeroclaw-memory/src/consolidation.rs
# (uses the module's existing helpers), then:
#   cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory --lib supersedes_nothing
#
# async fn supersede_outcome(update: &str) -> Vec<(&'static str, Option<String>)> {
#     let tmp = TempDir::new().unwrap();
#     let memory = SqliteMemory::new("sqlite", tmp.path()).unwrap();
#     seed_filler_facts(&memory).await;
#     store_core_fact(&memory, "dog", "User's dog is named Pixel").await;
#     store_core_fact(&memory, "phone", "User prefers Pixel phones").await;
#     // update_reply scripts history_entry = "Turn summary."
#     let provider = ScriptedProvider::update_reply(update);
#     run(&provider, &memory, &MemoryConfig::default()).await.unwrap();
#     let conn = open_db(tmp.path());
#     ["dog", "phone", "filler_editor", "filler_tz", "filler_lang", "filler_ci"]
#         .into_iter()
#         .map(|key| (key, superseded_by(&conn, key)))
#         .filter(|(_, marker)| marker.is_some())
#         .collect()
# }
#
# #[tokio::test]
# async fn unrelated_update_sharing_one_word_supersedes_nothing() {
#     let hidden = supersede_outcome("User is learning Pixel art techniques").await;
#     assert!(hidden.is_empty(), "unrelated Core rows were superseded: {hidden:?}");
# }
# // ...same for "User enjoys listening to jazz" and
# // "Enjoys listening to jazz on weekends"
```

### Impact

Affected users: installs where recall has no vector scores (the default `embedding_provider = "none"`) with `auto_save` on (also the default).
Frequency: intermittent; it depends on the wording of each turn's history entry relative to existing Core rows (see the table).
Consequence: curated Core memories silently disappear from recall, replaced by the newest auto-extracted entry. The rows are soft-hidden, not deleted (`superseded_by` can be cleared), but nothing tells the user it happened. The supersede took effect with #8570, first released in v0.8.3; before that the conflict result was computed and discarded.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
test consolidation::consolidate_turn_tests::unrelated_update_sharing_only_user_supersedes_nothing ... FAILED
test consolidation::consolidate_turn_tests::unrelated_update_sharing_one_word_supersedes_nothing ... FAILED
test consolidation::consolidate_turn_tests::update_sharing_no_words_supersedes_nothing ... FAILED
...
unrelated Core rows were superseded: [("dog", Some("core_a0ee87c3-1b5e-4576-8310-c91eb08743a4")), ("phone", Some("core_a0ee87c3-1b5e-4576-8310-c91eb08743a4"))]
...
unrelated Core rows were superseded: [("dog", Some("core_cc192077-62c3-41d6-83d5-fb1ac475ad1a")), ("phone", Some("core_cc192077-62c3-41d6-83d5-fb1ac475ad1a"))]
...
unrelated Core rows were superseded: [("phone", Some("core_e0ca6d07-24d1-4ca7-8911-82142d90f7d3")), ("filler_editor", Some("core_e0ca6d07-24d1-4ca7-8911-82142d90f7d3")), ("filler_tz", Some("core_e0ca6d07-24d1-4ca7-8911-82142d90f7d3"))]
...
test result: FAILED. 6 passed; 3 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 545 filtered out; finished in 0.24s
```

### ZeroClaw version

master d03325172 (also reproduced at 2cc26119d^, before #8898)

### Rust version

rustc 1.98.0

### Operating system

Not OS-specific (tested on Linux x86_64)

### Regression?

Yes, it worked before

issues.body:
## Summary

Add an opt-in output format for shell-type cron jobs so a job can return raw stdout instead of always using the current `status=... / stdout: / stderr:` wrapper.

## Problem statement

Discussion #8395 reports that shell cron jobs always wrap command output like this:

```text
status=exit status: 0
stdout:
<actual output>
stderr:
```

That wrapper is useful for debugging, but it is awkward when the cron job's output is meant to be consumed as the message payload, a tool result, or a simple human-readable report. Consumers then have to parse an ad hoc envelope just to recover the command's stdout.

Current source check on `master` at `48ce4ffe53` still shows `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/scheduler.rs` assembling that wrapper directly in `run_job_command_with_timeout()`.

## Proposed solution

Add a per-shell-job output format with a safe default:

- `wrapped` keeps the current `status/stdout/stderr` envelope and remains the default for compatibility.
- `raw` returns trimmed stdout on successful shell execution.
- Failed shell executions should still preserve enough status/stderr context for operators to diagnose the failure. The exact failure formatting can be decided during implementation, but raw mode should not silently hide command failures.

The config entry should be the source of truth. Runtime execution should resolve it from the current job/config path instead of caching a duplicate field in another runtime struct.

The dashboard/control panel should expose the choice when creating or editing a shell cron job, since this is a per-job decision and operators using the UI should not need to edit config by hand.

## Non-goals / out of scope

This should not change the default behavior of existing cron jobs.

This should not redesign cron delivery mode or final assistant-message delivery. That adjacent problem is tracked separately in #6510.

## Alternatives considered

Leave the wrapper as-is and ask users to parse it downstream. That keeps implementation simple but makes simple stdout-driven jobs unnecessarily clumsy.

Revive the old stripped-delivery approach from #5661 wholesale. That PR is useful prior art, but the current issue should be scoped around an explicit per-job output-format choice rather than an implicit behavior change.

## Acceptance criteria

- Existing shell cron jobs keep the current wrapped output by default.
- A shell cron job can opt into raw stdout output.
- Raw mode has tests for successful stdout, stderr, and non-zero exit behavior.
- The config/schema/docs path names the behavior clearly.
- The web control panel can set the option for shell jobs.
- The runtime resolves the option from the canonical job/config source instead of storing duplicate state.

## Architecture impact

Affected surfaces: cron config/schema, cron runtime execution, tests, docs, and dashboard cron-job editing.

## Risk and rollback

Risk is medium. Cron output feeds user-visible delivery and stored job history, so a default change could surprise users. Rollback is straightforward if the feature is default-off and the wrapped format remains the compatibility path.

## Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage.

## Next decision surface

This issue can carry the implementation scope. Discussion #8395 is the original request. Related prior/adjacent work:

- #5661
- #6510

## Breaking change?

No. Existing jobs should remain wrapped unless they explicitly opt into raw output.

## Data hygiene checks

- No personal/sensitive data is included.
- Examples use neutral placeholder output.

issues.body:
### Affected component

config / runtime sandboxing

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`firejail_args` is documented as extra arguments forwarded to firejail, and the config schema exposes it, but nothing applies it to the firejail invocation.

- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/firejail.rs:19` declares `pub struct FirejailSandbox;`, a unit struct with no fields, and `:23` is `pub fn new() -> std::io::Result<Self>`, which takes no arguments.
- `wrap_invocation` (`:151`) builds the command from a fixed argument list (`:162`) and then appends the caller's invocation (`:176`). No configured argument reaches it.
- The only production read of the field is `src/security_status.rs:409`, `firejail_args: policy.firejail_args.clone()`, which copies the value into the status output. It is reported, never applied, so a status read shows the arguments a user configured as though they were in effect.
- In `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/detect.rs` the field appears only in test initializers (`firejail_args: Vec::new()` at roughly ten sites), and `FirejailSandbox::new()` at `detect.rs:465` is the only production constructor.

I found this by reading the code rather than by running it, so I have not exercised a firejail sandbox here; the absence of any read path is the evidence.

### Expected behavior

Either the configured arguments are forwarded to the firejail command line, or the field stops being advertised as doing so. Right now it is both: the schema and the generated config reference present it as working, and the status output repeats the configured value back.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure `firejail_args` with something observable, for example `["--env=MY_ENV=XXX"]` or a hardening flag.
2. Run a tool through the Firejail sandbox.
3. Compare the firejail command line with the configured arguments, and read the sandbox status output.

### Impact

Anyone who sets the field gets no effect and no error. The security angle is the one that concerns me: a user who puts hardening flags or network restrictions into `firejail_args` will believe the sandbox applies them, and the status output will confirm it. A field whose entire purpose is to tighten the sandbox should not fail silently.

### Logs / stack traces

None. There is no runtime error to paste, because the failure is the absence of any effect rather than a failure to apply one.

### ZeroClaw version

master at `b9ec3e9a8`, read at that revision

### Rust version

N/A - this is configuration and runtime behaviour, not a build issue.

---

Two related notes. The documentation half is already being corrected in #11591, which removes the instruction to set the field; the generated `docs/book/src/reference/config.md` still advertises it because that page is generated from the schema, so the remaining fix is code or schema.

#5171 is not this report: it was closed by its own reporter after finding that firejail was not installed, so the field itself was never examined there.

I am not proposing a patch because both plausible directions look like your call: forwarding the arguments would be new functionality inside the transitional holding crate, and removing the field is a breaking config change.

issues.body:
### Affected component

channel

### Severity

S1 - workflow blocked

### Current behavior

When Telegram flood-limits a bot token (HTTP 429), the channel send path ignores the `retry_after` value Telegram returns and retries **immediately**, compounding the limiting:

1. `sendMessage` with Markdown fails on 429 → an immediate plain-text retry fires (`"Telegram sendMessage with Markdown failed; retrying without parse_mode"`), again without waiting out the penalty.
2. On a streamed answer (`stream_mode = "partial"`), `finalize_draft` failure falls back to "send as new message" immediately (`"Failed to finalize draft; sending as new message"`, `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs`).
3. When those immediate retries also hit 429, the reply is **dropped entirely** (`"failed to reply"`) — no requeue, no delayed attempt, no operator-visible error. The streamed draft the user was reading vanishes with it, so from the user's side the bot "erases its half-written answer".

Observed in production (2026-10-08, three episodes within 30 minutes — verbatim log lines, redacted):

```text
"Failed to finalize draft; sending as new message"
  error: Telegram sendMessage failed (markdown 429 Too Many Requests:
  {"ok":false,"error_code":429,"description":"Too Many Requests: retry after 536","parameters":{"retry_after":536}};
  plain 429 Too Many Requests: {... "retry_after":536}})
"failed to reply"
  error: Telegram sendMessage failed (markdown 429 ... "retry_after":468 ...; plain 429 ...)
"Failed to finalize draft; sending as new message"
  error: Telegram sendMessage failed (... "retry_after":1390 ...)
```

Note the escalating penalties (536s → 1390s): Telegram kept punishing because sends continued inside the penalty window.

### Expected behavior

Honor `parameters.retry_after` from 429 responses on the Telegram send path:

- Park the failed send and retry it **after** the penalty expires instead of firing immediate markdown/plain/fallback attempts into an active limiter.
- Never silently drop a finalized reply: if the channel stays limited, keep it queued (bounded) and surface an ERROR-level observability event when the bound is exceeded.
- Consider adaptive backpressure on draft updates: after a 429, raise the effective `draft_update_interval_ms` until sends succeed again.

Related: #7332 (draft-interval flooding guard), #11608 (sibling silent-failure theme on the inbound/listener side).

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Run a telegram channel with stream_mode = "partial",
#    draft_update_interval_ms = 1000.
# 2. Generate long streamed answers until Telegram returns 429
#    (or point api_base_url at a mock that returns
#    {"ok":false,"error_code":429,"parameters":{"retry_after":N}} on sendMessage).
# 3. Observe: markdown and plain retries fire immediately (retry_after ignored),
#    the finalize fallback fires immediately as well, and when those fail the
#    reply is dropped ("failed to reply") instead of being resent after N seconds.
```

### Impact

Affected users: deployments with streamed or long Telegram answers on busy bots. Frequency: intermittent (depends on Telegram flood control). Consequence: silent loss of user-facing replies; users see answers vanish mid-stream. Mitigated locally by raising `draft_update_interval_ms` 1000→4000.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
# Verbatim production events quoted in "Current behavior" above (redacted:
# chat ids and sender handles removed). No stack trace — the send path swallows
# the final failure without propagating.
```

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.5 (master b9ec3e9a8, 2026-10-07)

rustc 1.97.1

### Operating system

Windows 10 (Windows Service via WinSW)

### Regression?

Unknown

issues.title: [Feature]: Configurable target category for turn consolidation
issues.body:
### Summary

Add a `[memory] consolidation_category` option so automatic per-turn consolidation can write somewhere other than Core.

### Problem statement

`consolidate_turn` writes every non-empty `memory_update`, and every extracted typed fact when `consolidation_extract_facts` is on, to `MemoryCategory::Core`. The category is hard-coded at each step of the path in `crates/zeroclaw-memory/src/consolidation.rs` (importance, the policy gate, dedup and merge, the conflict check, and the store), and no config routes these writes elsewhere. `[memory.types] enabled` tags the kind but leaves the category as Core.

Core is the one category meant to be permanent, and it behaves differently from the others:

| Category | Score decay at injection | Default retention | Base importance | Conflict supersede |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core | none | none (`core_retention_days = 0`) | 0.7 | yes (only category) |
| Daily | 7-day half-life | none (`daily_retention_days = 0`) | 0.3 | no |
| Conversation | 7-day half-life | 30 days | 0.2 | no |
| Custom | 7-day half-life | none (hygiene never prunes or compacts custom categories) | 0.4 | no |

`MemoryCategory` documents Core as "Long-term facts, preferences, decisions". Consolidation instead runs after channel turns of at least 20 characters with `auto_save` on (the default), and on the gateway WebSocket chat path, asking the model for anything "worth remembering long-term". The model sees only that turn, including the assistant's own reply, and each result gets a fresh `core_<uuid>` (or `core_fact_<uuid>`) key. `core_max_rows` and `core_max_bytes` default to 0 (no cap). Per-turn inferences therefore accumulate as permanent Core memory, and once mixed in, they can't be aged out or capped without also removing deliberately stored entries (the `pinned` flag that exempts rows isn't exposed through `memory_store`). On my deployment, Core fills with auto-extracted entries I don't consider correct or worth keeping long-term. PR #9758 (closed) documented a related case, where a single refusal was stored as a permanent trait.

#11655 makes this worse while embeddings are off: each Core consolidation write can supersede unrelated Core rows.

### Proposed solution

Add `[memory] consolidation_category` (string, default `"core"`), accepting `core`, `daily`, or `conversation`, validated at config load.

- `consolidate_turn` and `store_typed_facts` use the configured category instead of the hard-coded `MemoryCategory::Core`.
- The rest of the write path follows it: `compute_importance`, `policy_gate::validate_store`, and the dedup candidate set (`dedup::core_candidates`) use the configured category, so quotas and dedup apply to the category actually written.
- `check_and_resolve_conflicts` already returns early for non-Core categories, so routing elsewhere also stops supersede for these writes.
- The config docs note that a non-Core target is usually paired with a retention setting (`daily_retention_days` defaults to keep-forever), and that Conversation rows are left out of memory injection for cron and daemon turns and for turns without a session (`resolve_inject_policy`).

The default is unchanged, so existing installs behave exactly as today. Custom category names could follow once custom categories have a retention mechanism.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Changing the default category. That is a behaviour change and should wait for evidence beyond one deployment.
- A usage-based promotion pass from Daily to Core. That is deliberate promotion, which #9048 places in phase 4 (v0.9.0) under #8891.
- Retention or compaction for custom categories.
- Changing the consolidation prompt or output schema (#6998), or provenance handling (#10007, #10755).
- Explicit Core writes (`memory_store` with `core`, or a user asking the agent to remember something) are unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

- `auto_save = false`: stops Core growth, but also stops the Daily history entries.
- `core_retention_days`: an absolute age limit from first write, which ages out deliberate Core entries along with auto-extracted ones.
- `core_max_rows` / `core_max_bytes`: cap size, but compaction evicts deliberate entries along with auto-extracted ones.
- `dedup_on_write`: catches near-identical text only.
- Workspace instructions telling the agent to use other categories: consolidation is a separate model call that receives only a fixed system prompt and the turn text, so these instructions reach it only indirectly, through the assistant's reply.

### Acceptance criteria

- `consolidation_category` is documented, defaults to `"core"`, and rejects any value other than `core`, `daily`, or `conversation` at config load.
- With the default, behaviour and existing tests are unchanged.
- With `"daily"`, `memory_update` and typed facts land in Daily; importance, quotas, and dedup use Daily; no supersede happens.
- Tests cover the default and each non-Core target.

### Architecture impact

`zeroclaw-config` (`MemoryConfig` field and validation) and `zeroclaw-memory` (`consolidation.rs`, possibly `dedup.rs`). No trait or API change. This touches the same `consolidate_turn` path as #10007 (blocked) and #10755 (accepted, v0.9.0), so implementation order should be agreed with those.

### Risk and rollback

Low. The default is unchanged; setting the option back to `"core"` or removing it restores current behaviour. Rows already written keep their category.

### Expected routing

Should attach to an existing roadmap/tracker issue

### Next decision surface

#8891 (persistent memory tracker); sequencing with #10007 and #10755.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.body:
### Summary

`Config::save_dirty` writes only the dirty paths onto the on-disk document and then unconditionally sets `schema_version = CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` (added in #7274 to fix the opposite case, a current-shaped body under a stale label). When the file on disk still has a pre-V3 body (top-level `default_provider`, `default_model`, no `[agents.*]`), the incremental save leaves that body as it is but relabels it V3. On the next start, migration sees V3 and does nothing, so the legacy fields are never turned into an agent.

### Observed

A config written by an external provisioner in the single-agent layout (top-level `default_provider = "openrouter"`, `default_model`, `[gateway]`, `[workspace]`, no `schema_version`). The daemon (v0.8.4, Homebrew) started, migrated it in memory, and a gateway pairing then saved `gateway.paired_tokens` through `save_dirty`. Afterwards the file has `schema_version = 3` at the top and the same legacy body.

- With the stamp in place, `zeroclaw --config-dir <dir> agents list` shows no agents.
- On a copy with the `schema_version = 3` line removed, the same command shows `default`, because load-time migration runs again and synthesizes the default agent.

### Expected

An incremental save of a file whose on-disk label is older than `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` should not produce a V3 label over a pre-V3 body. Either fall back to a full migrated `save()` for that file (the in-memory config is already migrated), or keep the on-disk label when the body was not migrated.

### Where

- `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs`, `save_dirty`: the `doc.as_table_mut().insert("schema_version", ...)` after `apply_dirty_path` (present at v0.8.4 and on master at 584d6da0).
- Regression test from #7274: `save_dirty_stamps_current_schema_version_on_stale_label` covers a V2-labelled file gaining a current-shaped section; there is no case for a legacy body that the dirty paths do not touch.

### Workaround

Remove the `schema_version = 3` line, run `zeroclaw --config-dir <dir> config migrate`, and check `agents list`.

### Related (separate, smaller)

The OpenRouter provider's error at v0.8.4 says "Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var", but v0.8.4 has no code that reads that variable (the string appears only in the error messages in `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/openrouter.rs`). The message is gone on master; worth confirming master does not tell users to set it elsewhere.

issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

Several built-in tools take a target identifier (`session_id`, `channel_id`) **from model-supplied arguments** and act on it with no per-agent ownership check. Any agent can therefore reach another agent's session/channel data. This violates ADR-011 (`docs/book/src/architecture/decisions/ADR-011-multi-agent-runtime-boundaries.md:24,56`), which declares agents must not share workspace, memory, or channel reachability by accident, and ADR-011:46,86, which require every cross-agent capability to define its own authorization boundary.

The ownership primitive **already exists** (`SessionOwnershipScope::authorize`, `crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/sessions.rs:90-126`) and is wired into `sessions_reset`/`sessions_delete` — but the read/write session tools and `discord_search` never call it. Verified by source inspection at commit `c1b04dbc0c` (master, v0.8.3):

| Tool | Location | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| `sessions_list` | `crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/sessions.rs:132` | Lists **all** sessions of all agents/channels; no security gate, no scope |
| `sessions_history` | `sessions.rs:216` | Reads **any** session by id; only a coarse `ToolOperation::Read` gate, no ownership |
| `sessions_send` | `sessions.rs:313` | Writes a user turn into **any** session; only a coarse `Act` gate, no `SessionOwnershipScope` |
| `discord_search` | `crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/discord_search.rs:57` | Reads **all** indexed Discord history; `channel_id`/`author_id` are optional filters; **no `enforce_tool_operation` at all** |

Registration confirms the session tools are all built via unscoped `::new` even though `agent_alias` is already in scope at the call site (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:1121-1127`, inside `all_tools_with_runtime(agent_alias, …)`).

Scope note: the 5 core memory tools (`memory_recall/store/forget/purge/export`) are **not** affected — they are correctly scoped via `AgentScopedMemory` with the alias bound from a trusted constructor; cross-agent sharing there is opt-in via `read_memory_from`. `send_via` (peer-group membership check) and `sessions_current` (trusted `TOOL_LOOP_SESSION_KEY` task-local) are the correct reference models to copy.

The shared knowledge-graph has the same class of gap but a different fix shape (schema + migration) and is filed separately.

### Expected behavior

Each tool must derive the caller's identity from a **trusted context** (constructor-bound `agent_alias` / task-local), never from arguments, and authorize the target before acting:

- `sessions_list` — filter results to sessions the caller owns (reuse the three-tier `SessionOwnershipScope` predicate).
- `sessions_history` / `sessions_send` — run `SessionOwnershipScope::authorize` before `load`/`append`; deny on foreign sessions. Register via `for_agent(...)` in `tools/mod.rs`.
- `discord_search` — add a tool-operation gate and constrain results to channels the calling agent is configured for.

**Legacy data handling — fail-closed with the existing channel fallback.** Reuse `SessionOwnershipScope::authorize` as-is: `agent_alias` match → owned-`channel_id` match → deny. Channel sessions never receive `agent_alias` (the orchestrator stamps only `channel_id/room_id/sender_id`, `orchestrator/mod.rs:4460-4465`), so the channel-ownership fallback prevents hiding an agent's own channels; only truly unattributed legacy sessions are denied. This matches the already-shipped `reset`/`delete` behavior.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Two agents in one deployment: [agents.rowan] and [agents.sable].
# Agent "sable" has an active channel session telegram__victim with private history.

# Acting AS agent "rowan", issue these tool calls:

# 1) Enumerate every session across ALL agents/channels (no ownership filter):
sessions_list {}
#   -> telegram__victim (owned by sable) appears in the list.

# 2) Read another agent's full private history:
sessions_history {"session_id": "telegram__victim"}
#   -> returns sable's conversation verbatim.

# 3) Inject a turn into another agent's session:
sessions_send {"session_id": "telegram__victim", "message": "..."}
#   -> appended as a user message in sable's session.

# 4) Read all indexed Discord history irrespective of channel membership:
discord_search {"query": "..."}          # channel_id omitted

# Verified by source inspection at commit c1b04dbc0c (master, v0.8.3):
#   sessions.rs:132 / :216 / :313        (list / history / send — no ownership scope)
#   discord_search.rs:57                 (no gate; channel_id optional)
#   runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:1121-1127   (session tools registered via unscoped ::new)
```

### Impact

```
Affected: any multi-agent deployment (>=2 configured agents, or agents + gateway/channel sessions).
Vector: a prompt-injected or low-trust agent can exfiltrate another agent's private
        conversation history and inject messages into foreign sessions.
Frequency: always -- deterministic, no race.
Consequence: cross-agent confidentiality + integrity breach; violates the ADR-011 isolation
        guarantee. Same confused-deputy class as #7947 and #8279; relevant to tracker #8290.
Not affected: the 5 core memory tools (AgentScopedMemory-scoped).
```

### Logs / stack traces

```text
Static authorization gap -- no runtime log. Primary evidence (v0.8.3, c1b04dbc0c):

sessions.rs:164  async fn execute(&self, args) {              // SessionsListTool
sessions.rs:171      let metadata = self.backend.list_sessions_with_metadata();  // ALL sessions, unscoped

sessions.rs:242  async fn execute(&self, args) {              // SessionsHistoryTool
sessions.rs:243      self.security.enforce_tool_operation(Read, "sessions_history")  // coarse gate only
sessions.rs:278      let messages = self.backend.load(session_id);   // arbitrary session_id, no ownership check
```

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.3 (commit c1b04dbc0c)

### Rust version

rustc 1.97.0

### Operating system

All platforms (source-verified on Windows 11; code path is OS-independent)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. (verified by source inspection of the v0.8.3 / c1b04dbc0c tree)
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content. (neutral placeholder aliases only)

issues.body:
### Affected component

memory

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

The `knowledge` tool exposes a **single, globally-shared** knowledge graph to every agent with no per-agent attribution and no ownership scoping. Any agent can read and mutate another agent's captured knowledge, client networks, and interaction logs. This is the knowledge-plane analogue of the session-tool ownership gap (#9646) and violates ADR-011 (`docs/book/src/architecture/decisions/ADR-011-multi-agent-runtime-boundaries.md:24,56,86`), which requires memory isolation per agent identity and that every cross-agent capability define its own authorization boundary.

Verified by source inspection at commit `c1b04dbc0c` (master, v0.8.3):

- `KnowledgeTool` holds a raw `Arc<KnowledgeGraph>` with no identity of any kind (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/knowledge_tool.rs:30-38`); `execute` dispatches on an `action` arg (`knowledge_tool.rs:126`) reaching `capture` / `search` / `relate` / `suggest` / `graph_neighbors` / `client_network` / `interaction_log`, all against the common store, with `node_id`/`client_id` taken from arguments.
- The graph is built once from a single global `root_config.knowledge.db_path` and handed to every agent unscoped (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:1370-1383`).
- `KnowledgeGraph` (`crates/zeroclaw-memory/src/knowledge_graph`) has no agent-attribution concept — nodes carry no owner column, so reads and writes cannot be filtered by agent.

Contrast: the 5 core memory tools ARE isolated via `AgentScopedMemory` (alias bound from a trusted constructor). The knowledge graph is the one memory-plane store with no per-agent partition.

### Expected behavior

The knowledge graph must gain a per-agent attribution dimension and the tool must scope by it, deriving the caller's identity from a trusted context (constructor-bound `agent_alias`), never from arguments:

- Add an owner/attribution column (e.g. `agent_alias`) to knowledge nodes (schema migration).
- Stamp new `capture`/`relate` writes with the trusted caller alias.
- Scope `search`/`graph_neighbors`/`client_network`/`interaction_log` reads and all mutations to the caller's own attribution (optionally widened by an explicit, operator-configured share, mirroring `read_memory_from` on the memory plane).

**Legacy data handling — cannot fail-closed.** No attribution exists today, so "legacy" = every node; hiding them all would break the feature. Required approach: run the migration, then either (a) default pre-existing nodes to a shared read-only scope with new writes per-agent, or (b) config-gate the `knowledge` tool until the operator opts in / migrates. Decide the default as part of this issue.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Two agents in one deployment: [agents.rowan] and [agents.sable], both with the `knowledge` tool.
# Agent "sable" has captured private knowledge (e.g. a client network).

# Acting AS agent "rowan":

# 1) Read another agent's captured knowledge on the shared graph:
knowledge {"action": "search", "query": "..."}
knowledge {"action": "client_network", "client_id": "..."}
knowledge {"action": "interaction_log", "client_id": "..."}
#   -> returns sable's captured nodes / client network / interaction history.

# 2) Mutate the shared graph (affects sable's knowledge):
knowledge {"action": "capture", "title": "...", "content": "..."}
knowledge {"action": "relate", "from_id": "...", "to_id": "...", "relation": "..."}

# Verified by source inspection at commit c1b04dbc0c (master, v0.8.3):
#   knowledge_tool.rs:30-38, 126        (raw Arc<KnowledgeGraph>, no identity, args-driven ids)
#   runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:1370-1383  (single global db_path, handed to every agent unscoped)
#   zeroclaw-memory/src/knowledge_graph (no owner attribution on nodes)
```

### Impact

```
Affected: any multi-agent deployment where more than one agent has the `knowledge` tool.
Vector: a prompt-injected or low-trust agent can exfiltrate another agent's captured
        knowledge, client networks, and interaction logs, and silently mutate shared nodes.
Frequency: always -- deterministic, no race.
Consequence: cross-agent confidentiality + integrity breach on the knowledge plane;
        violates the ADR-011 memory-isolation guarantee. Sibling of #9646 (session plane).
Not affected: the 5 core memory tools (AgentScopedMemory-scoped).
```

### Logs / stack traces

```text
Static authorization gap -- no runtime log. Primary evidence (v0.8.3, c1b04dbc0c):

knowledge_tool.rs:30  pub struct KnowledgeTool { graph: Arc<KnowledgeGraph> }   // no identity, no SecurityPolicy
knowledge_tool.rs:126 async fn execute(&self, args) { let action = args.get("action")... }  // args-driven, unscoped
tools/mod.rs:1370-1383  // one global KnowledgeGraph from knowledge.db_path, shared by every agent
```

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.3 (commit c1b04dbc0c)

### Rust version

rustc 1.97.0

### Operating system

All platforms (source-verified on Windows 11; code path is OS-independent)

### Regression?

Unknown

issues.body:
## Summary

Extract cron out of `zeroclaw-runtime` into a dedicated `zeroclaw-cron` crate, and retire the transitional exception that [ADR-016](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/master/docs/book/src/architecture/decisions/ADR-016-cron-extraction-and-transitional-exception.md) grants against this issue.

`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md` names cron as a subsystem awaiting extraction and forbids adding functionality to the holding crate. No destination crate exists, so accepted cron work has had nowhere permitted to live. ADR-016 records the extraction as the committed target and grants a narrow, expiring exception until it lands. This issue is what that exception is granted against: if it is closed without the extraction, or goes stale, the exception lapses and cron work returns to being blocked.

## Scope

`zeroclaw-cron` owns scheduling and job lifecycle:

- schedule parsing and next-run computation
- the job and run store, including migrations
- declarative reconciliation against config
- in-flight claim ownership, including owner-qualified startup recovery
- execution outcome classification and run history
- precondition (`pre_hook`) evaluation

It does **not** own agent execution, security policy construction, channel delivery, or configuration schema. It reaches those through existing contracts. In particular, the security policy that authorizes a cron command stays owned by the security layer and is resolved rather than reimplemented.

## What has to move

Current home: `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/` — `scheduler.rs`, `store.rs`, `schedule.rs`, `types.rs`, `precondition.rs`, `mod.rs`.

Known callers to re-point: the daemon scheduler startup, the gateway cron API handlers, the RPC cron methods, the `cron_*` tools, and the CLI cron subcommands.

Known outbound dependencies to resolve rather than absorb: `SecurityPolicy` construction and the per-agent action tracker, `RuntimeAdapter` shell execution, the delivery/announce path, the Fluent catalogue for operator-facing text, and `Config` cron declarations.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `crates/zeroclaw-cron` exists and owns everything under **Scope**.
- [ ] `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/` is deleted, not re-exported or shimmed.
- [ ] No dependency from security, config, or delivery onto cron. Cron depends on them, not the reverse.
- [ ] Every caller listed above builds against the new crate with no behavior change.
- [ ] Cron tests move with the code and pass, including the claim-ownership, precondition, and reconciliation regressions.
- [ ] `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md` no longer lists cron as awaiting extraction, and its active-exceptions table no longer lists `src/cron`.
- [ ] ADR-016 moves from `proposed` to `accepted`, or is superseded if the design changed during extraction.

## Debt accrued under the exception

Changes that landed in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron` under ADR-016 and must move with the extraction:

- #10220 — cron precondition gate (`pre_hook`), including `precondition.rs`, claim ownership on the manual path, typed run outcomes, the per-agent cron action tracker, and the Fluent keys for gate text.

Add to this list as further changes land under the exception. It is the running cost of not extracting yet, and it is deliberately visible.

issues.body:
### Affected component

channel

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

ZeroClaw's email channel can send to only one recipient and cannot represent or preserve an email conversation's recipient list. When replying to a message that has people in `Cc`, ZeroClaw replies only to the sender (or is forced to address every participant directly). The original To/Cc structure is silently dropped.

The one-off CLI has the same limitation: `zeroclaw channel send` exposes only one `--recipient` and provides no `--to`, `--cc`, `--bcc`, `--subject`, `--in-reply-to`, or `--references` options. Sending separate messages to each participant is not equivalent to Reply All and fragments the conversation.

Although the internal `SendMessage` type supports a single `in_reply_to`, the inbound email adapter discards `To`, `Cc`, `Reply-To`, and `References`, and the outbound adapter has no CC/BCC/References representation. Consequently a real RFC 5322 reply-all cannot be constructed through any standard email-channel surface.

Observed shape of an automatic reply to a message that carried `Cc` and `Reply-To`:

```text
To: alice@example.com
In-Reply-To: <message-1@example.com>
Subject: Re: Partnership discussion
```

Missing:

```text
To: alice-replies@example.com   # Reply-To should win when present
Cc: bob@example.com
References: <root@example.com> <message-1@example.com>
```

#### Root cause

The limitation exists across the message model, inbound adapter, outbound adapter, and CLI (line references re-verified on current master).

**1. Shared outbound message model is single-recipient** — `crates/zeroclaw-api/src/channel.rs:273-289`:

```rust
pub struct SendMessage {
    pub content: String,
    pub recipient: String,
    pub subject: Option<String>,
    // ...
    pub in_reply_to: Option<String>,
}
```

There are no recipient lists, CC/BCC fields, or References chain.

**2. Inbound channel model cannot retain the email envelope** — `ChannelMessage` has `sender`, one `reply_target`, and `subject`, but no email `to`, `cc`, `reply_to`, or `references` metadata. The email parser builds `ParsedEmail` with only:

```rust
struct ParsedEmail {
    msg_id: String,
    sender: String,
    subject: String,
    content: String,
    timestamp: u64,
    attachments: Vec<MediaAttachment>,
}
```

See `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/email_channel.rs:832-839`. `dispatch_email` then sets both `sender` and `reply_target` from `email.sender`, dropping the rest of the original envelope.

**3. SMTP builder emits one To and no CC/BCC/References** — `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/email_channel.rs:907-915`:

```rust
let mut builder = Message::builder()
    .from(self.config.from_address.parse()?)
    .to(message.recipient.parse()?)
    .subject(subject);
if let Some(ref reply_id) = message.in_reply_to
    && !is_synthetic_email_message_id(reply_id)
{
    builder = builder.in_reply_to(reply_id.clone());
}
```

There is no loop over To recipients and no `.cc(...)`, `.bcc(...)`, or References header construction.

**4. One-off CLI discards available email metadata** — `ChannelCommands::Send` exposes only `message`, `channel_id`, and one `recipient` (`src/lib.rs:316-325`), and `send_channel_message` always constructs `SendMessage::new(message, recipient)` (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs:8099`). Even the existing `SendMessage.subject` and `SendMessage.in_reply_to` fields cannot be set by the one-off command.

#### Relationship to #6883

RFC #6883 added `SendMessage::reply_to` so normal replies consistently carry one recipient, subject, and `In-Reply-To`. That work is useful but does not solve Reply All:

- `ChannelMessage` still does not retain email recipient headers.
- `SendMessage` still has only one recipient.
- Email still cannot emit CC/BCC/References.
- The one-off CLI still cannot use reply metadata.

This issue is therefore complementary, not a duplicate.

### Expected behavior

ZeroClaw should support standards-compliant email composition and Reply All:

1. Multiple `To` recipients.
2. Explicit `Cc` and `Bcc` recipients for outbound mail.
3. Inbound parsing of `To`, `Cc`, `Reply-To`, `Message-ID`, and `References`.
4. Reply should honor `Reply-To` before `From`.
5. Reply All should include:
   - the effective reply address (`Reply-To` or `From`) in `To`;
   - the original `To` and `Cc` participants, except ZeroClaw's own mailbox identities;
   - deduplication across recipient fields;
   - no propagation of inbound BCC recipients.
6. Outbound replies should set both:
   - `In-Reply-To: <parent-message-id>`
   - `References: <existing-reference-chain> <parent-message-id>`
7. CLI and agent/tool surfaces should expose the capability without forcing users to send separate emails.

#### Suggested design

Avoid encoding multiple addresses into the existing `recipient: String`. Use typed fields, for example:

```rust
pub struct EmailEnvelope {
    pub to: Vec<String>,
    pub cc: Vec<String>,
    pub bcc: Vec<String>,
    pub reply_to: Vec<String>,
    pub references: Vec<String>,
}

pub struct SendMessage {
    // existing cross-channel fields
    pub recipient: String,
    pub subject: Option<String>,
    pub in_reply_to: Option<String>,

    // channel-specific structured metadata
    pub email: Option<EmailEnvelope>,
}
```

An alternative is generic `recipients: Vec<Recipient>` with a `RecipientKind::{To,Cc,Bcc}`, but the API should remain typed and should not overload comma-separated strings. For inbound mail, retain the relevant envelope/thread metadata on `ChannelMessage`, either through a typed email metadata field or a channel-specific metadata enum.

Add explicit reply semantics rather than making every caller calculate recipients:

```rust
SendMessage::reply_to(&msg, content)
SendMessage::reply_all(&msg, content, own_addresses)
```

`reply_all` should prefer Reply-To over From; preserve original To/Cc participants; remove configured own addresses and aliases; deduplicate case-insensitively; never copy BCC from inbound metadata; and extend the References chain with the parent Message-ID.

Possible CLI surface:

```text
zeroclaw channel send ... \
  --recipient alice@example.com \
  --to second@example.com \
  --cc bob@example.com \
  --bcc audit@example.com \
  --subject 'Subject' \
  --in-reply-to '<id@example.com>' \
  --references '<root@example.com>'
```

For a mailbox-aware command, a safer follow-up could be `zeroclaw email reply --channel-id email.work --uid 123 --reply-all '...'` — the UID-based form lets ZeroClaw derive recipients and headers from the source message instead of making operators copy raw headers manually.

#### Security and privacy requirements

- Never expose BCC recipients from an inbound message to other recipients.
- Remove all configured identities for the sending mailbox from Reply All targets.
- Deduplicate addresses case-insensitively.
- Validate all mailbox strings with the existing email parser before SMTP.
- Preserve current recipient/peer authorization checks for every To/Cc/Bcc address rather than checking only the primary recipient.
- Avoid logging full recipient lists at info level if current privacy policy treats addresses as sensitive.

#### Recommended tests

1. Inbound parser retains From, Reply-To, To, Cc, Message-ID, and References.
2. Reply honors Reply-To over From.
3. Reply All includes sender + original To/Cc, removes self, and deduplicates.
4. Reply All never promotes inbound BCC.
5. SMTP output contains multiple To, Cc, Bcc, In-Reply-To, and References headers.
6. Standard reply remains backward-compatible for a single sender.
7. CLI parses repeatable/comma-separated To/Cc/Bcc flags and reply headers.
8. CLI-produced email is one MIME message, not one send per participant.
9. Authorization is enforced for every outbound recipient.
10. Existing non-email channel behavior is unchanged.

#### Workaround

Use an external mail client or SMTP implementation that supports recipient lists and RFC reply headers. Sending multiple one-off ZeroClaw messages is not a valid Reply All workaround because it fragments the conversation.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# --- Inbound/agent path ---
# 1. Send an email to a ZeroClaw mailbox with this envelope:
#
#    From: Alice <alice@example.com>
#    To: ZeroClaw <agent@example.com>
#    Cc: Bob <bob@example.com>
#    Reply-To: Alice Replies <alice-replies@example.com>
#    Message-ID: <message-1@example.com>
#    References: <root@example.com>
#    Subject: Partnership discussion
#
# 2. Let the email channel ingest the message and have the agent respond.
# 3. Inspect the outbound message: it carries only
#    "To: alice@example.com" + "In-Reply-To: <message-1@example.com>".
#    Reply-To is ignored, Cc is dropped, References is absent.

# --- One-off CLI path ---
# The help surface supports only a single recipient:
zeroclaw channel send --help
# Usage: zeroclaw channel send [OPTIONS] --channel-id <CHANNEL_ID> --recipient <RECIPIENT> <MESSAGE>
#
# Options:
#   --channel-id <CHANNEL_ID>
#   --recipient <RECIPIENT>

# There is no way to perform the equivalent of:
zeroclaw channel send \
  --channel-id email.work \
  --to alice-replies@example.com \
  --cc bob@example.com \
  --subject 'Re: Partnership discussion' \
  --in-reply-to '<message-1@example.com>' \
  --references '<root@example.com> <message-1@example.com>' \
  '...'
# (fails: --to/--cc/--subject/--in-reply-to/--references do not exist)

# Using the same "Re:" subject without RFC threading headers is not a true
# reply. Sending once to Alice and once to Bob produces two independent
# messages and can create duplicate or fragmented threads.
```

### Impact

Affected users: anyone using the email channel for multi-party threads (agent replies or `zeroclaw channel send`).

Frequency: always, whenever an inbound message has `Cc`, `Reply-To`, or an existing `References` chain.

Consequence: CC participants are silently dropped from conversations, `Reply-To` is ignored, and threads fragment in other participants' mail clients. Motivating incident: asked to reply to a two-party thread, ZeroClaw had to address both participants as direct recipients instead of keeping one on `Cc` — the capability to preserve the recipient structure does not exist.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

0.8.3 (source inspected at `3cb4ad183`; claims re-verified on master `90ae26b00`)

### Rust version

_No response_

### Operating system

macOS (arm64)

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

prs.title: fix(security): block high-risk shell commands even when allowlisted
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** `validate_command_execution_for_shell` skipped the `block_high_risk_commands` gate when a command was a literal `allowed_commands` entry, so the reported profile with the hard block on and `rm` in its allowlist could execute `rm -rf` after shell auto-approval. The gate now applies to every high-risk command, which is what the config schema documents the field to do. The Balanced and Locked Down preset help and the PowerShell sandboxing guidance are reworded in the same change, because they promised an explicit-allowlist exemption the code no longer gives.
- **Scope boundary:** The allowlist itself, the medium-risk approval gate, and the supervised high-risk approval gate are unchanged. The `"*"` + `block_high_risk_commands = false` escape hatch is unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** `SecurityPolicy::validate_command_execution_for_shell`, which the shell tool, the skill shell tool, and cron shell jobs all call. A profile that allowlists a high-risk command with the hard block on now gets it blocked instead of executed.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11058
- **Labels:** `bug`, `config`, `domain:security`, `needs-maintainer-review`, `risk:high`, `runtime`, `security:policy`, `size:S`, `tool:delegate`.

### What this does, simply

A profile lists the commands an agent may run in `allowed_commands`. Putting a command there used to do two things at once: it allowed the command, and if the command was high-risk it also switched off the `block_high_risk_commands` hard block for that command. Only the first effect is documented, and the second is how an allowlisted `rm` ran silently while the profile had the hard block turned on.

The config schema documents `block_high_risk_commands` as "Block high-risk commands even when allowlisted", so this makes the code match that sentence. The allowlist still decides whether a command may run at all; the hard block just applies on top of it. If you do want a high-risk command to run, `block_high_risk_commands = false` is the switch for that, and it's untouched.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — this is a pure policy function covered by the crate's own unit and integration tests; a manual agent run would exercise the same function without adding signal.

### How I tested

On `master`, before the change, the existing `validate_command_explicit_rm_bypasses_high_risk_block` passed. It builds a policy with `autonomy = Full`, `allowed_commands = ["rm"]`, `block_high_risk_commands = true` and asserts `validate_command_execution("rm -rf /tmp/test", true)` returns `Ok(CommandRiskLevel::High)`. That is the silent-execution path from the issue: the command clears validation and the shell tool runs it.

I added `validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk` (its comment quotes the schema sentence) and ran it before touching the code:

```
running 1 test
test policy::tests::validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk ... FAILED

---- policy::tests::validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk stdout ----
thread '...' panicked at crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:6588:13:
expected the hard block, got: Command requires explicit approval (approved=true): high-risk operation
```

That failure is the bug. The allowlist entry cleared the hard block, so an unapproved call fell through to the approval gate instead of being blocked; with `approved = true` the call returns `Ok` and the command runs.

After the change, on the tested revision:

```
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config
test result: ok. 1775 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out   (lib)
     Running tests/comment_writer.rs        — 8 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/migration.rs             — 99 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/nodes_mdns_config.rs     — 5 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/powershell_policy_probe.rs — 9 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/repro_8636.rs            — 1 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/schema_v4_external_saas.rs — 1 passed; 0 failed

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib validate_command
test result: ok. 15 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1760 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib independent_delegate_denies_prompt_required_skill_tools_without_approval_route
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5698 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib tools::shell::tests
test result: FAILED. 64 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5634 filtered out
# shell_child_cannot_open_owners_controlling_terminal is the failure: its own
# openpty() call returns EACCES in this sandbox before any ZeroClaw code runs,
# and the same denial reproduces with a standalone libc call outside the repo.
# The other 64 pass.

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
(clean)

$ scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
0 error(s)

$ scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh
No added links detected in changed docs lines.
```

The `validate_command` set covers the three cases the issue names: a high-risk command with an explicit allow entry is blocked for both `approved` values; an ordinary allowlisted command (`ls`) still returns `Ok(Low)` without approval; a high-risk command that is not allowlisted still fails with `Command not allowed by security policy`. One test also pins the opt-out: with `block_high_risk_commands = false`, an allowlisted `rm` still returns `Ok(High)`.

Five existing tests needed to move with the policy. Three asserted the old exemption directly and now assert the block. Two PowerShell allowlist-path tests set `block_high_risk_commands = false` so they keep exercising the path-match rule they exist for rather than the high-risk gate. `independent_delegate_denies_prompt_required_skill_tools_without_approval_route` used an allowlisted `rm` to reach the approval gate, so its fixture now turns the hard block off; with it on the command would stop at the high-risk gate instead of the prompt.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Rust quality gate (fmt + clippy) and the workspace test job cover the changed crate and its callers.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:** listed above.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I confirmed the risk classifier and the allowlist both live in `SecurityPolicy`, so the change sits in the function that owns the decision and covers all three callers (`tools/shell.rs`, `tools/skill_tool.rs`, `cron/mod.rs`) rather than one entry point. I did not run a live agent turn against a real model.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A`
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `c29e071cfd325c5b7bb6e6e14d016c54b21e8bba`, `zeroclaw-config` and `zeroclaw-runtime`, Linux x86_64, Rust 1.97.0. The branch is rebased onto current `master` (`d03325172eb6c64272f01042b60fd7f66d74c711`), so these runs are against the merged result rather than the old base.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: `N/A`

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `No`
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: keep `block_high_risk_commands = true` to retain the hard block. Profiles that previously relied on an explicit high-risk exemption will now receive `Command blocked: high-risk command is disallowed by policy`, with no process spawned. Choosing `block_high_risk_commands = false` permits allowlisted high-risk commands subject to the remaining approval, path and sandbox checks, but is an explicit security opt-out rather than an equivalent migration. With `"*"` in the allowlist, it also admits other high-risk commands and disables the existing shell syntax restrictions. Removing the wildcard and enumerating intended commands avoids that wildcard syntax bypass, but changes the previous broad low-risk allowance. This also affects allowlisted PowerShell executables classified as high risk.

  The Windows default profile is where a stock install feels this. `runtime.shell` defaults to PowerShell on Windows (#10956), and under PowerShell a command name the classifier doesn't recognize is high risk. 18 of the 27 entries in the Windows default allowlist are high risk, including `python`, `node`, `grep`, `find` and `where`. The `default` and `locked_down` profiles set `block_high_risk_commands = true`, so on Windows those 18 move from an approval prompt to a hard block that approval can't override, and a stock Windows install can no longer run them. POSIX defaults are essentially unaffected: the same names classify as low risk under the POSIX classifier. `block_high_risk_commands = false` restores them under the ordinary approval gates.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** revert the merged change using its landed commit SHA
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** none beyond the existing `block_high_risk_commands`; reverting restores the old allowlist exemption.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** shell tool results containing `Command blocked: high-risk command is disallowed by policy` for a command the profile previously allowlisted, with no process spawned.

prs.title: feat(memory): honor the preference subtype only for user-authored turns
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** The consolidation model labels each Core memory update with a semantic subtype, and `classify::kind_of_core` trusted a model-emitted `preference` unconditionally. `Preference` is a provenance claim — "the user themself expressed this" — but nothing verified a user was present in the turn. Both current consolidation callers (channel orchestrator, gateway WS chat) happen to be user-authored surfaces, so the claim holds by accident of wiring, not by contract; the first autonomous caller would silently mint preferences out of the model's own inference.
- This PR states the invariant at the layer that applies the label: `TurnOrigin::user_authored()` in `zeroclaw-api` (true only for `Interactive` and `Channel`; exhaustive match, no wildcard, so future origin variants force an explicit decision), `kind_of_core(result, origin)` downgrades an autonomous-turn `preference` to `Fact` (content survives, preference authority does not), and `consolidate_turn` / `MemoryStrategy::consolidate_turn` gain an `origin` parameter with each caller passing the origin its surface already stamps. The downgrade is logged at DEBUG.
- **Scope boundary:** No change to what gets stored, deduped, merged, or superseded — only to the `kind` metadata a non-user-authored `preference` receives. Non-preference subtypes are origin-independent. No config surface, no prompt change, no change to the verbatim autosave paths (heartbeat Daily stores, Conversation stores), which never classified.
- **Blast radius:** `MemoryStrategy` is a public trait in `zeroclaw-api` and its `consolidate_turn` gains a parameter — a compile-time break for external implementers (one implementer and two callers exist in-tree, all updated). Callers of `zeroclaw_memory::consolidation::consolidate_turn` likewise. Behavior changes only for a model-emitted `preference` on non-user-authored turns, a path no in-tree caller currently exercises.
- **Linked issue(s):** N/A
- **Labels:** `enhancement`, `agent`, `channel`, `gateway`, `memory`, `runtime`, `tests`, `distinguished contributor`, `channel:core`, `domain:security`, `priority:p2`, `risk:high`, `size:M`

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — the changed behavior (subtype metadata on a not-yet-wired autonomous consolidation path) has no user-visible surface today; the deterministic tests below are the observable contract.

### How I tested

Written test-first. With the `origin` parameter threaded but the downgrade not yet implemented, the new regressions failed and the negative controls passed:

```
failures:
    classify::tests::preference_alias_spellings_downgrade_identically
    classify::tests::preference_downgrades_to_fact_on_turns_no_person_authored
test result: FAILED. 7 passed; 2 failed
consolidation::tests::preference_from_the_model_is_stored_as_fact_on_autonomous_turns
  Daemon: stored kind must reflect turn provenance: left: Some(Semantic(Preference)) right: Some(Semantic(Fact))
```

After the one-match implementation, all green. New coverage:

- `user_authored_is_true_only_for_a_person_typing` + `default_origin_is_not_user_authored` (zeroclaw-api) — the full truth table per variant, and the serde fail-closed default is also provenance-fail-closed
- `preference_is_honored_when_a_person_typed_the_turn` — Interactive and Channel keep preference authority (negative control; passed at red)
- `preference_downgrades_to_fact_on_turns_no_person_authored` — Cron, Daemon, AgentDirect, SubTurn
- `preference_alias_spellings_downgrade_identically` — `pref`, `user_preference`, ` Preference ` get no side door
- `non_preference_subtypes_are_origin_independent` — facts/decisions/entities untouched (negative control; passed at red)
- `preference_from_the_model_is_stored_as_fact_on_autonomous_turns` — end-to-end through the real `consolidate_turn` store path with a scripted provider: the same model output stores as `Preference` for Interactive/Channel and `Fact` for Daemon/Cron, so the clause cannot silently detach from the store path

```sh
cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory     # 506 passed; 0 failed (+4, 0)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-api        # 166 passed; 0 failed (+1)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime    # 3737 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored
cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels   # 1391 passed; 1 failed (see note)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-gateway    # 436 passed; 0 failed (+9)
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-memory -p zeroclaw-runtime \
  -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-gateway --all-targets -- -D warnings   # clean
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                # clean
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                                   # passed
```

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the workspace test and lint gates over the five touched crates; the trait change is compile-checked by every consumer in the workspace matrix.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none specific to this change.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The full-suite `zeroclaw-channels` run had one failure, `tts::tests::edge_tts_timeout_kills_child_and_removes_temp_output` — a TTS child-process timing test this diff does not touch; it passes twice consecutively in isolation, so it is parallel-load flakiness, not a regression from this change. I verified both production call sites pass the origin their surface already stamps: the gateway stamps `TurnOrigin::Interactive` on its turn envelopes (`gateway/src/lib.rs`), and the orchestrator consolidates channel peer turns.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** no live-provider consolidation run; the scripted-provider e2e drives the identical store path.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No**
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No** — this narrows what a model-emitted label can claim: consolidation output can no longer assert user-preference provenance on turns no user authored.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **No** — `MemoryStrategy::consolidate_turn` and `zeroclaw_memory::consolidation::consolidate_turn` gain an `origin: TurnOrigin` parameter (compile-time break for external implementers/callers).
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **No**
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No**
- If backward compatibility is `No`: pass the `TurnOrigin` of the turn that produced the user message — `Interactive` for operator chat surfaces, `Channel` for channel peer messages, `Cron`/`Daemon` for scheduled work. If the origin is unknown, `TurnOrigin::default()` (SubTurn) is the fail-closed choice: consolidation still runs, but preference authority is withheld.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`; no data or configuration migration. Memories already downgraded to `Fact` keep that kind — no stored data changes shape in either direction.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** the downgrade only engages when `memory.types.enabled` is on (the only mode that classifies at all).
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a preference stated by a real user in chat being stored with `kind: fact` — grep DEBUG logs for "downgraded preference to fact" with an `Interactive`/`Channel` origin attribute, which would indicate an origin mis-stamped upstream.

prs.title: fix(cron): prevent shell diagnostics from leaking to channels
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** A scheduled shell command (`cron` with `job_type = "shell"`) forwarded the raw `status/stdout/stderr` envelope to the delivery channel. A failing command — or a successful one that prints to stderr — could therefore leak command text, file paths, and stderr diagnostics to the end user. This closes that leak.
- **What changed and why (mechanics):** `run_job_command_with_runtime_and_timeout` now returns bare stdout on success (logging any stderr internally at WARN with a sanitized diagnostic), and on failure returns the wrapped envelope only to a new `render_job_output` helper, which replaces it with a localized user-safe message and logs the sanitized failure. `execute_job_now_with_runtime` and `execute_and_persist_job` route their results through `render_job_output`, so both the channel and the persisted run history see only safe text. `cron run`'s tool-level policy rejection is likewise localized.
- **Scope boundary:** Shell jobs only. Agent jobs and non-shell outputs pass through unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** Cron shell job result rendering. No change to scheduling, retry, delivery routing, or command execution itself.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

A cron shell job that prints `internal-warning` to stderr and `public-output` to stdout now delivers only `public-output` to the channel; the stderr is recorded in the server log. A cron shell job that fails no longer sends its `status=`/`stdout:`/`stderr:` dump to the channel — the operator sees "The scheduled command failed. Check the server logs for details." while the sanitized details are logged server-side.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`; output-rendering change covered by unit tests and required CI.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required hosted CI covers the changed `zeroclaw-runtime` surface via `Test`, `Lint`, `Format`, and `Parallel Runtime Test`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The output assertions do not capture emitted diagnostic log attributes or verify credential scrubbing in those attributes.

- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(no output; formatting clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 4m 42s
(no warnings)

$ cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib cron::
test result: ok. 228 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5224 filtered out

$ cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib cron_run
test result: ok. 20 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5432 filtered out

$ git diff --check
(no output)
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** `execute_job_now_hides_shell_failure_diagnostics` and `execute_job_now_shell_success_returns_only_stdout` drive the real `execute_job_now` entry point and assert the failure output is the localized message (with no `wecom-leak-repro`, `status=`, or `stderr:` substring) and the success output is exactly `public-output`.
- **Visual interface changed?** Yes — cron shell failure/block messages are now localized; success output is bare stdout.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes. Shell diagnostics move from returned results to WARN log attributes. The sanitizer removes known token prefixes and URL credentials, but ordinary credential-bearing key/value text can remain in those logs.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No — this *reduces* what untrusted command output can reach the channel

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? The config remains parseable, but shell result text changes. Both `wrapped` and `raw` now return trimmed stdout on success and a localized message on failure; empty success returns a completion message. The accepted `shell_output_format` setting no longer selects execution output formatting.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No new fields or flags. Existing `shell_output_format` values remain accepted but are ignored during output rendering.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Revert the eventual merge commit to restore the previous shell output and logging behavior. No config or database migration is introduced.
