prs.title: fix(memory): preserve owner in delegation
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - An owner-bound RPC session routes its direct memory tools to the owner's private plane (`Agent::route_memory_to_principal`), but delegation replaced the child's memory tools with ones built by `DelegateTool::memory_for_target_agent`, which called `create_memory_for_agent` with no principal scope. A delegated `memory_recall` therefore read the target agent's shared rows and a delegated `memory_store` wrote there. Reverting the fix makes the new regression show exactly that (see How I tested).
  - `route_memory_to_principal` now binds the session's full `PrincipalScope` to the concrete `DelegateTool` the tool factory registered (`DelegateTool::bind_principal_scope`: set once, equality-checked, refuses a different scope). The cell is an `Arc<RwLock<Option<PrincipalScope>>>` that the background, parallel and nested bounded child instances clone, so every hop sees the same owner. The session binds its scope under its own agent alias (`memory_scope_for(owner, session_alias)`); a child re-selects it to the target agent, `owner.with_agent(target)`, and wraps the target handle in `PrincipalPlaneMemory`.
  - Two fail-closed branches: a bound delegate with no root config to build the target handle refuses, instead of handing the child the caller's shared fallback handle; and an owned session whose registry holds a `delegate` tool it has no handle for refuses to route instead of continuing unbound.
  - `AgentScopedMemory` and `RetrievalPipeline` now forward the nine `*_for_principal` operations to their backend. Before, they fell through to the fail-closed trait defaults, so every private-plane operation through the per-agent stack from `create_memory_for_agent` refused. That stack is also an owned session's own memory, so this changes more than delegation; see Blast radius and note 6. Private recalls skip the retrieval hot cache, whose key has no owner dimension; private writes invalidate it.
  - `delegate_tool` on `Agent`, `AgentBuilder` and `AllToolsResult` is production state now, so its `#[cfg(test)]` and `#[allow(dead_code)]` are removed. `AllToolsResult` therefore always carries a crate-private field, and the one out-of-crate struct literal (a `zeroclaw-channels` test helper) now calls `AllToolsResult::from_prebuilt_tools`, which builds the identical value.
- **Scope boundary:** No change to RPC plane selection or the explicit `plane: "shared"` path, grants and admission, delegation policy, `read_memory_from` behavior on the shared plane, the memory schema, or config. Unowned sessions (the shared operator, CLI, channels) never bind a scope and get exactly the handles they got before. **Known remaining gaps, pre-existing and not fixed here:** two other tools still give an owned session a path to the shared plane.
  - `spawn_subagent` builds its child with `memory: None`, and `agent::run` then creates the child's memory with an unscoped `create_memory_for_agent`. The tool is kept for administrators and for principals with wildcard agent selectors, and a delegated child, bounded or independent, can also reach it when its policies admit it.
  - The opt-in `execute_pipeline` tool (`[pipeline] enabled` with a memory tool in `pipeline.allowed_tools`; off by default) holds the memory tools captured before routing, which `rebind_memory_tools` does not reach.

  Both contradict the documented session-pinning contract and warrant a follow-up issue. This PR keeps to the delegate path the issue names.
- **Blast radius:**
  - Owner-bound RPC sessions, named administrators included, that delegate: bounded, independent, background, parallel and nested targets. This includes owned ACP and rehydrated sessions, whose delegate still carries the memory tools as parent tools.
  - Owned chat-mode sessions on SQLite (`session/new` without `exclude_memory`): their own memory tools, per-turn recall injection (where enabled) and `auto_save` (on by default) now work on the owner's private plane. On `master` they failed, as note 6 details. By default each such session now persists the user's messages to the owner's private memory and recalls them into later prompts. ACP and rehydrated sessions build with `exclude_memory` (`NoneMemory`, memory tools stripped, `auto_save` off), so their own memory is unaffected.
  - Non-SQLite backends: owned sessions' delegated memory tools now refuse. On `master` they reached the target agent's shared plane. The session's own memory tools already refused there, and still do.
  - Retrieval cache invalidation on private writes.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11198
- **Labels:** `agent`, `channel`, `channel:core`, `memory`, `runtime`, `size:L`, `tool:delegate` (applied by the path and size labelers; `risk:*` and domain labels are set by maintainers).

### What this does, simply

Each signed-in user of a ZeroClaw daemon has private memory: when their session stores or recalls a note, it goes to that user's private area, not the shared memory the operator's agents use. A session can also hand a task to another agent (delegation). The helper agent was given fresh memory tools, and those tools pointed at the helper agent's shared memory. So a user's delegated helper could read the operator's shared notes, and anything it saved landed in shared storage instead of the user's private area.

With this change the helper inherits the session's owner. Its memory tools work on the owner's private memory for the helper agent, whether the delegation runs inline, in the background, in parallel, or as a further hop. If the owner cannot be carried to the helper, the memory call is refused rather than falling back to shared storage.

Making that work also fixed a second problem. On the default SQLite backend, a signed-in chat session's own private memory was not working at all. Saving a note failed, and remembering past messages failed silently. Now those notes and auto-saved messages go to the user's private memory, which means chat sessions start keeping the user's messages there by default. Sessions with no signed-in owner behave exactly as before.

### Notes for review

1. **Constructor coverage.** `route_memory_to_principal` bails when the registry holds a `delegate` tool but the Agent has no handle to bind; `routing_refuses_a_registered_delegate_without_a_binding_handle` covers that branch. Its only production callers are the two RPC paths in `rpc/dispatch.rs` (session creation and reaped-session rehydration). Both build the Agent through `from_config_with_session_cwd_and_mcp_approval_mode`, which captures the registry's `DelegateTool` before assembly and passes it to `AgentBuilder::delegate_tool`. The only other non-test `Agent::builder()` site, the eval replay harness, never routes memory. Apart from that refusal test, the one hand-built test Agent that routes with a delegate registered calls `.delegate_tool(..)`. The early `microsoft365` return in `all_tools_with_runtime_on_thread` fires before the delegate is built, so it has neither the tool nor the handle.
2. **Why the scope is held in two places.** `Agent.memory_principal` is the session's record of where its memory is pinned. The delegate needs its own cell because child registries are built inside `DelegateTool::execute`, including inside the `'static` background and parallel workers, with no access to the Agent. The tool factory also builds the delegate before the session owner is known, hence a late-bound, write-once cell. `route_memory_to_principal` is the only writer; both sides compare the full scope and refuse a different one. A session's owner never changes after construction, so this is not live policy snapshotted into a handle.
3. **Administrators default to private.** `owner_principal_id` returns the authenticated principal's id whether or not it holds admin, and `effective_owner` feeds it to `route_memory_to_principal`. A named administrator's session and its delegates therefore work on the administrator's private plane. Shared access stays explicit (the RPC `plane: "shared"` path); delegation never selects it for an owned session.
4. **`read_memory_from` does not apply on the private plane.** `AgentScopedMemory` forwards `*_for_principal` calls unchanged, matching how `PrincipalPlaneMemory` already passes explicit scopes through. The SQLite private-plane predicate matches exactly one owner, agent alias, namespace and tenant, so a target's `read_memory_from` grants (agent UUIDs, applied only by `AgentScopedMemory`'s shared-plane reads) do not widen a delegated child's private reads. The child sees only the owner's rows for the target agent, and never another owner's rows.
5. **Dead-code attributes.** `delegate_tool` is now read in production (`route_memory_to_principal` and the factory capture), so the `#[cfg(test)]` and `#[allow(dead_code)]` are removed rather than kept, per AGENTS.md. The live-config plugin regression still reads the same field.
6. **What the wrapper forwarding changes for an owned session's own memory.** On `master`, an owned chat-mode session's routed handle is `PrincipalPlaneMemory` over `RetrievalPipeline(AgentScopedMemory(..))` from `create_memory_for_agent`. Neither wrapper overrode `*_for_principal`, so every private-plane operation hit the fail-closed trait defaults, with three effects:
   - The memory tools returned "this memory backend does not support principal-scoped memory".
   - Per-turn recall injection injected nothing, because `memory_inject` swallows recall errors.
   - `auto_save` failed silently: the turn succeeds, and only an observer event records the failed store.

   With the forwarding, all three work on the owner's private plane. `routed_session_memory_on_the_agent_stack_reaches_the_owners_plane` drives an auto-saved turn and `memory_store` through that production stack. With the wrappers reverted to `master`, the turn still succeeds and the test fails at its auto-save check. There is no cross-owner access. The forwarded scope is set only by trusted code (`route_memory_to_principal` via `memory_scope_for`), and the SQLite private predicate binds principal, agent, namespace and tenant. The scan and audit layers below already handle the private forms, and private recalls bypass the owner-less retrieval cache (`cached_pipeline_keeps_private_recalls_per_owner`).

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: the path needs an authenticated multi-principal RPC session with a delegation target. The regressions below drive the real delegate and memory stack, and reverting each fix shows the before/after.

### How I tested

New and updated regressions:

- `tools::delegate::tests::owned_delegate_child_recalls_and_stores_only_in_owners_target_plane`: bounded synchronous delegation. It binds `user:owner` under the caller's alias, as `memory_scope_for` does in production, and seeds four rows: the target agent's shared row, the owner's row under the target, the owner's row under the caller, and another owner's row under the target. The child stores and recalls. Its recall must return only the owner's target row and its own write, and the write must land under owner and target, not under owner and caller, and not on the shared plane.
- `owned_background_delegate_stores_only_in_owners_target_plane` and `owned_parallel_delegate_stores_only_in_owners_target_plane`: the same binding through the detached background worker and the parallel worker. Each rebuilds its delegate instance, and the child's write must land under owner and target only.
- `owned_delegate_without_target_config_refuses_instead_of_shared_memory`: an owned delegate with no root config refuses, and nothing reaches the shared plane.
- `agent::agent::tests::routing_refuses_a_registered_delegate_without_a_binding_handle`: routing errs, `memory_principal()` stays `None`, and the memory tools are not rebound.
- `agent::agent::tests::routed_session_memory_on_the_agent_stack_reaches_the_owners_plane`: an owned session over `create_memory_for_agent`. An auto-saved turn and `memory_store` land on the owner's plane and never on the shared plane.
- `retrieval::tests::cached_pipeline_keeps_private_recalls_per_owner`: with the hot cache enabled, two owners asking the same query each see only their own rows, and a shared recall sees neither.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `Test` and `Parallel Runtime Test` run the runtime, memory and channels suites, including the regressions above and the channels helper users. `Lint` runs the `-D warnings` clippy line. The `Check (plugins ...)` jobs run because `crates/zeroclaw-runtime` changed, and their runtime leg runs the live-config regression that reads `Agent.delegate_tool`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None known.
- **Commands run and tail output:** The first block ran at `cc958a0f6a`, this patch rebased onto current `master` with an unchanged patch-id. The second ran at `e5323c4e1a`, the same patch before that rebase. The third ran at `2a741e501c`, whose production code is identical to this patch's; every later change is inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`.

prs.title: fix(security): require tools:execute to run or approve SOPs over RPC
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `sops/run` and `sops/decide` both reach `refuse_constrained_tool_selector_for_sop` through `authorize_sop_agents`, before any run is started or resumed. That guard passed any non-admin principal whose `allowed_tools` contained `"*"` without checking the coarse `tools:execute` grant. A profile with `sops = ["execute"]` and `allowed_tools = ["*"]` but no `tools = ["execute"]` could therefore run a procedure, or approve a parked one, although the same grants give an interactive session no tools at all.
  - The guard now passes only when `principal_tool_ceiling(&auth.grants).is_none()`. That is the function sessions already use for their tool ceiling (admin first, then the required `tools:execute` grant, then the selector), so the SOP path and the session path can no longer disagree on the tool ceiling, and no admin or wildcard logic is restated.
  - The refusal branch is untouched: same `FORBIDDEN` code, same message, same `audit_auth_denial` call. Only the predicate and the doc paragraph that described it changed.
  - The SOP dispatch test fixture (`sop_scoped_ctx`) now grants `tools = ["execute"]` next to its wildcard selector. Its doc comment already said the principal has "unrestricted tools", which is only true with that grant. Without it the new rule would refuse every run in those tests, and their positive controls would stop proving anything about the agent selector.
  - Two new tests drive the real wire methods with an authenticated principal: `sop_run_and_decide_refuse_a_wildcard_selector_without_tools_execute` (run and approval refused, the parked run stays parked, and the trusted local operator is still admitted to the same procedure) and `sop_run_is_refused_once_tools_execute_is_revoked` (the same connection is admitted on `sops/run` and on `sops/decide`, then refused on its next run once only `tools:execute` is revoked). The admitted decision is a denial: the guard does not look at the decision, so a denial is admitted exactly as an approval would be, and approving here would resume the run into a real headless agent turn. Each admission control asserts the error an admitted run reaches after authorization, not merely the absence of `FORBIDDEN`.
- **Scope boundary:** Does not carry the principal's tool ceiling into the SOP engine; principals with a named tool list are still refused outright, as before. Does not change the refusal message, the audit event, SOP authoring checks, or the trigger sources (cron, webhooks, channels) that start procedures without an RPC principal. No docs change: `docs/book/src/security/authentication.md` already says SOP run and approval follow the session tool-selector rule and that a principal without `tools = ["execute"]` gets a tool-less session even with `"*"`. The `allowed_tools` doc on `PermissionProfileConfig` says the same.
  - **Pre-existing, left for follow-ups:**
    - *Nested tools.* This PR makes SOP execution match sessions on the tool ceiling only. Sessions also remove nested execution tools (`delegate`, `spawn_subagent`, `execute_pipeline`, and skill wrappers around them) from a principal whose agent selector is not `"*"`. SOP steps still run with the agent's own tool set, including those tools. The guard's doc comment now states this limit instead of claiming full parity.
    - *Unloaded procedures.* Both handlers skip `authorize_sop_agents`, this check included, when the engine does not hold the procedure. Nothing is started or resumed in that case: `sops/run` finds no procedure to start, and the approval broker fails closed (`PolicyUnavailable`) on a run whose procedure is not loaded. The remaining window is a reload that loads the procedure between the `sops/run` check and its dispatch; the RPC authoring methods do not reload the engine, so a caller cannot open that window through them. #11169 does not change either skip; its refusal of a scoped principal whose run's procedure is not loaded covers only its new `sops/cancel`.
    - *Refusal text.* It still says "constrained tool selector" for the newly refused case, whose selector is `"*"` but which lacks `tools = ["execute"]`. A reason-specific message fits better in the reconciliation with #11169, which rewrites this function.
- **Blast radius:** Only non-admin RPC principals that hold `sops:execute` and the wildcard tool selector but not `tools:execute` lose `sops/run` and `sops/decide`. Admin principals, and principals holding both the wildcard and `tools:execute`, behave as before. No executor, engine, or broker change.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11123. Related #11169: that draft rewrites this guard to take explicit grants and keeps the old `admin || wildcard` predicate. Whichever lands second should carry `principal_tool_ceiling(grants).is_none()` into the new signature, or this fix is undone.
- **Labels:** `runtime`, `risk:high`, `size:L`, `domain:security`.

### What this does, simply

Each client that connects to the ZeroClaw daemon gets a permission profile. Two separate grants matter here: permission to run SOPs (standard operating procedures: multi-step procedures that drive an agent), and permission to let agents execute tools. A tool selector can further narrow which tools a client may cause an agent to run, and `"*"` means all of them. The documented rule is that the selector only narrows the tool grant and never replaces it: a client without the tool grant gets an agent with no tools, even with `"*"`.

The check that guards starting or approving an SOP looked only at the selector, so `"*"` was enough. A client allowed to run SOPs whose tool permission had been removed could still start a procedure, or approve a waiting one, and the procedure's agents would then run their tools. This PR makes the SOP check apply the same tool ceiling as the interactive-session check, through the same function, so the two cannot disagree about whether tools are allowed at all. Admins, and clients holding both the tool grant and `"*"`, are unaffected. Clients with a narrower tool list were already refused and still are.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: the change is an authorization predicate on two RPC methods, and the new tests drive the real `sops/run` and `sops/decide` wire methods through `process_line` with an authenticated principal before and after revocation, which is the path a manual check would exercise.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Rust test jobs run the new and updated tests in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs`; the lint, fmt and rustdoc jobs cover the changed code; `check-plugin-backends` runs because the path is under `crates/zeroclaw-runtime`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None for the changed code.
- **Commands run and tail output:** see the list below.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** See below. Not verified: a live daemon with a real SOP.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A (no user-visible interface state changed; the refusal message is unchanged).
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `86dc953823` (this branch's single commit, rebased on current `master`); RPC authorization through the in-process dispatcher (`process_line`) in the `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs` tests; macOS host, rustc 1.98.0.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** see the red and green runs below.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** None.

**Red, then green.** With the fixture change and the two new tests on top of the old predicate, both new tests failed, and so did a decide-only variant I ran to watch the approval path on its own:

- `sops/run` got through authorization: `{"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"SOP subsystem not enabled"}}` (the test context has no SOP audit log, so an admitted run stops there);
- an approving `sops/decide` was accepted and resumed the parked run: `"status":"running"`.

With the fix both are `FORBIDDEN` (-32012) and the run stays `WaitingApproval`.

**What reviewers will want to check:**

- *The refusal happens before any run is created or resumed.* `handle_sops_run` calls `authorize_sop_agents(Method::SopsRun, &sop, true)` before it touches the audit logger or `dispatch_sop_event_to*`; `handle_sops_decide` calls it before `resolve_via_broker_deferred`. With `executes = true` the tool guard is the first check inside `authorize_sop_agents`. The new test asserts the parked run is still `WaitingApproval` after the refused approval, and the red run above shows the approval resuming it without the fix.
- *The fixture change does not weaken the selector tests.* With `tools:execute` granted, the tool check passes for the fixture principal, so in `sop_run_and_decide_refuse_a_procedure_run_as_an_agent_outside_the_selector` the `beta-sop` refusal can only come from the agent selector, as before. `sop_run_refuses_a_constrained_tool_selector_like_a_session` now differs from the admitted positive control only in `allowed_tools = ["calculator"]`, so it still isolates the named-selector refusal; without the grant it would be refused for the missing grant and prove less. The authoring tests never reach this guard (`executes` is false there).
- *The audit event still fires.* Only the `if` condition changed. Every refusal still runs the unchanged `audit_auth_denial` call, which records the `RPC authorization denied` WARN event with the method, reason, principal id and auth provider. The tests assert the `FORBIDDEN` code rather than the log record. The runtime does have a test log capture (`zeroclaw_log::try_install_capture_subscriber` with `subscribe_or_install`), but it is one process-wide sink. Every SOP refusal test emits an identical record for the same fixture principal (same method, reason and principal), so under the shared-process test runner an assertion could match a sibling test's record.

**Commands** (macOS, rustc 1.98.0, at this branch's head):

1. `cargo nextest run -p zeroclaw-runtime -E 'test(/sop_/)'`: `136 tests run: 136 passed, 5121 skipped`. Red run before the fix, with an earlier revision of these tests whose FORBIDDEN assertions were the same: `137 tests run: 134 passed, 3 failed` (the two new tests and the decide-only variant).
2. `./scripts/ci/rust_quality_gate.sh --strict`: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` is clean. Clippy stops at its only error, `unused import: std::sync::mpsc --> crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs:15:5`. That line is on master and untouched here: its uses are Windows- and Linux-only, so only a macOS lib-test build flags it, and Linux CI is unaffected. The script never reaches its provider-dispatch step after that error, so I ran that step on its own: `provider dispatch gate clean`.
3. `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets --features ci-all -- -D warnings -A unused_imports`: `Finished`, no warnings or errors.
4. `cargo test --no-run --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop`: passes. Its warnings are exactly master's two host-only ones (the `service/mod.rs:15` import above and a macOS linker `__eh_frame` note), so the allow in step 3 hides nothing new.
5. `cargo doc --no-deps --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop`: `Finished`, no warnings (the new intra-doc links resolve).
6. `./scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh`: `Comment hygiene gate passed.`
7. `TMPDIR=/private/tmp ZEROCLAW_PARALLEL_TEST_RUNS=1 ./scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh`: zeroclaw-runtime `5205 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored`, zeroclaw-channels `1957 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored`. `TMPDIR` is set because macOS temp dirs sit under the `/var` symlink. With the default temp dir, `rpc::dispatch::tests::forwarded_environment_demotion_while_queued_refuses_prompt_and_resume` fails: the session workspace check refuses the fixture's workspace spelling before the assertion the test expects. It fails the same way on the base commit with this change removed, and Linux CI's temp dir is not a symlink.
8. `check-plugin-backends` commands (this path triggers the job). These ran on the revision before the final one, which changed only the guard's doc comment and test code in `dispatch.rs`. Step 3 lints the final revision under `ci-all`, which includes `plugins-wasm-cranelift`, and step 4 builds it with default features:
   - `bash scripts/ci/plugin_backend_change_filter.test.sh`: `plugin backend change filter tests: pass`
   - `cargo check --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --no-default-features --features` with `plugins-wasm-cranelift`, `plugins-wasm-pulley` and `plugins-wasmtime`: all `Finished`
   - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --no-default-features --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib`: `260 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib -- plugin_runtime:: tools::tests::shared_ceiling tools::tests::repeated_loader tools::tests::auto_discover tools::tests::colliding_plugin`: `22 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test component -- plugin_info_cli`: `4 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --bin zeroclaw`: `548 passed; 3 failed` on the first run. The 3 were the `plugin_load_check` tests, which build a WASM fixture and need the `wasm32-wasip2` target, which this host lacked. After installing it, those 3 rerun with `--exact`: `3 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib agent::plugin_live_config`: `2 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test plugin_channel_runtime_e2e`: `4 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test channel_egress_e2e`: `3 passed; 0 failed`
   - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test channel_plugin_e2e --test egress_plugin_e2e --test tool_plugin_timeout_e2e --test reference_plugin --test reference_plugin_e2e --test tool_plugin_e2e`: `42 passed; 0 failed` across the six targets (14, 9, 5, 9, 3 and 2). The one ignored test is the existing subprocess helper in `reference_plugin_e2e`, which its parent test runs and which passed there.

   The last four ran after `wasm32-wasip2` was installed, and the code was unchanged.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. The change removes access: a principal lacking `tools:execute` can no longer run or approve SOPs over RPC.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No (fixtures use the synthetic `alice` roster principal and uid 4242).
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No, for one grant combination: a non-admin profile with `sops = ["execute"]` and `allowed_tools = ["*"]` but no `tools = ["execute"]` is now refused on `sops/run` and on every `sops/decide` decision (approve, deny, amend and revise). So an approver-only profile without `tools:execute` can no longer deny a parked run either; principals with a named tool list were already refused the same way. That combination contradicts the documented rule, so the old behaviour was the bug.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: a profile that should keep running or approving SOPs over RPC adds `tools = ["execute"]` to its `[permission_profiles.<name>.grants]`.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>` (one commit, no migration or persisted state).
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. Operators can restore access per profile by granting `tools = ["execute"]`.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** `sops/run` or `sops/decide` returning `FORBIDDEN` with "Principal has a constrained tool selector; procedures run outside per-session tool narrowing and are refused to it", and a matching `RPC authorization denied` WARN record carrying the method, principal id and auth provider.

prs.title: fix(rpc): stop pre-approving shell commands in cron/add and cron/patch
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `cron/add` passed `approved = true` ("RPC calls are pre-approved") into `add_shell_job_with_approval`. That skipped the supervised-autonomy gate that the CLI (`cron::add_shell_job`) and the gateway (`POST /api/cron`, `approved = false`) both apply. An RPC request is not an operator approval, so `cron/add` now passes `false`.
  - `cron/patch` validated a replacement command with `approved = true` for the same reason. It now also passes `false`, so the patch path cannot store a command that `cron/add` would refuse.
  - Two regression tests prove that a medium-risk command (`touch`, allowlisted but medium-risk under a supervised profile with `require_approval_for_medium_risk`) is refused by `cron/add` and `cron/patch` and never stored, while a low-risk command still succeeds.
  - Review follow-up: both handlers now recheck the caller's authority at the write, not only at the gate. The cron store writes synchronously and can wait out SQLite's five-second busy timeout, so a revocation published during that wait used to be ignored. After the agent selector passes, each handler now does three things in order:
    - takes the config write lock;
    - re-resolves the caller against the policy in force and repeats the agent selector with those fresh grants;
    - holds the lock through the store write.

    Every accepted-policy publication, from RPC or the gateway, takes that lock, so none can land between the recheck and the commit. `cron/patch` also reads the config again under the lock, so a replacement command is validated against the policy it commits under.
  - Review follow-up: `cron/patch` of an **agent** job is limited to the local operator. An agent job keeps its stored tool list and runs later under the agent's policy, so a new prompt from a narrower principal would run with tools that principal does not hold. A scoped principal or a named administrator now gets `FORBIDDEN`, with an audited denial, until the runtime can carry an editor's authority to the run and re-check it there. Shell jobs keep their policy-validated patch path. `cron/trigger` of an agent job follows the same rule, because a run on demand executes the stored prompt under the stored tool list.
  - Second review follow-up: the same workload could be installed through the agent-facing tools. `cron_add`, `cron_update`, `cron_run` and `schedule` now declare `requires_unrestricted_principal`, the marker `delegate`, `spawn_subagent` and `pipeline` already carry. Only the shared operator's RPC session keeps them. A named principal's session withholds every tool with this marker, whether it is scoped, a named administrator, or holds wildcard tools and agents, because its grants can be withdrawn while the work it started still runs. `send_message_to_peer` carries the marker too: a peer agent runs a detached turn with its own tools, so it could otherwise schedule the job for the principal. The rule and the peer fix are the same commits as on #11176: the shared-operator predicate is ported from it, and the peer fix is cherry-picked. The CLI and channels are unchanged.
  - Second review follow-up: wrappers no longer carry approval. The runtime writes a tool's `approved` argument only on the call it dispatched, under that call's own name. A `pipeline` step and a skill alias each call their child tool directly, and the model supplied that child's `approved: true`. Both wrappers now clear `approved` on a child that takes runtime approval, so a nested medium-risk command meets the supervised gate. The list of such tools moved to `zeroclaw_api::tool::takes_runtime_approval`, so the runtime's own sanitizer and the wrappers share it.
  - Second review follow-up: a paired-token revocation is ordered against these writes. The gateway's device revoke, token rotation, admin single-device revoke and revoke-all used to remove the token from the live set first and take the config write lock only to persist. A cron write that had checked the token under the lock could therefore commit after the token was gone. They now go through `PairingGuard::revoke_under_config_write_lock`, which takes the lock before anything changes. Under the lock it runs one synchronous closure that removes the device row (or clears the registry) and the live token together, then returns the guard so the token set is persisted under it. A write that checked the token first commits before the revocation lands, and one that checks after sees the token gone. Because nothing is deleted before the lock is held, a request the gateway's timeout drops while it waits has changed nothing and can simply be retried. The boundary also re-checks the requesting caller under the lock, before deleting anything, so a device revoked while its own request was queued is refused. Rotation holds the lock until its new pairing code is issued. The three per-device paths share `revoke_device_credential`, so another device surface can reuse the same step.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - Scheduled and manual execution are unchanged; they already re-validate with `approved = false`.
  - Agent-job support in `cron/add` is unchanged.
  - The gateway's cron routes and the CLI are unchanged; only the gateway's token revocation paths change.
  - Not changed here, and needs a design decision: a job keeps running after whoever installed it loses their grants. Named principals can no longer install agent work through RPC sessions or tools. Two cases remain: shell jobs a named principal adds through RPC `cron/add` with its cron grant, and jobs installed before this change. Closing it means storing the submitter's authority with the job and re-resolving it on every run. That is the cron site of the authority-recheck work, not a guard this PR can add.
- **Blast radius:**
  - RPC clients (zerocode/TUI, and a future external gateway) that add or patch shell cron jobs.
  - Under `autonomy = supervised`, a medium-risk (when `require_approval_for_medium_risk`) or high-risk command is now refused at creation with `requires explicit approval`, instead of being stored.
  - Full-autonomy profiles are unaffected.
  - A scoped or named principal can no longer patch an agent cron job over RPC.
  - `cron/add` and `cron/patch` now queue on the config write lock, as config writes and `session/new` already do.
  - A named principal's RPC sessions no longer offer `delegate`, `spawn_subagent`, `pipeline`, `cron_add`, `cron_update`, `cron_run`, `schedule` or `send_message_to_peer`. This includes named administrators and wildcard selectors. Its RPC `cron/*` methods are unchanged apart from the agent-job rules above.
  - A device revoke or rotation whose caller was revoked while it waited is refused with 401 and changes nothing.
  - Under supervised autonomy, a medium- or high-risk command inside a `pipeline` step or a skill alias is refused unless it is called directly, where the runtime's approval applies.
  - Gateway device revoke, rotation and revoke-all wait for any in-flight config write before deleting the device or removing the token. A request dropped while it waits leaves both in place.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #7432
- **Labels:** (set by maintainers)

### What this does, simply

A cron job scheduled over the RPC socket (zerocode/TUI) was treated as though a human had already approved its shell command. The CLI and the web dashboard both ask for approval under supervised autonomy. With this change the RPC path follows the same rule.

Related gaps are also closed:
- A permission removed, or a device revoked, while a cron write was waiting on the database now stops that write or waits for it to finish.
- Changing or running an agent cron job on demand is reserved for the local operator, because the job runs with its own stored tools, not the caller's. This applies over RPC, and a constrained session can no longer reach the cron tools that would do the same.
- A tool run inside a `pipeline` or a skill alias can no longer claim an approval nobody gave.

In practice the old behavior did not let the command *run*: every scheduled run re-checks the command without approval and refuses it. What it did was store a job the policy would not accept, which then failed on every tick. After this change the job is refused up front with the policy reason.

### Present in v0.8.5?

Partly.
- `git show v0.8.5:crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs` has the same `true, // RPC calls are pre-approved` in `handle_cron_add` (line 3143). It was introduced in #6848.
- v0.8.5 has no command validation in `handle_cron_patch` (no `validate_shell_command` call), so the patch half is master-only.

Because execution re-validates with `approved = false` in both v0.8.5 and master (`cron/scheduler.rs`, `execute_and_persist_job`), I do not think this alone justifies a v0.8.5 security patch. It is an approval-gate inconsistency that stores unrunnable jobs; it does not bypass execution.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The RPC tests drive the real handlers or `process_line`, and the tool tests go through the production tool dispatch. The revocation tests use deterministic pauses rather than sleeps: they hold a competing SQLite writer or the config write lock, and poll the revoking future once, before the change they race.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `CI Required Gate` runs the lib tests of every changed crate, including the new ones.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```
# merge 42b73abfc1: upstream/master f0ae8c8bd8 merged in (one conflict, check_agent_selector_with_grants added on both sides; master's copy kept)
$ cargo check -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-tools -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-gateway --all-targets   # exit 0

$ cargo clippy <same five crates> --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings
# one error, pre-existing on master and outside this PR: unused `std::sync::mpsc` in service/mod.rs,
# gated cfg(any(windows, test)); a --keep-going re-run reports nothing else

# head 88e4594791: caller re-check under the revocation lock; shared-operator predicate and peer fix shared with #11176
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib -- api::tests::device_ api::tests::revoke api::tests::rotate api::tests::a_device_request admin_paircode pairing

test result: FAILED. 2844 passed; 1 failed   # the one failure is the macOS-only forwarded_environment test noted below

# head 3cdebef0a1: the revocation boundary now covers the device-row deletion too
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib -- api::tests::device_ api::tests::revoke api::tests::rotate admin_paircode pairing
```

- **Other tests in the module:** after the master merge, `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- rpc:: agent:: tools:: cron::` gives 2913 passed and 0 failed on macOS; the earlier macOS-only `forwarded_environment_demotion_while_queued_refuses_prompt_and_resume` failure no longer reproduces.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - I confirmed that scheduled runs (`execute_and_persist_job`) and `cron/trigger` (`run_manual_job`) already validate with `approved = false`, so no execution path changes.
  - I confirmed that the gateway's `publish_persisted` publishes into the shared RPC authority under the same process-wide config write lock, which is what makes that lock the publication barrier.
  - In the daemon, the RPC context and the gateway both take their config write lock from `zeroclaw_config::write_lock::shared_config_write_lock()`. A gateway revocation holding it is therefore ordered against an RPC cron write holding it.
  - The four gateway paths that revoke a live token now use the ordered boundary: device revoke, rotation, admin single-device revoke and revoke-all. Each deletes its device rows inside the boundary, not before it. The compensating revokes of a token minted in the same failed pairing request are unchanged, because no connection can hold that token yet.
  - I did not run a live daemon.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** A full workspace `cargo test` and a workspace clippy were not run. Tests ran for each affected crate: `zeroclaw-tools`, `zeroclaw-runtime`, `zeroclaw-gateway` and `zeroclaw-config`. CI Lint covers clippy.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. This narrows them.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A. The change tightens an approval gate to match the CLI and gateway. It also rechecks authority at the cron write, narrows who may change or run an agent job, and removes a model-controlled approval path through wrappers. Pairing-token revocation keeps its semantics; only its ordering against in-flight writes changes.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes for full-autonomy and low-risk commands. Under supervised autonomy, RPC `cron/add` and `cron/patch` now refuse medium- and high-risk commands that were previously stored and then failed at run time. RPC `cron/patch` and `cron/trigger` on an agent job from a scoped or named principal now return `FORBIDDEN`. Named principals' RPC sessions lose the nested, scheduling and peer-messaging tools; only the shared operator keeps them. Wrappers no longer pass `approved` to a child, and a device request whose caller was revoked while it waited is refused.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No. `zeroclaw_api::tool` gains `takes_runtime_approval` and `clear_runtime_approval`, and `PairingGuard` gains `revoke_under_config_write_lock` and `revoke_token_hash_ordered`; nothing existing is removed.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:**
  - RPC `cron/add` returns `Cron add failed: blocked by security policy: Command requires explicit approval` for a command a client expects to schedule.
  - RPC `cron/patch` or `cron/trigger` on an agent job returns `FORBIDDEN` for a non-operator principal.
  - A named principal's session reports the cron, nested and peer tools as unavailable.
  - A nested medium-risk command in a pipeline or skill alias fails with `requires explicit approval`.

prs.title: refactor(rpc): extract the wire contract into zeroclaw-rpc-proto with an OpenRPC drift check
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Current reviewed head:** `ec00bf0a1287ea0192ac0d3e22da0f59c1ca83fd`, after the subsequent master merge. The tracked document now contains 99 methods and 160 component schemas. The `f74d25a0f4` counts and local command output below describe the earlier tested revision.

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions); rebased onto 4f93bf5399, then `upstream/master` f0ae8c8bd8 merged in (merge commit f74d25a0f4, not a rebase, since the PR is under review). The rebases and the merge carry master's later RPC additions into the proto: `config/set-many`, `events/history`, the memory `plane`/`agent` fields, the session-message cursor fields, and the bounded replayable subscription hub's surface (`events/subscribe`, `subscription/cancel`, the `events/event` and `subscription/lagged` notifications, `SubscribeParams`, the extended `LogsSubscribeResult`, `SubscriptionCancelParams`/`Result`, `SubscriptionLagged`), and the transport-hardening upload surface (`file/upload/begin`, `file/upload/chunk`, `file/upload/commit` with `FileUploadBeginParams`/`Result`, `FileUploadChunkParams`/`Result`, `FileUploadCommitParams`; commit returns the existing `FileEntryResult`). Merge conflicts were the registry (proto note kept, methods ported) and the moved types region (deletion kept, types ported); the tracked OpenRPC document was regenerated (97 methods, 157 schemas).
- **What changed and why:**
  - New crate `zeroclaw-rpc-proto`: the daemon RPC wire contract as pure data. It holds the `Method` enum with its single wire-name table, a per-method params/result contract (`Method::contract`, arm-complete like `authz`), every wire-stable request/response/notification payload type from `rt/rpc/types.rs`, the notification names, the error-code table, and the SOP graph projection re-exports. It depends on `zeroclaw-api`, `zeroclaw-config`, `zeroclaw-sop-graph` and serde, without depending on `zeroclaw-runtime`, so an RPC client can link the contract without linking the daemon. Its foundation dependencies still bring async I/O libraries transitively.
  - The runtime re-exports it. `zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::types::*` and `crate::rpc::dispatch::Method` keep resolving; `Method::authz()` becomes the `MethodAuthzExt` extension trait in `dispatch.rs` because it names runtime grants. Types whose fields are runtime-owned (doctor diagnostics, cron jobs, skill frontmatter, quickstart descriptors) stay in the runtime and are listed as external in the contract.
  - `cargo generate openrpc` renders the contract into `docs/book/src/architecture/zeroclaw-rpc.openrpc.json` (methods, params/result schema refs, authorization classification, notifications, error codes, component schemas). `cargo generate openrpc --check` runs in the `Installer Drift` CI job so the document cannot drift from the code.
  - Schema derives (`schema-export`-gated) added to the `zeroclaw-api` wire types the contract embeds: runtime status, plan entries, token-count source, model pricing.
- **Scope boundary:** No wire change. No method, field, name or default changes. No client (zerocode, gateway) switches to the new crate yet. `Method::authz` classification, dispatch, transport are unchanged. The zerocode exact-version gate, protocol negotiation and turn lifetime are separate PRs.
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw-runtime` (rpc types/dispatch/session import paths), `zeroclaw-api` (additive cfg-gated derives), `xtask`, CI `installer-drift` job, workspace manifest and lockfile. Every `use zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::types::…` in the gateway and zerocode compiles unchanged.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11000, #11001, #7432
- **Labels:** `ci`, `docs`, `dependencies`, `runtime`, `tests`, `distinguished contributor`, `domain:architecture`, `risk:medium`, `size:XL`, `type:refactor`, `release:v0.9.0`, `needs-author-action`

### What this does, simply

Until now, the only description of what the daemon's RPC accepts and returns was the Rust code inside the runtime. A client that wanted the types had to link the whole daemon or hand-copy them (zerocode hand-parses JSON for this reason). This PR moves the wire types and the method table into a small crate any client can depend on, and turns them into a machine-readable OpenRPC document that CI keeps in sync with the code.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, optional.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** none user-facing; the RPC contract document and crate boundary.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a checkout of this branch.
- **Steps to run:** `cargo generate openrpc --check`; then edit any `Method::contract` arm or wire type and rerun to see the drift failure; `cargo test -p zeroclaw-rpc-proto --features schema-export`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the check reports in sync; a contract edit makes it fail with the regenerate hint; the proto tests pass.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** no `zeroclaw-rpc-proto` crate, no `cargo generate openrpc` subcommand, no contract document.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `CI Required Gate` (fmt, clippy `ci-all`, workspace tests including the `architecture` test, `Installer Drift` with the new OpenRPC check).
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Local runs are macOS only.
- **Commands run and tail output:** (head `f74d25a0f4`, base `upstream/master` f0ae8c8bd8 merged in, rustc 1.96.1, macOS aarch64; affected crates only)

```text
$ cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-rpc-proto
test result: ok. 24 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
$ cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- rpc::
test result: ok. 658 passed; 0 failed
$ cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-rpc-proto --no-deps --all-targets -- -D warnings   # clean (xtask too)
$ cargo doc --locked --no-deps -p zeroclaw-rpc-proto                                  # 0 warnings
$ cargo test --locked -p xtask openrpc
test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed   # descriptors, Draft 7 walk + validator, required-first ordering
$ cargo run --locked -p xtask --bin generate -- openrpc            # debug build of xtask
openrpc: wrote docs/book/src/architecture/zeroclaw-rpc.openrpc.json
$ cargo run --locked -p xtask --bin generate -- openrpc --check

$ cargo test --locked --test architecture

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check                                        # clean
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh

```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The generated document lists all 97 `Method::ALL` entries once, 157 component schemas, 4 notifications and 17 error codes, with `info.version` equal to `RPC_PROTOCOL_VERSION`; per-method sides are 100 typed (schema `$ref`), 24 untyped (free-form JSON the daemon shapes at runtime) and 35 external (named runtime- or api-owned types with their owner recorded). The `authz` classification renders per method (`initialize` → handshake, `session/new` → `sessions:create`). A deliberate contract edit makes `--check` fail with the regenerate hint (verified while iterating on the generator). The reported local results above include the runtime `rpc::` suite and workspace `architecture` test at `f74d25a0f4`.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `f74d25a0f4`; commands above.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Workspace-wide clippy and the full runtime test suite were not run locally (disk discipline: affected crates only); CI runs them. `xtask` gains `jsonschema` as a dev-dependency at the version `zeroclaw-plugins` already pins, so the lockfile changes by one entry.

### Adversarial review findings (three MODERATE), fixed at this head

The review of head b1781f2149 found that the OpenRPC document exported every parameter-bearing method as one by-name descriptor named `params` whose schema was the whole params object, so a conforming OpenRPC client would send `{"params": {"params": {...}}}` and the daemon would reject it with `INVALID_PARAMS`. The generator now expands a typed params struct into one descriptor per property, named by the wire key with `required` from the schema (the struct's schema stays in `components`); shapes it cannot enumerate (free-form objects, types another crate owns without an exported schema) produce no descriptors and say so in `x-zeroclaw-params` rather than inventing a key. A contract test builds `session/close` and `initialize` requests from the descriptors and parses them with the daemon's own types.

The re-review of head 2f74e5d0ac found two more contract defects, both fixed here. (1) OpenRPC 1.3.2 schema objects are JSON Schema Draft 7 but the generator used the 2020-12 dialect, so tuple types were emitted as `prefixItems`, which a Draft 7 consumer ignores: the `LogsQueryResult.next_cursor` schema accepted `[1, 2]` although the wire type is `Option<(String, String)>`. The generator now uses Draft 7 settings and builds parameter descriptors from the definitions after the Draft 7 transforms run, records the dialect in `x-zeroclaw.schema_dialect`, and a test walks the whole document for later-dialect keywords and validates the cursor schema with a Draft 7 validator (accepts `null` and two strings; rejects `[1, 2]`, wrong lengths, mixed elements). (2) Nine methods listed optional parameters before required ones; descriptors are now ordered required first, alphabetical within each group, with an assertion across every method.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`No`)
- New external network calls? (`No`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`No`)
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: n/a. Authorization classification stays in the runtime and is untouched; the proto crate carries no policy.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? (`Yes`) Pure move plus additive derives; every wire name, field and default is unchanged and covered by the moved unit tests.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? (`No`) A new maintainer subcommand `cargo generate openrpc` exists; no user-facing CLI change.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? (`No`)

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the squash commit for this PR.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Compilation failures in consumers of the moved RPC definitions, or generated contract descriptions that disagree with daemon replies.

prs.title: feat(tools): agent-facing config authoring with operator-approved policy previews
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Moves JSON Patch parsing, typed coercion, property metadata, secret handling, and in-memory application into `zeroclaw-config`, so the gateway and CLI no longer maintain separate patch engines or error contracts.
  - Adds an agent-facing `config_patch` tool. The host renders the approval summary from the effective operations, including the affected agent's resolved-policy diff, persisted comments, and truncation. Secret values are redacted before approval, audit, logs, SOP capture, progress output, and client events.
  - Keeps authority with the operator. `locked_down` does not register the tool; `balanced` always asks; bounded delegates, pipelines, skill aliases, and unattended loops cannot acquire it; ordinary chat channels cannot approve it; authenticated paired clients and the terminal can.
  - Binds persistence to the reviewed config revision and changes only the file on disk. `config_patch` joins `master`'s process-wide `shared_config_write_lock()` from its fresh read through the save — after approval, never across the preview or an approval wait — and the save re-checks the exact source bytes before one atomic replace. The running process does not gain newly written permissions until reload or restart.
  - Gives every prompted patch an HMAC-authenticated, per-call preview binding over a fresh nonce, the exact operations, and the exact config bytes. Identical concurrent patches cannot overwrite each other, and there is no bounded preview map whose eviction can erase an outstanding review.
  - Routes denied, replaced, and hook-cancelled synthetic event pairs through the resolved tool's redaction boundary. Events now describe the effective post-hook call, retain the original ID only for correlation, and expose `{}` for unresolved tools instead of reflecting raw arguments.
- **Rebase note:** Rebased onto `master` c44909b1ed. Conflict resolutions keep both sides: the operator-only refusal wraps `master`'s narration flush barrier, which now runs only on the branch that actually prompts; `write_lock.rs` holds `master`'s transaction lock and this branch's per-path disk lock with one documented order (transaction first); both sides' new WebSocket regressions are kept. `master`'s new `TurnCtx::for_route` builds the context the tool phase receives, so it now carries the tool registry — an empty slice would have compiled and silently disabled operator-only gating and redaction on routed turns. `SOUL.md` and `USER.md` were removed from the branch history, not only the diff.
- **Scope boundary:** This does not add a proposal queue, asynchronous review UI, live config reload, new risk-profile semantics, or a general input channel for models. Approval remains synchronous within the turn.
- **Blast radius:** Shared config-patch ownership used by the gateway and CLI; the defaulted `Tool` approval/presentation methods and their wrappers; runtime tool assembly, approval routing, persistence, audit/log/SOP capture, and paired WebSocket approval.
- **Linked issue(s):** Supersedes #9828.
- **Labels:** `enhancement`, `docs`, `core`, `agent`, `config`, `gateway`, `runtime`, `skills`, `tool`, `tests`, `distinguished contributor`, `channel:core`, `tool:delegate`, `domain:security`, `domain:architecture`, `risk:high`, `size:XL`, `cli`

## Review map

Where each finding in @tidux's review (5202114133, on `5165efe2ac`) is addressed on this head (cb5b1d63cc). The zeroclaw-reviewer bot's comment on the same head raised the same issues.

| Finding | Addressed in | Pinned by |
|---|---|---|
| 🔴 Unauthenticated WebSocket treated as an operator approval surface | 2ef1450cd8 — `WsApprovalChannel` carries the connection's authenticated subject; `is_operator_approval_surface` is true only when one exists, and pairing-disabled sockets never have one | `anonymous_websocket_cannot_approve_config_patch` (real `/ws/chat`, pairing off, auto-approve profile: no prompt, denial, config bytes unchanged); `operator_surface_tracks_authentication_not_the_transport` |
| 🔴 Operator-only not structural: skill aliases, auto-approve profiles, delegates | a60fc20f3e — the gate forces a prompt for operator-only tools regardless of `NotRequired`, auto-approve, Full, or session grants, and denies with no approval manager; `SkillBuiltinTool` forwards the marker and summary; skill elevation rejects operator-only targets; independent/bounded delegate and pipeline registries drop them. aec285bd5b — route-specific turn contexts keep the registry the gate reads | `operator_only_config_patch_cannot_be_hidden_by_a_skill_alias`, `independent_delegate_excludes_direct_and_pipeline_config_patch_routes`, `bounded_delegate_excludes_config_patch_without_an_operator_surface`, `validate_rejects_operator_only_child_even_when_globally_allowed`, `full_profile_cannot_bypass_operator_only_approval`, `absent_manager_cannot_bypass_operator_only_approval`, `route_specific_context_keeps_the_tool_registry` |
| 🔴 Preview not bound to the bytes written; writers not serialized | a60fc20f3e — per-call HMAC binding over a fresh nonce, the operations, and the source bytes, required on every execution, with caller-supplied bindings stripped at the gate; one revision-checked atomic replace that fails closed on drift. 5cf3b620d9 — `config_patch` joins `master`'s `shared_config_write_lock()` from its fresh read through the save, only after approval. ecd3eab005 — forced agent-then-gateway regression | `drift_between_preview_and_execute_is_refused_and_nothing_is_written`, `model_supplied_preview_binding_is_rejected`, `preview_binding_rejects_operations_changed_after_review`, `concurrent_identical_previews_keep_distinct_config_bindings`, `concurrent_disjoint_previews_cannot_overwrite_a_new_revision`, `concurrent_agent_and_gateway_patches_preserve_the_gateway_write`, `gateway_patch_after_an_agent_patch_preserves_both_writes`, `execute_waits_for_the_process_wide_config_transaction` |
| 🔴 Denied, replaced, and hook-cancelled events leak raw patch arguments; unknown fields survive | a60fc20f3e — synthetic events are built from the post-hook name and the tool's redacted projection; the schema is `additionalProperties: false` at both levels and unknown fields are rejected before any sink | `denied_config_patch_emits_only_the_redacted_post_hook_call`, `replaced_config_patch_emits_only_the_redacted_post_hook_call`, `hook_cancelled_config_patch_uses_the_shared_redacted_pair`, `invalid_unknown_patch_fields_never_reach_synthetic_events` (sentinel secret on a real secret path) |
| 🔴 Unrelated identity files and a false PII answer | `SOUL.md` and `USER.md` are removed from the branch history, not only the diff: no commit on this head adds them. The PII answer below is accurate for both | — |
| 🔴 Public artifacts describe a different revision | This body: `Supersedes #9828` with the attribution section, the live label snapshot, and Testing regenerated from this head. The branch is rebased onto `master` c44909b1ed and merges cleanly | Required CI on this head: `CI Required Gate` success |
| 🟡 Comment-write failure still reports `saved: true` | a60fc20f3e — approved comments are written in the same atomic replace as the values; an approved comment whose target is not persisted is an error, not a log line | `approved_values_and_comments_are_saved_together` covers the joint write; the failure path is a code guard in `Config::save_patch_if_source_unchanged`, without a dedicated test |
| 🟡 XL shape carries unrelated files | The identity files are gone from history; the remaining diff is the patch engine, the tool, host previews, and the containment | — |

Two changes arose during the rebase rather than from the review: aec285bd5b (above), because `master`'s new `TurnCtx::for_route` predates the `tools` field and an empty slice would have compiled while disabling operator-only gating and redaction on routed turns; and the compatibility note below, because unknown per-operation members are now rejected in the shared parser that also backs `PATCH /api/config`.

The code-scanning alert on this head (`detect-insecure-websocket`, `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/ws.rs`) is the test's loopback `ws://` URL. The Semgrep job is report-only, and `.semgrepignore` routes inline-test WebSocket false positives to dismissal in the Security tab.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface: cli` for terminal approval and `surface: web` for paired WebSocket approval
- **Setup / preconditions:** Use a `balanced` agent with a disposable config. Pair the web client before testing its approval path; leave a second client unpaired for the refusal case.
- **Steps to run:** Ask the agent to change a policy-relevant setting such as another agent's `risk_profile`. Inspect the approval summary, approve from the terminal, repeat from the paired client, then repeat from the unpaired client. Include a secret-valued operation when inspecting emitted tool events.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The host-computed prompt shows the effective operations and resolved-policy before/after state, redacts secret values, and states that the change is not live until reload. Terminal and paired approval persist the reviewed patch. An unpaired or ordinary chat surface receives no operator prompt, leaves the config unchanged, and receives only redacted synthetic tool-call arguments.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** There is no agent-facing `config_patch` tool. An agent with shell access must perform a raw file edit without this host-computed preview, revision binding, or operator-surface boundary.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required CI on exact head cb5b1d63cc — https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/35980860123/job/107574582806 — `CI Required Gate`: success. It covers formatting, Clippy, all-target/default/no-default/plugin-backend builds, unit and parallel runtime tests, Security, Semgrep, cross-platform checks, and docs.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** CI does not drive a human terminal prompt or a real browser session. The anonymous-WebSocket path is covered at the production boundary by `anonymous_websocket_cannot_approve_config_patch` (real `/ws/chat`, pairing off, auto-approve profile). The live terminal and paired-browser smoke last ran on `68c828d` and was not repeated on this head.
- **Commands run and tail output:** on cb5b1d63cc, macOS, Rust 1.96.1 (CI's declared MSRV toolchain; CI's 1.98 `Lint` job is the Clippy authority):

```text
# full gates on ecd3eab005 (cb5b1d63cc changes only two test lines; see below)
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                   exit 0
cargo check --locked --all-targets -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-config \
  -p zeroclaw-gateway -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-tools -p zeroclaw
                                                             exit 0, 0 warnings
cargo check --locked -p zeroclaw --no-default-features       exit 0, 0 warnings
cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-config \
  -p zeroclaw-gateway -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-tools -p zeroclaw
  zeroclaw-api      268 passed; 0 failed
  zeroclaw-config  1681 passed; 0 failed
  zeroclaw-gateway  559 passed; 0 failed
  zeroclaw-runtime 4733 passed; 4 failed; 6 ignored
  zeroclaw-tools   2004 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored
  zeroclaw lib/main 276 + 392 passed; 0 failed
  all 43 binaries: 10580 passed; 4 failed; 17 ignored
  the 4 failures, none in code this branch touches:
    tools::delegate::tests::{background_task_result_persisted_to_disk,
      check_result_retrieves_persisted_background_result,
      list_results_includes_background_tasks}
      -> an unrelated local process holds localhost:11434 (Ollama's default)
         and never answers; all 3 pass with only that port denied
    rpc::local::tests::reload_replacement_generation_waits_for_durable_session_prompt_local
      -> "socket never appeared" under machine load; 5/5 pass in isolation

# on cb5b1d63cc (zeroclaw_spawn::spawn! for the disallowed tokio::spawn; nosemgrep on a loopback ws:// URL)
cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-config \
  -p zeroclaw-gateway -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-tools -p zeroclaw -- -D warnings
                                                             exit 0
execute_waits_for_the_process_wide_config_transaction        ok
anonymous_websocket_cannot_approve_config_patch              ok
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Mutation checks on this head's code, each restored byte-identical afterward: disabling skill-alias rejection of operator-only targets fails `operator_only_config_patch_cannot_be_hidden_by_a_skill_alias`; removing `config_patch`'s transaction-lock acquisition fails `execute_waits_for_the_process_wide_config_transaction`; giving routed contexts an empty registry fails `route_specific_context_keeps_the_tool_registry`; switching gateway persistence to a full-snapshot save fails `gateway_patch_after_an_agent_patch_preserves_both_writes`. The three `tools::delegate` background-task tests fail locally only because an unrelated process on this machine listens on Ollama's default port (`localhost:11434`) and never answers; with only that port denied to the test process they pass on this head's binary. None of them is touched by this branch.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A; this changes functional prompt and event content, not layout or rendering.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** cb5b1d63cc; runtime approval gate, gateway `/ws/chat`, and gateway `PATCH /api/config` via the tests named above.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** An anonymous WebSocket receives no operator prompt and the config file is unchanged; a paired surface or the terminal can approve; a denied, replaced, or hook-cancelled call emits only redacted arguments.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** The live terminal/paired smoke was not repeated on this head; the changed boundaries are covered by the mutation-checked tests above and required CI.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **Yes.** `config_patch` can write `config.toml`. Registration is risk-policy controlled, `balanced` always requires an operator, operator-only tools are excluded from unattended and bounded-delegation routes, persistence is revision-bound and serialized, and changes are disk-only until reload.
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **Yes.** The tool may set secret config paths. Secret values are rendered as `[redacted]` or `populated`, never echoed through approval, result, audit, log, SOP, progress, executed-event, or synthetic-event surfaces; dedicated tests cover both execution and pre-execution refusal paths.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **Yes.** Model-authored operations and comments appear only inside a host-structured, size-bounded approval summary. The model cannot supply the policy interpretation or free-form rationale shown to the operator, and approval remains on authenticated operator surfaces.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: The new write capability and model-authored content are constrained by host-owned rendering, redaction, policy registration, operator-only approval, exact-source persistence, writer serialization, and no live-process policy mutation.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **Yes**
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **Yes.** This adds the agent-facing tool and consolidates existing CLI/gateway patch behavior; existing config files and commands remain valid.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No**
- Backward compatible? **No, for one narrow case.** `PATCH /api/config` and `zeroclaw config patch` now reject a JSON Patch operation carrying members other than `op`, `path`, `value`, and `comment`. RFC 6902 §4 says such members are ignored; this API fails closed instead because patch operations reach approval, audit, and event sinks. Well-formed requests are unaffected.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: remove any members other than `op`, `path`, `value`, and `comment` from patch operations sent to `PATCH /api/config` or `zeroclaw config patch`. No config migration is required. To use agent-authored config patches, select a profile that registers `config_patch`; `balanced` presents every patch to an operator, while `locked_down` leaves the tool unavailable.
- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the eventual squash/merge commit with `git revert <merged-commit>` and deploy the prior binary. For immediate containment before redeploy, move affected agents to `locked_down`, where `config_patch` is not registered.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** No dedicated feature flag. The existing risk-profile registration boundary provides the containment toggle: `locked_down` excludes the tool.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A config-patch approval summary that does not match the persisted operation, unexpected operator prompts on unpaired/chat surfaces, raw secret values in `ToolCall` events, revision-drift or concurrent-write errors, or a config file changing after a refused request.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

- Superseded PRs + authors: #9828 by @JordanTheJet
- Scope materially carried forward: the shared JSON Patch engine, the agent-facing `config_patch` tool, host-computed approval previews, and the containment retained at #9828's head fbb244eeeb — authenticated-only WebSocket operator approval, structural operator-only exclusion from skill aliases, delegates, and pipelines, per-call HMAC preview binding with source-byte identity, serialized revision-checked persistence, and redacted synthetic events.
- `Co-authored-by` trailers added in commit messages for incorporated contributors? No
- If `No`, why: the superseded work has the same sole author; there is no other contributor to credit.

prs.title: fix(cron): move a declarative job's stored owner when its declaration moves
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - Cron ownership lives in `[agents.<x>].cron_jobs`, so an operator can move a declaration between agents while its id stays the same. `sync_declarative_jobs` resolves the owner with `config.agent_for_cron_job` on **insert**, but neither **update** path did — an existing row kept whichever alias it was first created under.
  - Every agent-scoped operation filters on that stored alias. `get_job_for_agent` selects `WHERE id = ?1 AND agent_alias = ?2`, and the agent-facing update and delete do the same, while the scheduler resolves the owner from live config. After a move the two disagree.
  - Consequence: the job executes as the new owner, but only the **old** owner can reach it through the cron tools. The new owner cannot see the job it owns; the old owner can still delete a job it does not.
  - An unclaimed declaration now skips rather than falling back, so a row no enabled agent owns does not stay reachable by whoever owned it last.
- **Scope boundary:** Only the two declarative-sync `UPDATE` statements and their owner resolution. No schema change, no change to insert, delete, the scheduler's own ownership resolution, or any imperative job path.
- **Blast radius:** Declarative cron rows whose `[agents.<x>].cron_jobs` membership changes between syncs. Rows that never move are written with the alias they already had.
- **Linked issue(s):** None filed; found while reviewing cron ownership.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — the behavior is fully covered by the two regressions below, and reproducing it by hand needs a config edit plus a sync cycle to observe a tool-visibility change.

### How I tested

```sh
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime cron::
test result: ok. 186 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 4213 filtered out

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check          # clean
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings   # clean
```
